International Business

Prof. Abdel Salam Abu Qahf, who teaches this course, gives a case in almost every lecture: a short report about a company that has a decision to make.

His first rule is that the report is never enough. "If you stick to this information or to this report, you will never ever realize the right decision."

You must collect more information, ask questions, make assumptions and develop different scenarios. Then you choose the scenario that solves the problem. His first case, Bill or Jane, shows how.

Bill or Jane?

This is the case as he told it in class.

The case

An American firm has a subsidiary in Saudi Arabia. A subsidiary is a company that the firm owns in another country. The subsidiary is five years old and needs a new marketing manager.

There are two candidates. Jane has 10 years of experience and an EMBA. Bill has 8 years of experience. Who should get the job?

The report gives you nothing more, and that is the point. He said nobody in the class asked the two key questions.

The question to askIf the answer isThen choose
Which industry?CosmeticsJane
Electronics, iron and steel, car assemblyBill (he can be trained for the gaps)
Which city?Riyadh (more conservative)Bill
Jeddah, or Abha (less conservative than Riyadh)Jane

So there is no single right name. The right answer is a set of scenarios: "if the industry is this and the city is that, then this candidate".

His closing line: "Neutrality is always required. Everywhere." You do not start with a favourite. You let the questions decide.

Rule 1: go outside the report

What he did with Bill or Jane is what he wants in every case. Four moves:

  1. Collect more information.
  2. Ask questions. What is missing from the report? Here: the industry and the city.
  3. Make assumptions. If nobody can answer your question, state what you assume.
  4. Develop different scenarios, then choose the scenario that solves the problem.
The mistake to avoid

Stereotyping التنميط: judging Jane or Bill by a fixed image, instead of asking the questions.

Rule 1, in his words

"If you stick to this information or to this report, you will never ever realize the right decision."

Collect more information, ask questions, make assumptions, develop different scenarios. Then choose the scenario that solves the problem.

Bill or Jane

The case: an American firm's five-year-old Saudi subsidiary needs a marketing manager. Jane: 10 years and an EMBA. Bill: 8 years.

The two questions nobody asked:

  • Industry. Cosmetics: Jane. Electronics, iron and steel, car assembly: Bill.
  • City. Riyadh: Bill. Jeddah or Abha: Jane.

"Neutrality is always required. Everywhere." Avoid stereotyping.

The report of a case is never enough. What four things must you do?

Collect more information, ask questions, make assumptions, and develop different scenarios. Then choose the scenario that solves the problem.

Bill or Jane? Each card is one answer to the two missing questions.

  • The industry is cosmetics
  • The industry is electronics
  • The industry is iron and steel
  • The industry is car assembly
  • The city is Riyadh
  • The city is Jeddah
  • The city is Abha

What were the two questions nobody asked in Bill or Jane, and how do they change the answer?

The industry (cosmetics: Jane; electronics, steel, cars: Bill) and the city (Riyadh: Bill; Jeddah or Abha: Jane).

How did he close the Bill or Jane discussion?

  1. "Experience is always the first criterion."
  2. "Neutrality is always required. Everywhere."
  3. "A woman cannot manage in Saudi Arabia."
  4. "Always choose the candidate with the EMBA."

You do not start from a favourite. You ask the missing questions and let each scenario decide.

What is stereotyping, and why is it the opposite of his method?

Stereotyping is judging a person, here Jane or Bill, by a fixed image. His method is to ask the questions (which industry, which city) instead of judging by the image.

The case page handed out with the lecture comes from the textbook. It is about the Colorado Computing Company and a deal worth 35 million dollars. The candidates are Jane Adams and Bill Smith, and it also names Robert Donner and Jeanette Falcon.

The version he told in class differs in its details. Your own full written answers to this case are kept in the course's case folder.

What disappointed him in the written answers

After reading the class's first written case answers he said plainly what disappointed him: "most of you summarizes the report. And then try to touch to answer the questions." Too general.

Right after the Bill or Jane case, Prof. Abu Qahf gave the class four small puzzles. All four make one point: if you stick only to the information you are given, you will never reach the right decision.

"In international business, if you have an opportunity to become an international manager, you are required to be a creative person."

Four puzzles, one lesson

1. Nine dots

Join 9 dots with 3 straight lines without lifting the pen. The dots are like the short case report: as long as you stay inside them, it is impossible. You have to go outside the box.

2. How many cubes?

The question is simply: how many cubes? Not one: six. Each face is a square, and each square is a cube. "This is creativity."

3. The highest point of a handkerchief

Where is the highest point of a handkerchief? Pull it up from its centre. He linked this to الوسطية (the middle way): the middle is the top, not a weak point between two extremes.

4. How many rectangles?

How many rectangles are in a drawn square? More than you first see.

The link with a case is direct. Judging Bill or Jane from the few lines of the report is staying inside the nine dots. Asking about the industry and the city is going outside them.

The point of the puzzles

If you stick only to the information you are given, you will never reach the right decision. Ask questions, make assumptions, build scenarios.

An international manager is "required to be a creative person".

The four puzzles

  1. Nine dots, 3 straight lines: go outside the dots.
  2. How many cubes? Six, not one.
  3. The handkerchief's highest point: its centre. The middle is the top.
  4. Rectangles in a square: more than you first see.

What one point do the four puzzles make about solving a case?

If you stick only to the information you are given, you will never reach the right decision. You must ask questions, make assumptions and build scenarios.

To the puzzle "how many cubes?", his answer was:

  1. One
  2. Four
  3. Six
  4. Nine

Six: each face is a square, and each square is a cube. "This is creativity."

In the nine dots puzzle, what do the dots stand for?

The short case report. Staying inside the dots makes the puzzle impossible, just as staying inside the report makes the right decision impossible.

Where is the highest point of a handkerchief, and what did he link it to?

Its centre: pull it up from the middle. He linked it to الوسطية: the middle is the top, not a weak point between two extremes.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

The verse he quoted with the handkerchief

For the idea that the middle is the top he quoted: وكذلك جعلناكم أمة وسطا.

The word to avoid: stereotyping

Stereotyping التنميط means judging by a fixed image. Judging Jane or Bill by a fixed image, instead of asking the questions, is exactly what the puzzles warn against.

The first lecture of Prof. Abu Qahf came with four case pages. Two are full cases to hand in: Bill or Jane, and Illy against Starbucks. Two are short "discussion examples" for class discussion only, numbered Example 2 and Example 4 on their page.

Each one leaves a lesson. Together they say the same thing: what works in one country can fail in another, because everything around the product is different.

The two cases to hand in

Illy against Starbucks

Illy is an Italian espresso firm. Starbucks is the American coffeehouse chain. The lessons:

  • Country-specific advantages stay home. Firm-specific advantages travel. A strength that comes from the home country does not move with the company. A strength that belongs to the company itself does.
  • A concept that wins in the USA (paper cups, sweet milky drinks, coffee to go) meets a different "ecology" in Italy.
  • Related diversification, which means adding products close to the main one, strengthens a company's market position.
Bill or Jane

Ask about the industry and the city. Stay neutral. And notice that culture shapes management decisions: the same two candidates get a different answer in Riyadh and in Jeddah.

The two discussion examples

Example 2: the plastics maker

A British plastics maker copied American products under licence, which means with the American owner's permission. The products had succeeded in the USA. In Britain they failed.

Why? Disposability, the habit of using a thing once and throwing it away, was not yet accepted there. And the price limited the product to the "AB" segment: the richest buyers, social grades A and B.

Example 4: the sewing machine

The same sewing machine is a hobby in the USA, a basic need in Nigeria, and an heirloom and status symbol elsewhere.

It is the same formal product (the same machine, with the same features) but a different core benefit, which is the reason people buy it. So the marketing mix must be differentiated: a different message for each market.

Marketing ecology

The whole environment around a product in a market: the culture and habits, the income and prices, what people use the product for, the competition, and the infrastructure.

One lesson from each case

  1. Illy against Starbucks: country-specific advantages stay home, firm-specific advantages travel. A concept that wins in the USA meets a different ecology in Italy. Related diversification strengthens market position.
  2. Bill or Jane: ask about the industry and the city; neutrality; culture shapes management decisions.
  3. Example 2 (British plastics maker): success in the USA failed in Britain, because disposability was not yet accepted and the price limited it to the "AB" segment.
  4. Example 4 (sewing machine): a hobby in the USA, a basic need in Nigeria, an heirloom and status symbol elsewhere. Same formal product, different core benefit, so the marketing mix must be differentiated.

Marketing ecology

The whole environment around a product in a market: culture and habits, income and prices, what people use it for, competition, infrastructure.

In the Illy against Starbucks case, which advantages stay home and which travel?

Country-specific advantages stay home. Firm-specific advantages travel.

The British plastics maker copied products that had succeeded in the USA. Why did they fail in Britain?

  1. The licence was too expensive
  2. Disposability was not yet accepted, and the price limited the product to the "AB" segment
  3. The British government banned plastic
  4. The quality was lower than in the USA

The habit of throwing things away was not yet accepted in Britain, and only the richest buyers (social grades A and B) could afford the product.

What does the sewing machine example show?

The same formal product can have a different core benefit in each country: a hobby in the USA, a basic need in Nigeria, an heirloom and status symbol elsewhere. So the marketing mix must be differentiated.

What is "marketing ecology"?

The whole environment around a product in a market: culture and habits, income and prices, what people use the product for, competition, and infrastructure.

Of the four case pages of the first lecture, which two were for class discussion only?

  1. Bill or Jane, and Illy against Starbucks
  2. Example 2 and Example 4
  3. Bill or Jane, and Example 2
  4. All four

Bill or Jane and Illy against Starbucks were full cases to hand in. Example 2 (the plastics maker) and Example 4 (the sewing machine) were short discussion examples.

Two names for the mistake in Example 2 (an added note, not his words)

Judging a foreign market through home eyes is called the self-reference criterion. It is also an ethnocentric mindset. The word ethnocentric comes back in the part on global management.

Where the full method for answering a case is

How to write the answer to a case (a short brief of each company, then a fact sheet, then the answers) was taught in Lecture 2, with his feedback on the Illy against Starbucks reports.

Prof. Abu Qahf gave two definitions of international business. The first is the managerial one: international business "is the application of all managerial functions and theories and principles in different environments."

The meaning: an international manager does the same job as a local one. What changes is everything around the job. His story of an incentive plan that worked in Egypt and failed in the UAE shows it.

The same job, in a different place

Definition 1: the managerial one

"[International business] is the application of all managerial functions and theories and principles in different environments."

An international manager does the same job as a local one: plan, organize, direct, lead, decide and control, using the same principles and theories. But in different environments. The difference is the environment, not the job.

Even the steps of making a decision stay the same, he said: specify the problem, develop alternatives, evaluate the alternatives, select one, and issue your decision. "The same steps, but in different situations."

The key phrase

"Different environments" is the key phrase. Without it, the definition just describes ordinary management.

Explain it simply

Think of yourself at MIDOR, the oil refinery company in Alexandria. If you moved to a refinery in the UAE you would still plan, organize, motivate and control. What changes is everything around you: the culture, the laws, the economy, what motivates people. Definition 1 says exactly that.

The incentive plan that failed in the UAE

His story

An HR manager at MIDOR designs an incentive scheme based on money. It works very well. She moves to a company in the UAE and copies the same scheme. It fails.

Why? The standard of living there is higher, so extra money motivates people less ("take it for yourself"). In Egypt, with a lower standard of living, money motivates well.

The function is the same (motivating people). The environment is different, so the same plan gives a different result.

This was his main lesson of the first lecture. The functions and principles of management are the same everywhere, but divergences between countries change how you plan, decide and motivate. Divergences are differences: in culture, in the economy, in politics and in society. A manager must recognize them.

Definition 1, word for word

He insists on exact words, so learn it as he said it:

"International business is the application of all managerial functions and theories and principles in different environments."

What it means

  • Same functions: plan, organize, direct, lead, decide, control.
  • Same theories and principles, same steps of making a decision.
  • Different environments: culture, economy, politics, society.

The example to quote

The MIDOR incentive plan: money-based, worked at MIDOR, failed in the UAE because the higher standard of living makes money motivate less.

"International business is the application of ... in different environments." Complete it.

... all managerial functions and theories and principles ...

Which phrase makes Definition 1 about international business and not about ordinary management?

  1. "all managerial functions"
  2. "theories and principles"
  3. "in different environments"
  4. "the application of"

Without "in different environments", the definition just describes ordinary management.

Why did the MIDOR incentive plan fail in the UAE?

The standard of living there is higher, so money-based incentives motivate less. Same function (motivation), different environment.

He said "divergences between countries" change every decision and plan. In which four areas?

Culture, the economy, politics and society.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

His exact words
"In other words, the international manager is practicing the same functions of the local one. But, and a big but: in different environments! In different environments!"
"You are going to follow the same steps of making a decision ... specify the problem ... develop alternatives ... evaluate alternatives ... select an alternative, and ... issue your decision. The same steps, but in different situations."
"Divergences between countries, not only in culture, but also in economic-wise, and political-wise as well, and social-wise as well, all of these will impact all the decisions, all plans, all tasks you are going to perform in each foreign firm."
Another version of the story you may meet

In some class notes the second company in the incentive story is Aramco. The point is the same: a higher standard of living makes money motivate less.

The successful manager in global companies: seven qualities

The revision material for his exams lists seven qualities of the successful manager in global companies:

  1. A global mindset: "think globally and act locally".
  2. Long-term vision.
  3. Negotiation skills.
  4. Understanding the national culture of each market.
  5. Emotional intelligence: "the ability to manage individuals emotionally".
  6. The ability to motivate everyone to excel.
  7. The desire and ability to take on burdens and foreign assignments.

Even the biggest brands change their names, their colours and their recipes to fit a country. Prof. Abu Qahf gave four examples: Libya, the Philippines, India and Egypt.

Each one is the first definition at work: the same business, bent by a different environment.

Brands that changed their names or looks

Libya: new names

Under Gaddafi, foreign drinks had to change their names. 7-Up became السبعة "Al-Sab'a" (the seven). Mirinda became "Mrada", the name of a Libyan village. Coca-Cola became الشافي "Al-Shafi" (the healer).

The Philippines: a new colour

Pepsi was asked to make its cans mostly blue, because Filipinos preferred blue.

India: a new menu

Cows are sacred in India. So McDonald's replaced beef with chicken, fish and soy burgers, rather than give up a huge market.

Egypt: a new recipe

Cadbury replaced animal fat (pig fat) with vegetable oil.

The differences are not only in products. A manager must also watch verbal habits and body language: the hands, the eyes, the facial expressions.

His four examples of adapting to local culture

CountryCompanyWhat changed
Libya7-Up, Mirinda, Coca-ColaThe names: Al-Sab'a, Mrada, Al-Shafi
The PhilippinesPepsiThe can: mostly blue
IndiaMcDonald'sThe menu: no beef; chicken, fish and soy burgers
EgyptCadburyThe recipe: vegetable oil in place of pig fat

Also watch verbal habits and body language (hands, eyes, facial expressions).

In Libya under Gaddafi, Coca-Cola was sold under the name:

  1. Al-Sab'a
  2. Mrada
  3. Al-Shafi
  4. Its own name, in Arabic letters

Al-Shafi, "the healer". Al-Sab'a ("the seven") was 7-Up, and Mrada was Mirinda.

What did McDonald's change in India, and why?

It replaced beef with chicken, fish and soy burgers, because cows are sacred in India. It changed the menu rather than give up a huge market.

What did Pepsi change in the Philippines?

  1. Its name
  2. The colour of its cans: mostly blue
  3. Its recipe
  4. Its price

Filipinos preferred blue, so the cans became mostly blue.

What did Cadbury change in Egypt?

It replaced animal fat (pig fat) with vegetable oil.

Besides the product itself, what else must an international manager watch?

Verbal habits and body language: hands, eyes and facial expressions.

Where Mrada is

Mrada is a village between Benghazi and Ras Lanuf. He visited it himself, in 1991 or 1992.

Prof. Abu Qahf set two ways of managing people side by side. Unity of command: each worker takes orders from one boss only. Management by consensus: no decision is made until everyone agrees.

Management by consensus was developed in America. The Americans failed to apply it. The Japanese succeeded. The reason is culture: Japan is collectivist, America is individualist.

One worker, one boss

Unity of command وحدة الأمر

Subordinates A, B, C, D "must be ordered, must be directed, must be instructed through the marketing manager only", "to avoid the contradiction of orders".

Each worker has one boss. Picture a marketing manager with four people under him. Nobody else may give them orders.

Why? If two managers give a worker opposite orders, whichever one he obeys, the other becomes an enemy.

The principle is old: he dated it to 1916, "110 years ago". It is built on individualism, a culture where the individual comes first, and it is widely applied in the USA, in the West and in Egypt.

Nothing is decided until everyone says yes

Management by consensus الإدارة بالإجماع

"There is no decision to be made and to be issued ... without a 100% yes from all people. If just one opposes, the decision will be stopped."

In Japan a worker can take directions from several managers without conflict, because nothing is decided until everyone agrees.

Its doctrine: "success is the responsibility of all; failure is the responsibility of all."

He said this system was developed in America, but the Americans failed to apply it while the Japanese succeeded. Why? Culture.

  • Japanese culture is collectivist: the group comes first. Think of Kaizen, which means continuous improvement. You can name Japanese companies like Toyota, but rarely a single Japanese innovator.
  • American, Egyptian, Arab and British cultures are individualist.
Explain it simply

The same management "rule" works in one culture and fails in another. In an individualist culture people want personal credit, so "everyone must agree" feels slow and nobody owns the result. In a collectivist culture the group comes first, so consensus feels natural. That is why the international manager must study the environment before copying a system from home.

Unity of command

USA and the West, 1916

One subordinate, one boss: orders come through one manager only, "to avoid the contradiction of orders".

Built on individualism. Widely applied in the USA and in Egypt.

Management by consensus

Japan

No decision "without a 100% yes from all people". A worker can take directions from several managers.

"Success is the responsibility of all; failure is the responsibility of all."

Built on collectivism and Kaizen.

The lesson

Consensus was developed in America, failed there, and succeeded in Japan. The cause is culture: collectivist Japan, individualist America (and Egypt, the Arab world, Britain).

Which system does each line describe?

  • Orders come through one manager only
  • It avoids the contradiction of orders
  • Built on individualism
  • Widely applied in Egypt and the USA
  • No decision without a 100% yes from all
  • If just one person opposes, the decision is stopped
  • Built on collectivism
  • Success and failure are the responsibility of all
  • A worker can take directions from several managers

Why did management by consensus succeed in Japan but fail in America?

Culture. Japan is collectivist: success and failure are everyone's responsibility. America is individualist.

Which cultures did he call individualist?

  1. Japanese only
  2. Japanese and Egyptian
  3. American, Egyptian, Arab and British
  4. None of them

American, Egyptian, Arab and British cultures are individualist. Japanese culture is collectivist.

What problem does unity of command avoid?

The contradiction of orders. If two managers give a worker opposite orders, whichever he obeys, the other becomes an enemy.

Whose principle unity of command is, and the date

Unity of command is one of Henri Fayol's principles of management (France, 1916). He gave 1916 in class ("110 years ago"). Some class notes say 1915; use 1916.

His exact words
"This is an American-developed management system, and the American failed to apply it ... But it has been succeeded in many Japanese companies ... the Japanese culture is based on the idea of collectivism. While the American one, and Egyptian one, and Arabic one, and the British one, is mainly based on individualism."
Where the textbook covers this

The textbook covers individualism against collectivism inside Hofstede's framework, a well-known way of comparing national cultures.

Two pages of class notes

Prof. Abu Qahf's second definition is the practical one: international business is "any organization that is doing business in one or more than one foreign market ... either in a direct way or indirect way."

One foreign market is enough. There is no cut-off point.

He rejects a famous definition by a scholar named Vernon, who demands six or more foreign countries and sales of 100 million dollars a year. And he reminds the class that the name is new but the practice is very old.

An old practice with a new name

Start with a camel caravan. Long before anyone wrote a textbook, the merchants of Quraysh took goods north to Syria in summer and south to Yemen in winter, buying in one country and selling in another. That is international business.

  • The term "international business", as a school or a science, is new. The practice has "a long, long history".
  • The Phoenicians and the Greek merchants sent representatives abroad to buy and sell.
  • The winter and summer journeys رحلة الشتاء والصيف of Surah Quraysh, from Hijaz to Syria and to Yemen: he calls them the first indirect form of international business, which is trade, export and import.

One foreign market is enough

Definition 2: the professional (practical) one

"International business represents any organization that is doing business in one or more than one foreign market, or foreign country ... either in a direct way or indirect way."

One foreign market is enough. There is no cut-off point: "no 'at least' or 'at most'".

Definition 1 told you what an international manager does. Definition 2 is the test you use to decide whether a company is international: has it done business in at least one country outside its home? Then yes.

He added: "There is no common definition for international business." No single definition is accepted worldwide. All are acceptable, except extreme ones like the next one.

The definition he calls "completely wrong"

Vernon's definition of an international firm

A firm is international if it invests in six or more foreign markets and makes an annual turnover of 100 million dollars. Turnover means sales. Both conditions are required.

Vernon is a well-known scholar, and the definition is well known. Prof. Abu Qahf calls it "a very funny way" to define the international firm, and "completely wrong, from my own viewpoint".

His reason: the cut-off is arbitrary. Why should a firm in 5 countries not count? What about a firm that makes 99 million dollars?

He said he debated this with his own professor at Strathclyde University, Prof. James Dennison, "and I won the debate".

Do not mix them up

His definition: one or more foreign markets. Vernon's: six or more, plus 100 million dollars of annual turnover.

Definition 2, word for word

"International business represents any organization that is doing business in one or more than one foreign market, or foreign country, either in a direct way or indirect way."

No cut-off point: no "at least" or "at most". And "there is no common definition for international business".

Vernon, and the criticism

Vernon: six or more foreign markets and an annual turnover of 100 million dollars.

His criticism: "completely wrong". The cut-off is arbitrary (what about 99 million dollars, or 5 countries?).

Old practice, new name

The term is new; the practice has a long history: the Phoenicians, the Greek merchants, and the winter and summer journeys of Quraysh, "the first form of indirect international business".

Give his two definitions of international business.

(1) The application of all managerial functions, theories and principles in different environments. (2) Any organization doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly.

What makes a firm international in his professional definition?

Doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly. There is no cut-off point.

State Vernon's definition and his criticism of it.

Six or more foreign markets AND an annual turnover of 100 million dollars. "Completely wrong": the cut-off is arbitrary (what about 99 million dollars?). There is no single accepted definition.

An Egyptian company sells in one foreign country only. By his definition it is:

  1. Not international: it needs at least six foreign markets
  2. Not international: it needs 100 million dollars of turnover
  3. International: one foreign market is enough
  4. International only if it owns a factory there

One or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly. Six markets and 100 million dollars are Vernon's conditions, which he rejects.

What did he call the winter and summer journeys of Quraysh?

The first indirect form of international business: trade, export and import, from Hijaz to Syria and to Yemen.

His exact words
"International business as a terminology is new ... But in practice, it has a long, long, long history ... since the Phoenician civilization."
"The winter trip and the summer trip represent the first form of indirect international business ... Trade. Export and import. From Hijaz to Syria and Lebanon and Jordan ... And to Yemen as well."
"There's no cut-off point in the number of countries to be served by the firm concerned ... there is no 'at least' or 'at most'."
"Vernon ... has defined the international firm in a very funny way ... completely wrong, from my own viewpoint."
Vernon's 100 million: another version you may meet

Some class notes write "100 million dollars of investment". He said annual turnover. Use "annual turnover".

A third, shorter definition from the textbook

The textbook defines international business as "any commercial transaction that crosses the borders of two or more nations".

Other definitions of the international company (revision material for his exams)

Foreign company: a company that owns, manages or indirectly practises an investment activity (production, marketing or services) outside the home country, regardless of the number of host countries.

Livingstone: the international company has an independent legal personality (it is not controlled by any home government) and chooses to invest in one or more foreign countries. Vernon focused on size; Livingstone on freedom (choice).

Hood and Young: a company that owns and manages investment projects in more than one foreign country.

Rolfe: a company is international when its foreign sales, foreign employees or foreign investment reach about 25% of the total.

Livingstone, Hood and Young, and Rolfe are scholars quoted in that material.

A question from the same material: are the offices abroad of airlines, tourism companies and commercial agencies international companies? No (Livingstone). The nature of their business forces them to have offices, so there is no element of choice. And a commission agent or a distributor abroad is not an international company.

Five groups of international markets (revision material)
  1. Advanced economies: USA, Japan, Germany, France.
  2. Developing economies: Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea.
  3. Economies in transition: Hungary, Czech Republic, Poland.
  4. Emerging economies: Argentina, Brazil, China, India.
  5. Less developed countries: Middle East, Central Africa, Central America. The poorest and least stable.
What the strategic approach requires: seven points (revision material)
  1. Flexibility more than size.
  2. Awareness of "hyper competition".
  3. Focus on ideas and on the organization's ability to learn.
  4. Managing non-commercial risks.
  5. Not expecting stability over time.
  6. Discovering the opportunities that lead to success.
  7. Foreign investment and its management.

Prof. Abu Qahf's second definition ends with "either in a direct way or indirect way". These are the two major options of a company that wants to go international.

Indirect: sell abroad without building your own operation there. His example is exporting.

Direct: build your own factory, subsidiary or branch in the foreign market.

In short: indirect means my goods travel. Direct means my company travels.

My goods travel, or my company travels

Indirect غير مباشر

Sell abroad without building your own operation there. His example: exporting.

Faragalla, the Egyptian juice and food company, becomes an international firm once its product is sold in Sudan, Libya, Kuwait or Lebanon.

The company owns nothing abroad.

Direct مباشر

Build your own factory, plant, subsidiary, affiliate or branch in the foreign market. This is direct foreign investment.

Faragalla builds its own plant in Saudi Arabia, Libya or Sudan. "Just one country" is enough.

The operation is wholly owned, or a joint venture (JV) with a local partner.

"Once the company succeeded in exporting its product to a certain ... foreign market, it becomes an international firm."

A joint venture without paying

A joint venture is a project owned together with a local partner. The foreign firm can join one without investing money: the local partner pays the cost of the project, and the foreign firm contributes its know-how.

This is only the start

There are more indirect forms ("more than four") and more direct forms. They come later in the course under modes of entry into foreign markets, together with an entry model of his own that he called the "Egyptian model".

The two major options

Indirect: selling abroad without your own operation there. Example: exporting (Faragalla sold in Sudan). No ownership abroad.

Direct: your own factory, plant, subsidiary, affiliate or branch abroad, wholly owned or a joint venture (Faragalla builds a plant in Libya). One country is enough.

The joint venture point

A foreign firm can enter a joint venture without investing money: the local partner pays, the foreign firm brings know-how.

To remember it

Indirect = my goods travel. Direct = my company travels.

What is the difference between direct and indirect international business? Give his example.

Indirect: selling abroad without your own operation there, for example exporting (Faragalla sold in Sudan). Direct: your own plant, subsidiary or branch abroad, wholly owned or a joint venture (Faragalla builds a plant in Libya).

Indirect or direct?

  • Faragalla's juice is sold in Sudan
  • Exporting
  • The winter and summer journeys of Quraysh
  • Faragalla builds its own plant in Libya
  • A wholly owned subsidiary abroad
  • A joint venture with a local partner
  • The company's own branch in the foreign market

A foreign firm enters a joint venture without investing any money. What does it contribute?

  1. The land
  2. The workers
  3. Know-how
  4. Nothing at all

The local partner pays the cost of the project. The foreign firm participates with its know-how.

In how many foreign countries must Faragalla build a plant to count as direct international business?

Just one country is enough.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

His exact words on the joint venture
"The company can enter a JV, or joint venture basis, without investing money. The cost of investment project ... is actually paid by the local partner, while the foreign firm is participating, let's say, by know-how."
Another way to draw the line: ownership of 10% or more

The revision material for his exams uses ownership as the test.

Foreign direct investment (FDI): a resident entity in one economy gets a lasting interest in an enterprise in another economy. It is recorded as FDI at 10% or more ownership. It is long-term and gives the right to manage.

Indirect investment: dealings with no ownership share: exporting, licences, concessions, management contracts.

It is the same idea as his class version ("direct = own plant or joint venture; indirect = export"), with ownership as the test: 10% or more is direct.

Once a company crosses the border, people give it different names: multinational, multidomestic, global, transnational. They are not synonyms. Each name describes how the company runs its units in other countries.

Prof. Abu Qahf defined all four. In short: a multinational is a family of companies held by one head office. A multidomestic lets each country run itself. A global company does the same thing everywhere. And transnational is the softer name the United Nations chose for the same firms.

Held by headquarters, or run country by country

Multinational corporation (MNC) الشركة متعددة الجنسيات

"A cluster of companies spread in different countries and hold by the headquarters."

A family of companies in several countries, all controlled by one head office, for example in the USA or in France. It is not necessarily worldwide.

Multidomestic company

"An organization with multicountry affiliates ... where each ... affiliate ... has its own strategies. Its own marketing policies, production policies, human resources management policies, and logistics policies" ... "based on the perceived differences between countries."

An affiliate is a company's unit in a country. Here each country unit runs almost like a separate local company, because each country is seen as different. The unit in Egypt and the unit in Lebanon may have completely different policies.

The same everywhere, and a softer name

Global company الشركة العالمية / الكونية

"A very large company ... that attempts to standardize, and integrate its own operations, products, marketing activities, marketing policies, HR policies, etc., ... on worldwide basis."

Very large, and it does things the same way everywhere, with only minor changes. To standardize means to make the same. His examples: Coca-Cola, Pepsi (even in chips), McDonald's: "what you are going to eat in the USA is the same you are going to eat in Egypt".

Transnational corporation (TNC) الشركة عابرة القوميات

"An international firm, just like the multinational. But this terminology has been developed by the United Nations ... instead of using multinational, or foreign firm ... For cultural reasons."

The same kind of firm, under a softer name. He explained why. Most foreign investment flows from developed countries (the USA, Portugal, Spain, France, Britain) into developing ones. Most of those were once occupied, and there the word "foreign" sounds like "colonization". The United Nations chose "transnational" to avoid that negative image.

The four names, in his words

Multinational: "a cluster of companies spread in different countries and hold by the headquarters."

Multidomestic: an organization with affiliates in many countries, where each affiliate has its own strategies and policies (marketing, production, human resources, logistics), "based on the perceived differences between countries".

Global: "a very large company that attempts to standardize, and integrate its own operations, products, marketing activities, marketing policies, HR policies, on worldwide basis." Coca-Cola, Pepsi, McDonald's.

Transnational: an international firm, just like the multinational. The term was developed by the United Nations, for cultural reasons, in place of "multinational" or "foreign firm".

Multidomestic or global?

  • Each affiliate has its own strategies
  • Based on the perceived differences between countries
  • The unit in Egypt and the unit in Lebanon may have completely different policies
  • Each country unit runs almost like a separate local company
  • Standardizes and integrates on a worldwide basis
  • What you eat in the USA is the same you eat in Egypt
  • Coca-Cola, Pepsi, McDonald's
  • Only minor changes from country to country

Define a multinational and a global company in his words.

Multinational: a cluster of companies in different countries held (controlled) by the headquarters. Global: a very large company that attempts to standardize and integrate its operations, products, marketing and HR policies on a worldwide basis.

Why did the United Nations invent the word "transnational"?

For cultural reasons. Most foreign investment flows from developed countries into developing ones, most of them former colonies, where "foreign" or "multinational" carries the negative image of the colonial era.

In his meaning, a transnational corporation is:

  1. A company that works in one industry only
  2. A company owned by the United Nations
  3. The same kind of firm as a multinational, under a softer name
  4. A company with no head office

"An international firm, just like the multinational." Only the name is different, chosen by the United Nations to avoid the colonial image.

"A cluster of companies spread in different countries and held by the headquarters" defines the:

  1. Multinational corporation
  2. Multidomestic company
  3. Global company
  4. Trading house

The multinational: a family of companies in several countries, all controlled by one head office.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

Global does not mean "in one industry"

He said Coca-Cola also invests in tourism, hotels and fast food, and still standardizes inside each industry. Keep the point. The examples are his own claim: today Coca-Cola is known as a drinks company.

His view of the United Nations

"Of course they are fooling people ... It only serves the major countries, and the rest of the countries are victims of the five ... that have the veto right."

Another classification you may meet: five types

The revision material for his exams lists five types:

  1. Multi-local: each branch designs its own strategy for its market. This is his "multidomestic".
  2. Global: coordinates and integrates operations, products, marketing, finance and HR worldwide (Coca-Cola).
  3. International: may be global or multi-local.
  4. Multinational: a "cluster organization" of companies controlled by one head office.
  5. Transnational: has the characteristics of the global or the multinational company. Its new name: "multicultural and multinational companies".

The same material also says the United Nations prefers "transnational" to reduce the psychological and political effect of "multinational" in developing countries.

"Transnational": another version you may meet

In class: the same kind of firm as a multinational, under a softer name chosen by the United Nations.

In the revision material, and in most textbooks: a distinct type that combines global integration (the savings of large scale) with local responsiveness.

What to write: his meaning first. Add the other as "another view" if the question asks for types.

Prof. Abu Qahf defines a product by what it does for people, not by what it is made of: "The product is anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need."

Every product has three levels. The core is the benefit, the reason you buy. The formal level is the features. The augmented level is the extra services around it.

The next lesson uses these three levels to answer a big question: can my product travel?

Anything that satisfies a human need

Product المنتج

"The product is anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need."

Tangible means you can touch it, like a pen. Intangible covers services, ideas, persons, organizations and impressions.

His examples of intangible products: a candidate for parliament "markets himself". And you market an impression when you dress your best to meet your fiancé.

The point

A product is defined by the need it satisfies, not by being a physical thing.

His example: water

Water is a liquid with no colour, no smell and no taste. Exactly these characteristics make it drinkable and keep us alive. He quoted: وجعلنا من الماء كل شيء حي.

Core, formal, augmented

He explained the three levels with a mobile phone.

LevelHis wordsIn a mobile phone
1. Core product المنتج الجوهري"The product why": the function, the benefit you enjoy.To communicate, to connect people.
2. Formal product المنتج الشكليThe features.Size, depth, width, colour, weight.
3. Augmented product المنتج المدعمThe extra services around it.Guarantee, instalments, a free cover.

Product, word for word

"The product is anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need."

Intangible includes services, ideas, persons, organizations and impressions.

The three levels

  1. Core: the "why", the function or benefit (a phone: to communicate).
  2. Formal: the features (size, depth, width, colour, weight).
  3. Augmented: the extra services (guarantee, instalments, a free cover).

Define "product" and give its three levels.

Anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need. Levels: core (the "why", the function or benefit), formal (the features), augmented (the extra services: guarantee, instalments, free cover).

A mobile phone. Which level is each one?

  • To communicate
  • To connect people
  • Its size
  • Its colour
  • Its weight
  • Its depth and width
  • The guarantee
  • Paying in instalments
  • A free cover

Which of these is an intangible product in his examples?

  1. A pen
  2. A mobile phone
  3. A candidate for parliament marketing himself
  4. A bottle of water

Intangible products are services, ideas, persons, organizations and impressions. The candidate "markets himself".

What does his water example show?

A product is its characteristics that satisfy a need. Water is liquid, with no colour, smell or taste, and exactly these characteristics make it drinkable and keep us alive.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

"By-product": a word you may see in class notes

One classmate's drawing of the three circles has the word "by-product" in it. Here it means the product's secondary functions beside its core function. A phone is for communication; its other functions are by-products. It does not mean a by-product of manufacturing.

Before any company goes abroad it must answer one strategic question. Prof. Abu Qahf made it sound almost like a law: can the core of our product be internationalized?

"If the answer is yes, go international. If the answer is no, stay home."

The other two levels, formal and augmented, can take minor changes from country to country.

The core decides. The surface adapts.

Recall the three levels of a product: the core (the benefit, the reason anyone buys), the formal level (the features) and the augmented level (the extra services).

His test looks only at the core:

  • If the core can be internationalized: go international.
  • If it cannot: stay home.

The formal and the augmented levels do not decide anything. They "can be changed, minor changed from one country to another country".

His example: the marker

The instructions on his board marker are in English. In an Arab country they can be translated into Arabic. That is a minor change. The core is not touched.

Explain it simply

The core is the reason anyone buys. If people in the new country want that same benefit, you can sell there and adjust the surface: the labels, the colour, the service. If the core benefit itself does not exist there, no amount of surface change will help.

A twist: the core itself can differ

One of the short discussion examples of the first lecture is about a sewing machine. The same machine had a different core in different countries: a hobby in the USA, a basic need in Nigeria, a status symbol elsewhere. So the promotion had to change.

The strategic question

"Can the core of our product be internationalized or not?"

Yes: go international. No: stay home.

The other two levels

The formal and the augmented levels can get minor local changes from one country to another. Example: translating the instructions on a marker from English into Arabic.

What strategic question must a firm answer before going international? What follows from yes and from no?

Can the core of our product be internationalized? Yes: go international, with minor changes to the formal and augmented levels. No: stay home.

Which levels of the product can be changed a little from one country to another?

  1. The core only
  2. The formal and the augmented levels
  3. All three, freely
  4. None of them

The core is what must travel as it is. The formal and augmented levels can take minor local changes.

What is his example of a minor change to the formal level?

The instructions on a marker are in English. In an Arab country they can be translated into Arabic.

A sewing machine is a hobby in the USA and a basic need in Nigeria. What is different between the two countries?

  1. The formal product
  2. The augmented product
  3. The core benefit
  4. Nothing

The machine and its features are the same. The reason people buy it, the core, is different, so the promotion had to change.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

His exact words
"The company that is planning to become an international one ... is actually required to answer a strategic question. That is: can the core of our product be internationalized or not? If the answer is yes, go international. If the answer is no, stay home."
"The remaining levels, I mean the formal level and the augmented level, can be changed, minor changed from one country to another country. The instruction on this marker is in English. In an Arab country ... this can be translated into Arabic."

He repeated the rule in the following lecture:

"If your core can be globalized ... okay go international ... If cannot ... stay local."

For Prof. Abu Qahf a market is not a building, a street or a city. It is people: "A group of people ... with needs to satisfy, and desire to buy, and they have purchasing power."

Three conditions: a need, a desire to buy, and money. If one is missing, there is no market.

"The market is not a place"

Market السوق

"A group of people ... sized by tens, or millions, or billions ... with needs to satisfy, and desire to buy, and they have purchasing power."

Purchasing power means having the money to buy.

The definition has three conditions:

  1. A need to satisfy.
  2. A desire to buy.
  3. Purchasing power.

Missing any one of them, there is no market.

His example: one pen, two places

Two students bought the same pen, one in Al-Agami and one in Borg El Arab, two districts of Alexandria. They are the same market, in different places. So "the market is not a place".

Market, word for word

"A group of people, sized by tens, or millions, or billions, with needs to satisfy, and desire to buy, and they have purchasing power."

"The market is not a place."

To remember it

N-D-P: Need, Desire, Purchasing power. People, not a place.

Define "market". Why is it "not a place"?

A group of people (tens to billions) with needs to satisfy, desire to buy and purchasing power. The same pen is bought in different places by the same market.

Millions of people need a product and want to buy it, but they cannot afford it. Is this a market?

  1. Yes: the need is enough
  2. Yes: need and desire are enough
  3. No: purchasing power is missing
  4. Yes, if they all live in one city

All three conditions are required: a need, a desire to buy, and purchasing power. Missing any one, there is no market.

What do the letters N-D-P stand for?

Need, Desire to buy, Purchasing power: the three conditions of a market.

"The market is not a place." Then what is it?

  1. A list of products
  2. A group of people with needs to satisfy, desire to buy and purchasing power
  3. A country
  4. The total of all sellers

A market is people. The two students who bought the same pen in Al-Agami and in Borg El Arab are one market in two places.

Everyone says "the world has become a small village". Prof. Abu Qahf calls that "junk", "a joke": globalization is a big myth.

Not because nothing has changed. His reason is simple: globalization means that everything moves freely between countries, without any restrictions. And in real life nothing moves freely.

What we really live in, he says, is "the death of distance".

The definition he tests

He gave two definitions of globalization:

  1. Free mobility: "the free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions". Everything means people, products, services, capital, wealth, technology, the results of scientific research, "even poverty, even problems".
  2. Integration: the tendency toward integrating the world.

He builds his argument on the first one, and he reads it strictly. If anything at all needs permission to cross a border, the definition is not met.

So the test is easy to state: does everything move freely? Is it a fact? His answer: "No. Big no."

Explain it simply

His test is strict on purpose. Globalization means everything moves freely. So one visa, one standard, one border check is enough to say "not yet".

Nothing moves freely

  • People. You need a visa for Saudi Arabia, France, Britain or the USA. The USA even restricted Mahmoud Abbas, the Palestinian president, from going to the United Nations General Assembly.
  • Products. The European Union sets its own standards. A charger carries the letters CE, which mean it is certified to European standards. Without them it can "never ever" enter the EU.
  • Blocs are not globalization. The EU is an agreement among the countries it has accepted, and only among them. From outside it, you still need a visa.
  • Disputes everywhere. The USA and Iran, Iran and the Gulf, Egypt and Ethiopia, Algeria and Morocco, Afghanistan, Kashmir. "To talk about a tendency toward unification of the world, nonsense."
  • Knowledge. Research results, technology and innovation do not move freely either.

His rule: "As long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization." And: "As long as you have 'no', you will have also a big 'myth'."

The death of distance

The death of distance

"We are living in the death of distance ... rather than globalization."

Transport and communication make everything feel close. A flight to the USA takes 8 to 10 hours. Calling a friend in the USA is easy. Saudi Arabia is a couple of hours away, instead of weeks by camel.

But geographic distance and cultural differences are still the same. "The world will never ever become a small village or just one market."

Do not mix them up

Easier contact is the death of distance. It is not globalization. Travel and talk have become fast and cheap, which makes the world feel smaller. The borders, the rules and the cultural differences are still there.

The claim

"Globalization is a myth. And a big myth." Definition: the free mobility of everything among countries without any restrictions. "Is it a fact? No. Big no."

The evidence

  1. People need visas (Saudi Arabia, France, Britain, the USA).
  2. Products must meet standards: the EU's CE mark.
  3. Blocs like the EU are regional agreements, not globalization.
  4. Disputes between countries everywhere.
  5. Research results, technology and innovation do not move freely.

His rule: "As long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization."

The death of distance

Transport and communication have made distance feel smaller, but geographic and cultural distance remain. So "we are living in the death of distance, rather than globalization".

Why is globalization a myth? Give three pieces of evidence.

Visas restrict people. EU standards (the CE mark) restrict products. Blocs like the EU are regional, not global. There are disputes between countries everywhere. Technology and research do not move freely. "As long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization."

The letters CE on a charger show that:

  1. Products move freely into Europe
  2. Products must be certified to European standards to enter the EU
  3. The charger was made in Europe
  4. The EU has no restrictions on imports

Without the CE mark a product can "never ever" enter any European country. A standard is a restriction, so it is evidence against free mobility.

People move freely between the countries of the European Union. For him this is:

  1. Proof that globalization is a fact
  2. A regional agreement among accepted countries, not globalization
  3. A driving force of globalization
  4. The death of distance

The EU is an agreement among the countries it has accepted. From outside it, you still need a visa.

What does "the death of distance" mean?

Transport and communication have made distance feel smaller, but geographic and cultural distance remain. So we live in the death of distance, not in globalization.

Give his rule about restrictions.

"As long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization." Also: "As long as you have 'no', you will have also a big 'myth'."

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

His exact words
"Globalization, gentlemen, is a myth. Is a myth. And a big myth."
"Once again: globalization, free mobility of everything among countries without any restrictions. Is it a fact? No. Big no."
"If you look at this charger you will find two letters CE ... Certified according to the European standards ... If it is not ... never ever be able to enter any European country."
Where the two definitions are taught in full

He came back to the two definitions of globalization in Lecture 2, with their exact wording and with more on trade between rich and poor countries. That is in Lecture 2.

Prof. Abu Qahf says people mix up three different things: the concept of globalization itself, the forces pushing toward it, and its surface symptoms.

The forces are trade agreements and technology. The symptoms are burgers, jeans and Coca-Cola. Neither one is globalization.

Keep the three apart and his whole argument becomes easy.

Concept, forces, symptoms

CategoryWhat belongs here
The concept (the core)Free mobility of everything, with no restrictions. Or: integration of the world.
Driving forces القوى الدافعة (they push toward it)GATT and GATS; the drastic development of transportation and communication technology, and information technology; political, economic and technological forces.
Superficial symptoms (they look like it, but are not it)Eating a hamburger in Egypt like in the USA; jeans; drinking Coca-Cola or Pepsi; Pizza Hut, Starbucks, Domino's, McDonald's; easy communication.

GATT and GATS

GATT is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. It is for goods. GATS is the General Agreement on Trade in Services. Both are world trade agreements.

Why are they only forces, and not globalization itself? Because GATT and GATS "just ... encourage trade between countries, no more. But still there are restrictions imposed."

And the burgers and jeans? "These represent superficial symptoms of globalization ... but they are not representing globalization." Superficial means on the surface.

To remember it

Concept, Causes, Costumes. The concept is the idea. The causes push toward it. The costumes (burgers, jeans) only dress like it.

Three things not to mix up

  1. The concept: free mobility of everything without restrictions, or the integration of the world.
  2. The driving forces: GATT (goods), GATS (services), the drastic development of transportation and communication technology. Political, economic and technological forces.
  3. The superficial symptoms: hamburgers, jeans, Coca-Cola and Pepsi, Pizza Hut, Starbucks, Domino's, McDonald's.

His line on the agreements

GATT and GATS "just encourage trade between countries, no more. But still there are restrictions imposed."

Driving force or superficial symptom?

  • GATT
  • GATS
  • The development of transportation technology
  • The development of communication technology
  • Eating a hamburger in Egypt like in the USA
  • Wearing jeans
  • Drinking Coca-Cola or Pepsi
  • Pizza Hut and Domino's
  • Starbucks
  • McDonald's

Name two driving forces and two superficial symptoms.

Forces: GATT (goods) and GATS (services); the development of transport and communication technology. Symptoms: McDonald's hamburgers, jeans, Coca-Cola, Pizza Hut, Starbucks.

GATT and GATS are trade agreements. Which one is for goods and which for services?

  1. GATT for goods, GATS for services
  2. GATT for services, GATS for goods
  3. Both for goods
  4. Both for services

GATT: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (goods). GATS: General Agreement on Trade in Services.

GATT and McDonald's: which is a driving force and which a symptom?

GATT is a driving force. McDonald's is a superficial symptom.

Why are GATT and GATS not globalization itself?

They "just encourage trade between countries, no more. But still there are restrictions imposed." And as long as there are restrictions, there is no globalization.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

His exact words
"People sometimes make a mishmash or mix up ... between the core of the concept of globalization ... and the driving forces toward such a phenomenon."
"Jeans trousers, Pizza Hut, Starbucks, Domino's Pizza, McDonald's ... these represent superficial symptoms of globalization ... but they are not representing globalization."
A longer list of driving forces exists

The three forces above are the ones he gave in class. His past exams also use a longer list of eight driving forces, together with "conditional" and "governing" factors. They are in lesson 4 of this part.

Prof. Abu Qahf's past exams ask about four indicators of globalization, also called its four types: globalization of demand, of supply, of competition and of strategy.

He did not explain them in the first lectures, but several of his past exams ask for them, often as "give the term" or "answer in two words". Each indicator has its own signs. Learn which sign belongs to which indicator.

Four places where globalization shows

1. Globalization of demand عولمة الطلب

The same product is offered to different geographic segments, which means to customers in different parts of the world. Local demand adds up into global demand.

Examples: jeans, fast-food restaurants, Pepsi and Coca-Cola.

2. Globalization of supply عولمة العرض

A new international division of labour. Specialization in making components. Fast movement of the factors of production. Subcontracting. Concentrated research and development. Technology exchange between the USA, the EU and Japan.

3. Globalization of competition عولمة المنافسة

A move from comparative advantage to competitive advantage. A move from local to international competitiveness. Booms and recessions spread fast. Strategic alliances.

Comparative advantage is a country's natural edge, such as cheap labour or raw materials. Competitive advantage is an edge that firms build, such as quality, a brand or technology.

4. Globalization of strategy عولمة الاستراتيجية

A move from economies of scale to economies of scope. Activities are moved between countries as wages and material costs change. Subsidiaries support each other when a product is launched.

Scale and scope

Economies of scale: cheaper per unit because you make more of one product.

Economies of scope: cheaper because you make several related products with the same resources.

The four indicators (types) and their signs

IndicatorSigns
DemandThe same good for different geographic segments; local demand added up into global demand. Jeans, fast food, Pepsi and Coca-Cola.
SupplyNew international division of labour; specialization in components; fast movement of production factors; subcontracting; concentrated research and development; technology exchange.
CompetitionFrom comparative to competitive advantage; from local to international competitiveness; fast spread of booms and recessions; strategic alliances.
StrategyFrom economies of scale to economies of scope; moving activities between countries; subsidiaries supporting each other in launches.
To remember it

D-S-C-S: Demand, Supply, Competition, Strategy. "Don't Sell Cheap Stuff."

Name the four indicators of globalization.

Globalization of demand, of supply, of competition and of strategy.

Each line is a sign of globalization. Of which kind?

  • The spread of fast-food restaurants and jeans
  • Adding up the demand for the same good across many customer segments
  • Companies subcontracting the making of goods
  • Specialization in making components
  • Fast movement of production factors and technology exchange
  • The spread of strategic alliances
  • From comparative advantage to competitive advantage
  • Booms and recessions spreading fast
  • From economies of scale to economies of scope
  • Moving activities between countries as wages change
  • Subsidiaries supporting each other in launches

What is the difference between economies of scale and economies of scope?

Scale: cheaper per unit because you make more of one product. Scope: cheaper because you make several related products with the same resources.

"The widening of the phenomenon of strategic alliances." In two words, this is:

  1. Globalization of demand
  2. Globalization of supply
  3. Globalization of competition
  4. Globalization of strategy

Firms move from comparative to competitive advantage and ally with each other to compete worldwide.

What is the difference between comparative advantage and competitive advantage?

Comparative advantage is a country's natural edge, such as cheap labour or raw materials. Competitive advantage is an edge that firms build, such as quality, a brand or technology.

Optional. Open what you want.

Jeans and fast food: a symptom in class, an indicator in the exam

In class he called burgers and jeans "superficial symptoms" of globalization. But when his exam asks, in two words, what "the spread of fast-food restaurants and wearing jeans" means, the label to write is the indicator: globalization of demand.

Prof. Abu Qahf's past exams ask for three lists about globalization: its driving forces, its conditional factors and its governing factors. They also ask for the three centres of globalization.

In class he gave the short version of the driving forces: GATT, GATS and technology. The longer lists in this lesson are the ones his exam answers use. The work here is to know which item belongs to which list.

The eight driving forces

Driving forces push the world toward globalization. The exam list has eight:

  1. The information-technology revolution.
  2. GATT and the talks to liberalize trade, which means to free it from restrictions.
  3. The end of the Cold War.
  4. Progress in transport, communication and printing.
  5. Sudden global problems: pollution, AIDS, Covid-19.
  6. Poor countries cannot be sources of flows to rich ones.
  7. Wealth concentrated in a few countries, and the dominance of multinational companies.
  8. A United Nations environment that lets America act as "the world's policeman".

His class version is inside this list: GATT is number 2, and transport, communication and information technology are numbers 1 and 4.

Conditional factors, governing factors, centres

The five conditional factors العوامل الشرطية

  1. The retreat of the state's power.
  2. The efforts of the USA to break up big countries (the Soviet Union).
  3. The widespread belief that globalization is inevitable.
  4. The belief that everything, "things and non-things", can be globalized.
  5. Globalization needs national culture to be negated.

The governing factors العوامل الحاكمة

These are the ways the centres of globalization press Third World countries:

  • Debt.
  • The forced sale of assets.
  • Exporting only raw materials.
  • Aid that supports consumption.
  • Threats of force or sanctions (Iraq).

The three centres

North America, the European Union, and the Far East (Japan; now also China and South Korea).

Driving forces (8)

The information-technology revolution; GATT and trade liberalization; the end of the Cold War; progress in transport, communication and printing; sudden global problems (pollution, AIDS, Covid-19); poor countries cannot be sources of flows to rich ones; wealth concentrated in a few countries and the dominance of multinationals; a United Nations environment that lets America act as "the world's policeman".

Conditional factors (5)

The retreat of the state's power; US efforts to break up big countries (the Soviet Union); the belief that globalization is inevitable; the belief that everything can be globalized; the negation of national culture.

Governing factors

The centres pressing Third World countries: debt, forced sale of assets, exporting only raw materials, aid that supports consumption, threats of force or sanctions.

Centres

North America, the European Union, the Far East.

Which list does each factor belong to?

  • The information-technology revolution
  • GATT and trade liberalization
  • The end of the Cold War

  • The retreat of the state's power
  • The belief that globalization is inevitable
  • The negation of national culture
  • The break-up of big countries such as the Soviet Union
  • Drowning countries in debt
  • Forcing countries to sell their assets
  • Aid that encourages consumption

Name the three centres of globalization.

North America, the European Union, and the Far East (Japan; now also China and South Korea).

"The retreat of the state's power, the belief that globalization is inevitable, and the negation of national culture" are:

  1. Driving forces
  2. Conditional factors
  3. Governing factors
  4. Indicators

They are the conditional factors. The multiple-choice questions in the revision material for his exams mark them as NOT driving forces.

What are the governing factors of globalization?

The ways the centres of globalization press Third World countries: debt, the forced sale of assets, exporting only raw materials, aid that supports consumption, and threats of force or sanctions.

The short class version of the driving forces

In class he named: GATT (the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, for goods), GATS (the General Agreement on Trade in Services), and the drastic development of transportation and communication technology. The eight in this lesson are the longer list used in the model answers to his exams.

The third centre: another name you may meet

One model essay in the revision material calls the third centre "South-East Asia" in place of "the Far East".

Four of Prof. Abu Qahf's past exams ask the same thing: is there a theory of globalization? The answer is no.

The main reason: globalization is a phenomenon, and "a phenomenon is not characterized by permanence". A theory needs stable, general relationships. And even the definition of globalization is not met in real life.

The model answer then adds a list of justifications. This lesson gives them, with the ways of confronting globalization.

Why there is no theory

First, it is a phenomenon. A phenomenon is not permanent, and a theory needs stable, general relationships.

Second, it is not even a fact. There is no free mobility of people, goods, technology or research: visas, EU standards and disputes stand in the way. So it is a myth more than a fact.

Then come the justifications:

  1. Its governing principle is utilitarianism النفعية: judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings. This leads to "market fundamentalism", where the market and profit rule everything, or "economic barbarism".
  2. It produces more prohibitions, more impossibilities and more dependency.
  3. It leads to alienation and the loss of freedom.
  4. It conflicts with liberalism and with diversity, because it means extending influence and standardization.
  5. The power of the world "springs from diversity, not from standardization".
  6. Glocalization shows the contradiction.

Glocalization

Global plus local: a global firm gives its products a local character. Ford, Coca-Cola and McDonald's standardize, while Toyota lets the consumer decide what is produced.

What globalization leads to, and how it is confronted

The justifications name four results of globalization as it is now. His exam has asked for them "by drawing only":

Repercussions are the results that follow from something. Three of them are named together as the repercussions: more prohibitions, more impossibilities, and dependency. Alienation is named as its "inevitable result".

Confronting globalization

  • Regionalism: regional blocs.
  • Nationalization, or localization الوطننة, which "is not a war on globalization".

The link with what he said in class

People mistake the driving forces (GATT, GATS, technology) and the superficial symptoms (burgers, jeans) for the phenomenon itself.

The answer

No. Globalization is a phenomenon, and "a phenomenon is not characterized by permanence". Its definition is not met in reality, so it is a myth, not a fact.

The justifications

  1. Utilitarianism, leading to "market fundamentalism" or "economic barbarism".
  2. More prohibitions, impossibilities and dependency.
  3. Alienation and loss of freedom.
  4. Conflict with liberalism and with diversity.
  5. The world's power "springs from diversity, not standardization".
  6. Glocalization: Ford, Coca-Cola and McDonald's standardize; Toyota lets the consumer decide what is produced.

Confronting it

Regionalism (regional blocs), and nationalization or localization, which "is not a war on globalization".

Is there a theory of globalization? Give the answer and the main reason.

No. It is a phenomenon, and "a phenomenon is not characterized by permanence"; a theory needs stable, general relationships. Also, its definition is not met in reality: there is no free mobility, so it is a myth.

Utilitarianism, the governing principle of globalization, means:

  1. Respecting every national culture
  2. Judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings
  3. Protecting the poor countries
  4. Sharing technology freely

It leads to "market fundamentalism", where the market and profit rule everything, or "economic barbarism".

What is glocalization, and which companies show the contradiction?

Global plus local: a global firm giving its products a local character. Ford, Coca-Cola and McDonald's standardize, while Toyota lets the consumer decide what is produced.

Name the two ways of confronting globalization.

Regionalism (regional blocs), and nationalization or localization, which "is not a war on globalization".

Which of these is NOT one of the repercussions of globalization in the drawing?

  1. More prohibitions
  2. More impossibilities
  3. Dependency
  4. Free mobility of people

The drawing shows more prohibitions, more impossibilities, dependency (the subjugation of poor countries) and alienation (the loss of freedom).

A global firm, said Prof. Abu Qahf, needs a global management team. The team has three major objectives: to search the world for opportunities, to keep a presence in key markets, and to look for similarities among countries.

The third objective is why global firms enjoy economies of scale: one product for many similar countries means producing far more units.

Search, keep, similarities

  1. Search worldwide for opportunities to be exploited. This is a global vision.
  2. Keep (maintain) a presence in key markets.
  3. Look for similarities among countries to be exploited.
His example for the third objective

There are 22 Arab countries. A global firm does not make one advertisement for Jordan, another for Egypt and another for Morocco. One advertisement in Arabic, or one product, serves all 22.

Objective 3 is why global firms enjoy economies of scale, which means a lower cost per unit because you make more. One product for 22 countries means producing 100 million units instead of 1 million.

To remember it

S-K-S: Search, Keep, Similarities. And similarities lead to scale.

The 3 objectives of the global management team

  1. Search worldwide for opportunities to be exploited (a global vision).
  2. Keep (maintain) a presence in key markets.
  3. Look for similarities among countries to be exploited (one Arabic advertisement for the 22 Arab countries).

Objective 3 gives the firm economies of scale.

What are the three objectives of a global firm's management team?

Search worldwide for opportunities (global vision). Keep a presence in key markets. Look for similarities among countries to exploit, which leads to economies of scale.

One advertisement in Arabic for the 22 Arab countries is his example of:

  1. Searching worldwide for opportunities
  2. Keeping a presence in key markets
  3. Looking for similarities among countries
  4. A multidomestic company

The countries share a language, so one advertisement or one product can serve all of them. That is exploiting a similarity.

Why do global firms enjoy economies of scale?

Because they exploit similarities among countries. One product for 22 countries means producing 100 million units instead of 1 million, so each unit costs less.
