Multinational corporations can be classified in many ways. The best-known way, said Prof. Abu Qahf, is by the orientation of headquarters. Orientation here means mindset: whose way of doing things wins?

Ethnocentric: headquarters decides everything. Polycentric: each subsidiary decides for itself. Regiocentric: organized by region. Geocentric: one large, integrated company.

Each pattern has a weak point, and his exams ask for both.

Whose way of doing things wins?

Multinationals can be classified on many bases: technological, political, technical, nationality. This is the best-known one.

Ethnocentric مركزي / متمركز حول الوطن الأم

Centralized. All decisions and strategies are made at headquarters. The subsidiaries, which are the company's units abroad, have no freedom to shape their own strategies. In one line: "Home knows best."

Polycentric لامركزي

Decentralized. Each subsidiary formulates its own policies and strategies, in production, in marketing, in everything. In one line: "Each country knows best."

Regiocentric (regional)

Organized by region: "focused on regional integration". In one line: "Each region knows best."

Geocentric جغرافي / عالمي

A large, integrated company: integrated horizontally, vertically, or both. The next lesson explains these two words. In one line: "The world is one system."

Explain it simply

Ask one question: whose way of doing things wins? Ethnocentric: headquarters' way, everywhere (a branch is a copy of home). Polycentric: each country's own way (each branch is almost a local company). Regiocentric: one way per region (one plan for the Gulf, another for Europe). Geocentric: the best way from anywhere, inside one integrated world company.

The first one is the easiest to run and the worst at adapting. The second adapts well but is hard to control.

Three patterns, three weaknesses

The classification comes from Howard Perlmutter, a management professor at Wharton in the USA, in 1969. His original scheme had three patterns: ethnocentric, polycentric and geocentric. His exams use these three, each with its weakness.

PatternDescriptionWeakness
Ethnocentric (centralized, single-nationality)Basically a national company with production branches abroad. All main decisions are taken at the head office at home.Cannot adapt to the host environment.
Polycentric (decentralized)High decentralization and freedom of action in the branches. Weaker control by the parent. Many owning nationalities.Hard to control the branches.
Geocentric (geographic)Integration and geographic spread worldwide. Large, with material, human and technical resources.Influenced by the home country's culture, especially early on, and tries to impose it on the hosts.
To remember the weaknesses

Ethno: can't adapt. Poly: can't control. Geo: imposes home culture.

The four types, in his meaning

  • Ethnocentric: centralized. All decisions and strategies are made at headquarters.
  • Polycentric: decentralized. Each subsidiary has its own policies and strategies.
  • Regiocentric: organized by region.
  • Geocentric: a large company characterized by integration, horizontally, vertically or both.

The three patterns and their weaknesses

  • Ethnocentric: cannot adapt to the host environment.
  • Polycentric: difficulty of control over branches.
  • Geocentric: influenced by the home country's culture, and tries to impose it on the hosts.

Ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric or geocentric?

  • All decisions and strategies are made at headquarters
  • Subsidiaries have no freedom to shape their own strategies
  • Weakness: cannot adapt to the host environment
  • Each subsidiary formulates its own policies and strategies
  • Weakness: hard to control the branches
  • One plan for the Gulf, another for Europe
  • A large company integrated horizontally, vertically or both
  • Weakness: tries to impose the home culture on the hosts

Ethnocentric, polycentric and geocentric: one line each.

Ethnocentric = centralized at headquarters. Polycentric = decentralized, each subsidiary sets its own strategy. Geocentric = large and integrated (vertically, horizontally, or both).

Weakness of the polycentric pattern, in four words?

Difficulty of control over branches.

Which of these is a pattern of headquarters' orientation, and not a name of a kind of firm?

  1. Multinational
  2. Multidomestic
  3. Polycentric
  4. Transnational

Do not mix the two lists. Multinational, multidomestic, global and transnational are names of firms. Ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric and geocentric classify firms by the mindset of headquarters.

His exact words
"The ethnocentric is representing a centralized firm ... all decisions, all strategies are actually made in the headquarters."

Three types or four? Where "regiocentric" comes from

Perlmutter's original scheme (1969) had three types: E, P and G. Regiocentric was added later (Heenan and Perlmutter, 1979), which gives the four letters "EPRG".

In class he said "three major groups" and then listed four: ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric "and even geocentric". The revision material for his exams gives the three.

The textbook uses the same words for staffing policies, which means who gets the jobs in the units abroad.

Another grouping: Vernon and Livingstone's three groups

The revision material also gives a grouping by Vernon and Livingstone, based on the degree of integration, the nature of activity and the type of technology:

  • Group I (GI): vertically integrated, high technology, extractive and manufacturing industries.
  • Group II (GII): horizontally integrated, high technology, less politically sensitive.
  • Group III (GIII): companies that transfer advanced technology to developing host countries through direct investment (Volkswagen making cars in Brazil).

It was not taught in class.

A page of class notes

One slip on this page: it says "there is one common definition". He said there is no common definition of international business.

Prof. Abu Qahf described the geocentric company as a large company that is integrated "horizontally, or vertically, or both". To integrate means to join things together.

Vertical integration: the company owns more steps of the same chain, upward toward the market or downward toward the raw material.

Horizontal integration: the company does the same thing in more places.

Vertical: owning more steps of the same chain

A company "integrates" when it grows by taking over more of the work itself, instead of paying other companies to do it. Let us follow one clothes company.

Making a shirt takes a chain of steps: cotton farm, then thread, then cloth, then shirt factory, then shop, then customer. Usually different companies do different steps. Say our company only weaves cloth. It buys cotton thread from someone else and sells the cloth to someone else.

Vertical integration means the company takes over steps above or below it in that chain:

  • Toward the customer: it opens its own shirt factory and its own shops, so it sells directly to people.
  • Toward the raw material: it buys its own cotton farm, so nobody can cut off its supply.

Picture the chain standing up like a ladder. The company climbs up and down its own ladder. That is why it is called vertical.

Vertical integration التكامل الرأسي

"Upward, I mean toward the market. Downward, toward the raw material."

His example: a spinning and weaving company opens its own garment factory and its own stores (upward, toward the market), or its own sheep or cotton farms (downward, toward the raw material).

Horizontal: the same step in more places

Here the company does not add new steps. It copies the same step somewhere else.

Our cloth company has one factory in Alexandria. It opens another cloth factory in Tanta, another in Damanhur and another in Marsa Matruh. It still does exactly the same work, just in more places. Picture factories standing side by side in a row. That is why it is called horizontal.

Horizontal integration التكامل الأفقي

"The same process, the same operation can be spread out in different places."

His example: the same factory again in Alexandria, Damanhur, Tanta and Marsa Matruh.

How this connects to "geocentric"

He described the geocentric company as a very big company whose parts are joined together in these two ways, across many countries. For example, it owns its farms in one country, its factories in several others and its shops around the world, and all of them work as one company.

Vertical integration

"Upward, I mean toward the market. Downward, toward the raw material."

A spinning and weaving company: its own garment factory and stores (upward), its own sheep or cotton farms (downward).

Horizontal integration

"The same process, the same operation can be spread out in different places." The same factory in Alexandria, Damanhur, Tanta and Marsa Matruh.

In one line

Vertical means owning more steps of the chain. Horizontal means the same step in more places. A geocentric company is a big company that does one or both of these.

Use his words

Upward = toward the customer. Downward = toward the raw material. Textbooks call these forward and backward integration. In his exam, use his words.

A spinning and weaving company grows. Which kind of integration is each move?

  • It opens its own stores
  • It opens its own garment factory
  • It buys its own cotton farms
  • It buys its own sheep farms
  • It opens a second weaving factory in Tanta
  • It opens the same factory again in Damanhur and Marsa Matruh

Vertical integration upward and downward: which is which?

Upward = toward the market (its own garment factory, its own stores). Downward = toward raw materials (its own cotton or sheep farms).

Give his definition of horizontal integration and his example.

"The same process, the same operation can be spread out in different places." The same factory in Alexandria, Damanhur, Tanta and Marsa Matruh.

Which type of multinational did he describe as "characterized by integration ... horizontally, or vertically, or both"?

  1. Ethnocentric
  2. Polycentric
  3. Regiocentric
  4. Geocentric

The geocentric company: a large company whose parts in many countries are joined together and work as one.

Prof. Abu Qahf opened his second lecture by separating two words that people mix up.

The mission is what the company aims to be, and why it exists. The strategy is the paths the company selects to reach its objectives.

Mission answers "why are we here?" Strategy answers "how will we get there?"

Why we exist, and how we get there

Mission الرسالة

His words: "What the company is aiming to be, and why the company is existing (the reason)."

In plain words: the reason the company exists. It answers "why are we here?"

Strategy الاستراتيجية

His words: "The different types of paths the company will select to achieve its objectives."

In plain words: the roads chosen to reach the objectives. It answers "how will we get there?"

A third word sits between the two. An objective is the long-term result the company wants, for example staying in business. The strategy is the road to that result.

Do not mix them up

Mission = why we exist. Strategy = how we reach our objectives. Objective = the long-term result.

Mission

What the company is aiming to be, and why the company is existing (the reason).

Strategy

The different types of paths the company will select to achieve its objectives.

In three words

Mission: why. Strategy: how. Objective: the long-term result.

Mission and strategy: what is the difference?

Mission = what the company aims to be and why it exists (the reason). Strategy = the paths it selects to achieve its objectives.

"We will enter three Arab markets through local agents in the next five years." This sentence is about the company's:

  1. Mission
  2. Strategy
  3. Reason for existing
  4. Culture

Strategy. It describes a path the company selects to reach its objectives. The mission would say why the company exists.

Which word does each line describe?

  • Why the company exists
  • The paths the company selects
  • What the company is aiming to be
  • It answers "how will we get there?"
  • It answers "why are we here?"

What is an objective, in his course?

The long-term result the company wants, for example staying in business. The strategy is the set of paths chosen to reach it.

Objective against target

He also separates the objective from the target. An objective is a long-term result, for example business continuity. A target, aim or goal is a short-term result, for example "immediate profit". This pair is taught again with total quality management, in Lecture 3.

Where these two words come back

A final exam of his from a doctorate programme asked for the "basic company mission" and the strategy of an ethnocentric firm, which is a firm that takes all its main decisions at the head office in its home country. The question and its answer are in the exam questions of Lecture 1, part 6 (Global management).

Prof. Abu Qahf gives a case in almost every lecture. After reading the first reports the class handed in, he said plainly what disappointed him: most of them summarized the case, then barely touched the questions. "Too general."

His method has three moves: a short briefing on each company, then a fact sheet (a table that compares the companies), and only then the answers, with suggestions and lessons drawn from the table.

A summary is not an answer

The homework case was about Illy, an Italian espresso firm, facing Starbucks, the American coffeehouse chain.

Most reports retold the story of the case and then wrote a few general lines under each question. His verdict:

"The way you are actually deal with or treated this case is just too general. Too general. I think I realize that most of you summarizes the report. And then try to touch to answer the questions."

A case answer must show that you organized the facts before you judged them. That is what the fact sheet is for.

Three moves, always in this order

  1. Briefing. A short summary of each company in the case. A few lines, not a retelling.
  2. Fact sheet. A comparison table of the companies on chosen factors: where each comes from, what it sells, who its customers are, and so on.
  3. Then answer. Answer the questions from the table. From the same table draw suggestions, courses of action, advice, and lessons for similar companies.

Why the table comes first: once the facts sit side by side, the answers become easy to see. In his words, after the fact sheet "it will be very much easy for you": you can make suggestions, develop advice, and realize lessons.

To remember it

Brief, Table, Then answer. Never answer a case before the table.

His method for any case

  1. Briefing: a short summary of each company.
  2. Fact sheet: a comparison table of the companies on chosen factors.
  3. Then answer the questions, and draw suggestions, courses of action, advice and lessons from the fact sheet.

What he criticised

Reports that summarize the case and then only touch the questions: "too general".

What are the three steps of his case method?

Brief each company; build a fact sheet (a comparison table); then answer, suggest and draw lessons.

What did he criticise in most of the first reports?

  1. They were too short
  2. They used a table
  3. They summarized the case and then barely touched the questions
  4. They gave too many suggestions

"Too general": a summary of the report, then a light touch on the questions. He wants the facts organized in a table first.

What should come out of the fact sheet, besides the answers to the questions?

Suggestions, courses of action, advice, and lessons for similar companies.

In which order does he want a case answer written?

  1. Answers, then a summary, then a table
  2. Briefing, fact sheet, then answers with suggestions and lessons
  3. Fact sheet, then briefing, then answers
  4. A long summary, then the answers

Brief, table, then answer. The table comes before any answer.

However the way you are actually deal with or treated this case is just too general. Too general. I think I realize that most of you summarizes the report. The questions page of the Illy and Starbucks case
The other rule for cases

The first rule, that the facts given in a case are never enough (ask, assume, build scenarios), is in Lecture 1, part 1.

A fact sheet is a table. Each row is a factor, each column is a company. Prof. Abu Qahf suggested about thirteen factors, from the country of origin to the competitive advantages, and called the list "endless": add or drop factors as the case needs.

He calls it "more comprehensive than the bloody SWOT". SWOT is not thrown away. It sits inside the fact sheet as four of its rows.

The rows of the table

The factors he suggested:

  1. Country of origin
  2. Nature of business
  3. Degree of diversification
  4. Type of customers: B2B or B2C
  5. Degree of international commitment
  6. Strategies (modes) of entry
  7. Competitors
  8. Strengths
  9. Weaknesses
  10. Opportunities
  11. Threats
  12. Potential
  13. Competitive advantage (the firm-specific advantages)

Some words. B2B means business to business: the company sells to other companies. B2C means business to consumer: it sells to the end consumer. Diversification is how many different lines of products the company has. The degree of international commitment is how deeply the company is involved abroad.

The list is open. He called it an "endless list": add a factor that matters in the case, drop one that does not.

The fact sheet and SWOT

SWOT means Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats. The fact sheet is "more comprehensive than the bloody SWOT": SWOT is rows 8 to 11 of it. PESTLE (the political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors around a company) sits inside it too. SWOT is "just a suggested way" to organize information, and there are many others.

Starbucks against Illy, row by row

These rows are built from his own remarks in class. Notice the last line of each: a row is not finished until it says "so what?"

Country of origin

Starbucks: the USA. "USA is a brand." Illy: Italy.

So what? The American origin is a strength for Starbucks.

Customers

Starbucks: B2C first, also B2B. Illy: mainly B2B.

So what? Illy could serve the end consumer too.

Diversification

Starbucks: wide, in related lines: food, sweets, mugs, gifts, music, the in-store "complete circle" of services. Illy: focused on one product, espresso.

So what? Each Starbucks line is a niche that strengthens its market position.

Niche تسويق النيشات

A distinct, special corner of the market "in a place on its own". A student said Illy is the niche (great espresso). He answered that the sweets and gifts of Starbucks are niches too.

And one weakness he pointed at: Starbucks has very high prices.

The factors of a fact sheet (an open list)

Country of origin; nature of business; degree of diversification; type of customers (B2B or B2C); degree of international commitment; modes of entry; competitors; strengths; weaknesses; opportunities; threats; potential; competitive advantages.

Two lines to quote

"More comprehensive than the bloody SWOT": SWOT and PESTLE sit inside the fact sheet.

"USA is a brand": the country of origin can be a strength.

Every row ends with "so what?"

Illy is mainly B2B, so it could serve end consumers too. Starbucks diversifies into related niches, so its market position is stronger. Its weakness: very high prices.

Name at least eight factors he suggested for a fact sheet.

Country of origin; nature of business; degree of diversification; type of customers (B2B or B2C); degree of international commitment; modes of entry; competitors; strengths; weaknesses; opportunities; threats; potential; competitive advantages.

How does the fact sheet relate to SWOT?

  1. It replaces SWOT, which is wrong
  2. It is more comprehensive: SWOT sits inside it
  3. It is a shorter form of SWOT
  4. They are the same thing

"More comprehensive than the bloody SWOT". Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats are four of its rows, and PESTLE sits inside it too.

Illy sells mainly to other businesses. What did he suggest from that row?

Illy could serve the end consumer too (add B2C to its B2B).

What is a niche? Which company has niches in this case?

A distinct, special corner of the market "in a place on its own". Illy's great espresso is one. But the sweets and gifts of Starbucks are niches too, and each one strengthens its market position.

Which company does each fact describe?

  • "USA is a brand"
  • Focused on one product
  • Mainly B2B
  • Wide diversification into related lines
  • Very high prices
  • Italian origin

6. Modes of entryForeign direct investment, joint ventures, wholly owned subsidiariesExporting, B2B partnerships, some franchising
7. CompetitorsGlobal and local cafes, fast-food chainsPremium bean suppliers, espresso makers
8. StrengthsGlobal brand, product range, comfortable experienceQuality, espresso expertise
9. WeaknessesVery high prices (his joke: for that price you could buy a galabeya)Narrow range, reliance on B2B
10. OpportunitiesMore B2B services and related merchandiseEnter B2C directly
11. ThreatsLocal competition, economic swings in luxury spendingBean prices, diversified chains
12. PotentialityExpand the "chain of services"High if B2C entry succeeds
13. Competitive advantagesThe complete experience and related nichesPurity, focus and reputation of one product

Factors 1 to 4 and the remark on prices come from his words in class. Several other cells, for example Illy's modes of entry, are a classmate's own reading of the case.

Later in the course Prof. Abu Qahf came back to the fact sheet "again", for a case about choosing a country to invest in. This time the fact sheet became a weighted scoring table.

List the factors. Give each factor a weight out of 100, which is its relative importance. Score the country on each factor, out of that weight. Add up the scores. With one column for each country, the highest total is chosen.

A report card for countries

The case was "Going to Gdansk": a family firm from Chicago that makes computer chips wants to build a plant in Gdansk, a city in Poland.

He drew the fact sheet as a table with weights:

Factors to be consideredWeightPolandEgypt
Political stability (sub-factors A, B, C, D)2015...
Economic environment (A: market size, B, ...)60......
... (other factors).........
Total100calculatedcalculated

How to read it:

  • The weight is the relative importance of the factor. All the weights add up to 100.
  • The score is what the country actually earns on that factor, out of the weight. Poland gets 15 of the 20 for political stability.
  • Add the scores, and each country has one number out of 100.

"We can also add another market": one column for Poland and one for Egypt, and the highest total is chosen.

Only the 20, the 60, the 15 and the 100 are his numbers. The Egypt column shows how a second market is added.

The factors follow PEST

He framed the factors as PEST: Political, Economic, Social, Technological.

  • Political stability, measured by indicators A, B, C.
  • The economic environment, measured by market size, inflation, growth rate and so on.
  • Then the social and cultural factors.

His advice about the table: "Make this as a methodology through which you can arrange and organize the way you are thinking."

Explain it simply

It is a report card for countries. The weight says how much a factor matters to this company. Here the economy counts three times as much as politics. The score says how much of that weight the country earns. The scores add up to one number per country out of 100, so the choice can be defended in a table and not just by feeling.

The weighted fact sheet

  1. List the factors (PEST: political stability, economic environment, social and cultural factors).
  2. Give each a weight, its relative importance. The weights total 100.
  3. Score each country on each factor, out of the weight.
  4. Add up. One column per country. The highest total is chosen.

His numbers

Political stability 20, economic environment 60, total 100. Poland earns 15 of the 20 for political stability.

His sentence

"Make this as a methodology through which you can arrange and organize the way you are thinking."

Describe the weighted fact sheet in four steps.

List the factors; give each a weight out of 100 (its relative importance); score each country on each factor out of that weight; add up the scores. With a column for each country, the highest total is chosen.

In his table, political stability has a weight of 20 and Poland has 15. What does the 15 mean?

  1. Poland is ranked 15th in the world
  2. Poland earns 15 of the 20 points available for political stability
  3. Political stability matters 15 percent
  4. Poland has 15 indicators of risk

The weight (20) is how much the factor matters. The score (15) is how much of that weight the country earns.

Which factors did he put in the table, and how is each measured?

He framed them as PEST. Political stability, measured by indicators A, B, C. The economic environment, measured by market size, inflation, growth rate and so on. Then social and cultural factors.

The company compares Poland and Egypt in the same table. Which country is chosen?

  1. The one with the highest score on political stability
  2. The one with the largest market
  3. The one with the highest total
  4. The one with the lowest weight

Each country gets one total out of 100. The highest total is chosen.

His feedback on the Gdansk reports

Show the indicators first. A student recommended an integrative approach: local staff, and good relations with the government and the parties. He asked: did the case really show that Poland is politically unstable? The integrative approach protects against political risk, not economic risk. So first "tell me some sort of indicators through which you can say that Poland is politically unstable". Recommending the integrative, protective or defensive approach without that evidence is "quite risky". These approaches are the ways of managing political risk, taught in Lecture 3.

This case is "out of assumptions". The student said "make an assumption", which was his own advice in the first lecture. He answered: "This case is actually ... out of assumptions!" It "is completely representing an application of the political risk ... a real world case". So in this kind of case, argue from the facts in the report.

On the papers. "I have gone through the paper you have actually submitted. You have analyzed it quite well, really." A student admitted: "We did the fact sheet, but not like the standard that you did."

More about the Gdansk case

Andrzej Jaworski, in Chicago, and his brothers make patented, specialized computer chips. They expect sales of 147 million dollars within three years, and 200 million if they expand internationally. They prefer a plant in Gdansk, Poland, where the family has its roots, over Belgium, to export to the European Community (today's European Union). The risks: expropriation, blocked profits, and an investment of 20 million dollars. The case comes from the printed chapter on political risk.

From a grocery shop to an iron and steel giant or EgyptAir, every organization lives inside a total business environment.

Prof. Abu Qahf splits it in two. The internal environment is inside the company. The external environment is outside it, and has two parts: the public (general) environment, which touches all companies, and the task environment, which is specific to the company's own business.

Inside, outside for everyone, outside for you alone

He says any organization, "apart from its size ... nature of business ... nationality ... age ... owners", operates within the total business environment.

  • The internal environment is inside the company. The company controls it.
  • The external public environment (also called general): the economic, political, cultural, social, technological and even international variables. They affect any organization, "directly or indirectly".
  • The external task environment (also called competitive or specific): the company's own customers, suppliers, competitors and government agencies.
To remember it

Public factors: PEST + C + I (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, plus Cultural and International). Task factors: C-S-C-G (Customers, Suppliers, Competitors, Government agencies).

Political instability touches everyone

The clearest example of a public factor is political instability. It does not choose one company. It hits all of them.

"Unstable countries cannot attract any foreign investment. Even domestic investment."
His example: Egypt, 2011 to 2013

Foreign firms withdrew. No newcomers arrived. And most of the big Egyptian businessmen moved their money abroad.

So an unstable country loses twice: the foreign investor leaves, and the local investor leaves with him. This is the door to the next lecture's topic, political risk.

The total business environment

  1. Internal environment: inside the company.
  2. External public (general) environment: economic, political, cultural, social, technological, international.
  3. External task (competitive, specific) environment: customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies.

The example to quote

Egypt 2011 to 2013: "Unstable countries cannot attract any foreign investment. Even domestic investment." Foreign firms withdrew, no newcomers came, and Egyptian businessmen moved their money abroad.

Draw the total business environment (say it aloud as a tree).

Total = internal + external. External = public, or general (economic, political, cultural, social, technological, international) + task, or competitive, specific (customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies).

The task environment: list its four elements.

Customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies.

Public (general) environment or task (specific) environment?

  • The company's suppliers
  • Political instability in the country
  • The company's competitors
  • The technology of the age
  • The culture of the society
  • The government agency that supervises its industry
  • The company's customers

What did Egypt 2011 to 2013 show about political instability?

Unstable countries attract neither foreign nor domestic investment: foreign firms withdrew, no newcomers came, and Egyptian businessmen moved their balances abroad.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

A fuller version of the drawing

A classmate's compiled notes fill the boxes with more items:

  • Internal: management, employees, organizational culture, structure, financial resources, technology and capabilities, core competencies.
  • General (macro), or public: economic, political, legal, cultural and social, technological, international, natural or environmental.
  • Task (micro), or competitive: suppliers, customers, competitors, governmental agencies, strategic partners such as alliances and distributors.

The extra items (legal, natural, strategic partners, and the list of internal items) look like the note-taker's additions, not words from class.

Another version you may meet: the environment of international management

The revision booklet passed on from earlier classes describes the environment of international management under five headings.

Changes affecting international business. NAFTA (the USA, Canada, Mexico); the European Union and Turkey's attempts to join; new GATT changes; the Asian tigers and ASEAN; Eastern Europe moving to market economies; Latin American growth and the Andean Pact; growth in India, Pakistan and Egypt.

The political environment. China's transformation; changing politics in Russia and Poland; many countries moving to market economies and democracy (an opportunity and a threat); changes in the Balkans and the Caucasus.

The legal environment. It is confusing, because laws differ. Sources of law: Islamic Sharia; socialist law; common law; civil law (with Roman origins). Principles of international law: sovereignty (each state makes its own laws), nationality (a state may prosecute its citizens anywhere), territoriality (its laws apply inside its borders), protection (laws to protect national security), plus others such as refusing visas.

The economic environment. Big economic blocs and strategic alliances; foreign direct investment as a main tool of development; wider markets; developing economies growing faster than advanced ones.

The technological environment. Biotechnology, satellites, instant translation, chips and supercomputers, e-cash, better communications in developing countries.

Prof. Abu Qahf told a story: one man buys a can of Pepsi, then a Kia car, on the same day. For the Pepsi he asks nothing and overpays. For the Kia he asks about everything.

His conclusion: "the customer of Kia is not the customer of Pepsi", even when it is the same person, because the motives behind the decision to buy and the purchasing power are different. So the two companies live in two different task environments.

One man, one day, two customers

His story

Ahmed finishes his EMBA. His father gives him money for a car.

On the way to the showroom he is thirsty. He buys a Pepsi at a grocery, pays 30 pounds (too much) and asks nothing.

At the Kia showroom he asks the salesman, Mr. Hanafi, everything: the price, cash or instalments, durability, maintenance, spare parts (available? expensive?), the guarantee, the options, the fuel consumption.

Why the difference? The motives.

  • Pepsi: emotional motives. He wants to quench his thirst, "to keep alive". No questions. He even accepts a higher price.
  • Kia: rational, or economic, motives. Price, fuel, durability, spare parts. Every question, or its answer, "can be translated into money".

And the purchasing power differs. Almost everyone can buy a Pepsi. A car needs substantial money, savings or instalments. "The purchasing power for Pepsi is not equal to the purchasing power of the Kia. Totally different."

"When dealing with Kia you are Ahmed. When dealing with Pepsi you are not Ahmed."

So the two task environments differ

Lay the two companies side by side, the way he wants it done in every case answer:

FactorPepsiKia
Nature of businessBeverages: fast-moving consumer goodsAutomotive, engineering: car manufacturing and assembly
Decision processVery fast, impulsive, no negotiationLong and complex, a high financial commitment
Competitors ("different enemies")Coca-Cola, local drinksOther car makers (BMW, Hyundai) and all means of transport: tuk-tuks, trains, aircraft
SuppliersSugar, carbonation, packaging, bottlingParts, steel, electronics, engines
Government agenciesThe food and beverage tax authority (his example), health regulatorsThe engineering industry authority (his example), traffic licensing

Notice the wide view of competition. A car competes with every other way of getting from A to B, not only with other cars.

His conclusion: the task environment of Pepsi is not the task environment of Kia. The customers differ, and so do the competitors, the suppliers and the government agencies.

His sentence

"The customer of Kia is not the customer of Pepsi", even when it is the same person.

Why

  1. Motives. Pepsi: emotional. Kia: rational, or economic ("all of these questions mean money").
  2. Purchasing power. Almost everyone for Pepsi; substantial money for Kia.

What follows

Their task environments differ: the competitors (Pepsi against Coca-Cola; Kia against car makers and even tuk-tuks, trains and aircraft), the suppliers, and the government agencies (food against engineering).

Why is "the customer of Kia not the customer of Pepsi"?

Different motives (rational or economic against emotional) and different purchasing power behind the decision to buy, even if it is the same person. The suppliers, the competitors and the government agencies differ too.

Which purchase does each line describe?

  • Emotional motives
  • Every question can be translated into money
  • The buyer accepts an overcharge
  • Competes even with tuk-tuks, trains and aircraft
  • Cash or instalments? Spare parts? Guarantee?
  • A very fast decision, no negotiation
  • A long and complex decision

Who are Kia's competitors, in his wide view?

  1. Only other Korean car makers
  2. Only other car makers
  3. Other car makers and all means of transport: tuk-tuks, trains, aircraft
  4. Pepsi and Coca-Cola

A car competes with every other way of getting from A to B.

What did the buyer ask about at the Kia showroom, and what do the questions have in common?

The price, cash or instalments, durability, maintenance, spare parts, the guarantee, the options, the fuel consumption. They reflect rational, or economic, motives: each answer can be translated into money.

Which government agencies did he name for each company?

For Pepsi: the food and beverage tax authority. For Kia: the engineering industry authority.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

Explain it simply

A "customer" is not a person. It is a person in a buying situation. For a 30-pound drink you act on feeling. For a car you act like an accountant. So a company must study the motives, the purchasing power and the decision process of its buyers, not just who they are.

In class the students suggested other differences: "level of involvement", "different needs", "purchasing power", "number of people in the decision". He kept stressing the difference in purchasing power and in motives.

His words
"All of these questions reflect what is called Rational motives. Economic motives ... Or the answer can be translated into money."
"The motives that lie behind the decision to buy Pepsi is completely different from the motives that lie behind the decision to buy Kia motor car."
"The purchasing power for Pepsi is not equal to the purchasing power of the Kia. Totally different."
Which cells of the table are his

The motives, the competitors, the two government agencies and the purchasing power are his points from class. The other cells (nature of business, decision process, the lists of suppliers, health regulators and traffic licensing) were filled in by a classmate's notes.

Prof. Abu Qahf gives two definitions of globalization. The first: the free mobility of everything between countries, without any restrictions. The second: the tendency toward integrating the world, on an economic, political and cultural basis.

He builds his argument that globalization is "a big myth" on the first one. If anything at all needs permission to cross a border, the definition is not met.

Free mobility: everything moves, nothing is stopped

Definition 1: free mobility العولمة: حرية الانتقال

"The free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions."

Everything means: people, products, services, capital, wealth, technology, the results of scientific research, "even poverty, even problems".

Read it strictly, as he does. If anything at all needs permission to cross a border, this definition is not met.

He called this definition "a very simple definition" and "the core of globalization". It is the one he tests against real life, and the one his "myth" argument stands on.

Integration: the world as one

Definition 2: integration

"The tendency toward integrating the world ... on economic basis ... political basis ... and cultural basis."

He also said it this way: "the international integration of goods, services, technology, labor, capital ... on worldwide basis".

In plain words: the world working as one economy, one political space and one culture.

What he repeated about the myth

With the two definitions in hand, he repeated three warnings:

  • Do not confuse the concept with its driving forces. These are GATT (the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, for goods), GATS (the General Agreement on Trade in Services), and the revolution in information technology and transport.
  • McDonald's, Pizza Hut, Starbucks and jeans are only superficial symptoms.
  • It is a myth: people need visas, the European Union has its own standards (the CE mark), and trade blocs are closed clubs. What exists is the "death of distance". Geographic and cultural distance remain, and the world is never one small village.

Definition 1: free mobility

"The free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions": people, products, services, capital, wealth, technology, scientific research results, "even poverty, even problems".

Definition 2: integration

"The tendency toward integrating the world" on an economic, a political and a cultural basis.

Which one he uses

Definition 1 is "the core of globalization". He tests it against real life, finds restrictions everywhere, and concludes that globalization is a myth.

Give his two definitions of globalization.

(1) The free mobility of everything (people, goods, services, capital, technology, research, even problems) between countries without any restrictions. (2) The tendency toward integrating the world on an economic, political and cultural basis.

Which definition does he build his "myth" argument on?

  1. Free mobility of everything without any restrictions
  2. Integration of the world
  3. The textbook's definition
  4. Neither

Free mobility. It is easy to test: one visa, one standard, one border check is enough to say it is not met.

In definition 1, what does "everything" include?

People, products, services, capital, wealth, technology, the results of scientific research, "even poverty, even problems".

Which definition does each line belong to?

  • "Without any restrictions"
  • One economy, one political space, one culture
  • "Even poverty, even problems"
  • "On economic basis, political basis and cultural basis"
  • "The core of globalization"

Which three things must not be confused when talking about globalization?

The concept itself (free mobility, or integration); its driving forces (GATT, GATS, the revolution in information technology and transport); and its superficial symptoms (McDonald's, Pizza Hut, Starbucks, jeans).

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

Which one is the "scientific" definition?

He used the word for both. In the first lecture he called free mobility "the scientific definition", "a very simple definition" and "the core of globalization". In the second lecture he introduced integration with "scientifically speaking", and then called free mobility "maybe much easier".

Either way, definition 1 is the one he builds his "myth" argument on.

The textbook's exact definition

"The trend toward greater economic, cultural, political, and technological interdependence among national institutions and economies."

The revision material passed on from earlier classes of Prof. Abu Qahf is harsher than his words in class. It calls globalization "colonialism in a new garment made in the United States", built on principles such as market fundamentalism.

It also gives a list that one past exam asked for: the seven things economic globalization depends on. He did not explain either point in class, so learn them as they are written.

"Colonialism in a new garment"

In this view, "Globalization is colonialism in a new garment made in the United States". It is also Westernization: making the world look like the West.

It does not respect the individual's intellectual integrity or national identity, and it assumes that cultures will not survive.

Its principles:

  1. Market fundamentalism. "If the commodity does not fit the market, the market will be modified to fit the commodity". So globalization is "a trap for consumption".
  2. One-sided utilitarianism النفعية: judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings.
  3. The individual is an economic unit, not a cultural one.
  4. Similarity of tastes, and the media.
  5. Consumerist materialism.

And one sentence that matches his own "death of distance": distances die through communications, "but distances do not die from the geopolitical or geostrategic point of view, and the comprehensive power of the world springs from diversity, not from standardization".

What economic globalization depends on

The same material lists seven factors. A past exam asked to "mention them without explaining", so a clean list is the whole answer.

  1. Information technology and the Internet.
  2. Companies' social and ethical responsibility.
  3. A global product or a global customer.
  4. Global business standards and products.
  5. The growth of trade, of investment, and of their agreements.
  6. New competitors from emerging economies.
  7. The fading of borders.
To remember it

Walk from the tool to the result: technology, responsibility, a global product or customer, global standards, trade and investment, new competitors, fading borders.

The harsher view

"Globalization is colonialism in a new garment made in the United States", and Westernization. Principles: market fundamentalism ("a trap for consumption"); one-sided utilitarianism; the individual as an economic unit; similarity of tastes and the media; consumerist materialism.

The power of the world "springs from diversity, not from standardization".

Economic globalization depends on (7)

  1. Information technology and the Internet.
  2. Companies' social and ethical responsibility.
  3. A global product or a global customer.
  4. Global business standards and products.
  5. Growth of trade, investment and their agreements.
  6. New competitors from emerging economies.
  7. The fading of borders.

Mention, without explaining, the seven factors economic globalization depends on.

Information technology and the Internet; companies' social and ethical responsibility; a global product or a global customer; global business standards and products; the growth of trade, investment and their agreements; new competitors from emerging economies; the fading of borders.

"If the commodity does not fit the market, the market will be modified to fit the commodity." Which principle is this?

  1. Utilitarianism
  2. Market fundamentalism
  3. Consumerist materialism
  4. Westernization

Market fundamentalism. It is why this view calls globalization "a trap for consumption".

What is one-sided utilitarianism?

Judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings.

Complete the sentence: "Globalization is colonialism in ..."

"... a new garment made in the United States."

In this view, where does "the comprehensive power of the world" spring from?

  1. Standardization
  2. The death of distance
  3. Diversity
  4. The media

From diversity, not from standardization. Distances die through communications, but not from the geopolitical or geostrategic point of view.

Where the same material continues

The rest of what this revision material says about globalization (its four indicators, its driving, conditional and governing factors, and why there is no theory of globalization) is in Lecture 1, part 5. The past exam question on the seven factors is worked out in that part's exam questions.

Agreements between developed and developing nations, Prof. Abu Qahf says, "ensure equal opportunities ... but never ever secure equal results".

On paper both sides may export the same value. In reality the poor country's products are tested against the rich country's standards and often rejected, while its own market stays open. He calls signing the world trade agreements without asking for help "the big crime", and he puts the blame on the government that signed.

The same right to export is not the same result

His example: the partnership between Egypt and the European Union

On paper, both sides may export the same value to each other.

In reality, Egyptian potatoes are examined against the European standards and often rejected. Even a pen's length, weight or diameter can get a product refused.

Why does the poor side lose?

  • Developing countries lack the competitive advantage and the competitive conditions to compete in the rich markets.
  • Meanwhile their own markets are open to the rich countries' goods.
  • So the rich countries "play safe": they give an equal opportunity that the other side cannot use.

A competitive advantage is something that makes a company's product win against its rivals, such as quality, price or technology.

Aid that feeds consumption, and "the big crime"

Aid creates dependency. Aid from rich countries tends to encourage consumption. It comes as support in kind, which means goods, not as local factories that would stop imports. The result is dependency تبعية: the poor country keeps needing the rich one.

His view on the trade agreements. GATT is the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, for goods. GATS is the General Agreement on Trade in Services. Signing them, he says, was "the big crime committed worldwide" against the third-world countries.

But notice where he puts the blame. Not on the rich countries. The blame is on the government that signed without asking the other side to help it develop its production factors, so that its products could meet their standards.

His sentence

Agreements between developed and developing nations "ensure equal opportunities ... but never ever secure equal results".

The example

The Egypt and European Union partnership: Egyptian potatoes are tested against European standards and often rejected, while Egypt's market is open.

Why

  1. Developing countries lack the competitive advantage and the competitive conditions. Rich countries "play safe".
  2. Aid encourages consumption, not local factories: dependency.
  3. Signing GATT and GATS without asking for help to upgrade production was "the big crime". The blame is on the government that signed.

"Equal opportunities but never equal results": explain with his example.

The Egypt and European Union partnership: both may export equally on paper, but Egyptian potatoes are tested against European standards and often rejected, while European goods enter Egypt's open market.

Whom does he blame for "the big crime" of signing GATT and GATS?

  1. The rich countries
  2. The World Trade Organization
  3. The government that signed without asking for help to develop its production
  4. The multinational companies

The government that signed. It should have asked the other side to help develop its production factors, so that its products meet their standards.

How does aid create dependency?

Aid tends to encourage consumption (support in kind), not local factories that would stop imports. So the poor country keeps depending on the rich one.

Why can the rich countries "play safe" when they sign such agreements?

  1. Because they export nothing
  2. Because developing countries lack the competitive advantage and conditions to compete in rich markets
  3. Because the agreements forbid exports from poor countries
  4. Because they pay for the poor countries' factories

The opportunity is equal on paper, but the developing side cannot use it: its products do not meet the standards, while its own market is open.

More on this lesson

Optional. Open what you want.

One more point about aid

A classmate's notes of the lecture add that such subsidies "eventually return to the donor country".

Prof. Abu Qahf told a story from an English mall. Egyptian cotton undershirts sold out there. The shop ordered more from Egypt. The new order came by sea, the pins rusted, and the whole order was rejected.

The lesson: standards and quality are the real border. A market can be won by a good product and lost by one small detail.

Sold out, ordered again, rejected

His story: the Egyptian undershirts in England

In an English mall he found undershirts made of 100% Egyptian cotton by Gil, a maker from Alexandria. They were expensive.

He bought 4. A colleague bought the rest. A third man came and found none.

So the shop ordered Egyptian cotton shirts from Egypt. They arrived by sea. The humidity rusted the pins. That spoiled the shirts, and the order was rejected.

The product was wanted. The price was accepted. The market was open. What lost it was one small detail.

By air, or with decent pins, it would have worked. His word for it: الغباء, stupidity.

To remember it

One rusty pin can lose a whole export market: standards and quality are the real border.

The story fits his sentence about trade agreements: the opportunity was equal, the result was not.

The story in four lines

  1. Gil's 100% Egyptian cotton undershirts sold out in an English mall, at a high price.
  2. The shop ordered more from Egypt.
  3. They came by sea; humidity rusted the pins; the shirts were spoiled.
  4. The order was rejected.

The lesson

Standards and quality are the real border. By air, or with decent pins, it would have worked.

Tell the undershirts story in four steps.

Gil's Egyptian cotton undershirts sold out in an English mall. The shop ordered more from Egypt. They came by sea and the humidity rusted the pins, which spoiled the shirts. The order was rejected.

Why was the second order rejected?

  1. The cotton was of low quality
  2. The price was too high
  3. The pins rusted at sea and spoiled the shirts
  4. England banned Egyptian products

The product itself was wanted and had sold out. One small detail, pins that rust in sea humidity, lost the order.

What would have saved the order?

Sending it by air, or using decent pins.

What does the story teach about exporting?

Standards and quality are the real border. One rusty pin can lose a whole export market, even when the product is wanted and the market is open.

Competition is now worldwide, so a company must adopt a global perspective. For Prof. Abu Qahf, the key to success is to develop a global product: a product that can be marketed worldwide, because it satisfies customer needs on a worldwide basis.

His examples: Coca-Cola, Pepsi, shaving blades, pens, pencils. Small changes are still allowed, as long as the core of the product stays the same.

One product the whole world can buy

"The key success in a world of growing tendency toward internationalization is ... the development of what can be called a global product."

Global product

"A product that can be marketed worldwide ... mainly based on satisfying customer needs on a worldwide basis."

His examples: Coca-Cola, Pepsi, shaving blades, pens, pencils. People everywhere need them for the same reason.

Small changes are still allowed. 7UP or Coca-Cola written in Arabic script "doesn't make any difference ... because the core is okay".

The core of a product is the main benefit the buyer gets from it, the "why" of buying. So the test is the same one he gave for going international: if the core can be globalized, go.

Global product

"A product that can be marketed worldwide", based on satisfying customer needs on a worldwide basis.

His examples

Coca-Cola, Pepsi, shaving blades, pens, pencils.

The test

If the core can be globalized, go. Minor changes (the name in Arabic script) make no difference, "because the core is okay".

Define a global product in his words, and give three of his examples.

"A product that can be marketed worldwide ... mainly based on satisfying customer needs on a worldwide basis." Coca-Cola, Pepsi, shaving blades, pens, pencils.

Coca-Cola writes its name in Arabic script on cans sold in Egypt. Is it still a global product?

  1. No, any change makes it a local product
  2. Yes: it "doesn't make any difference ... because the core is okay"
  3. Only if the price is also the same
  4. Only outside the Arab countries

Yes. The change touches the outside of the product, not its core. The core is what must be the same worldwide.

What does he call "the key success" in a world that is becoming more international?

The development of a global product. Because competition is now worldwide, a company must adopt a global perspective.

What decides whether a product can be a global product?

Its core, the main benefit the buyer gets. If the core can be globalized, go.

The core (the main benefit, the "why"), the formal level (features, size, colour) and the augmented level (extra services such as a guarantee) are taught in Lecture 1, part 4.

Prof. Abu Qahf says any company has three options. Think local, act local: a domestic company that stays home. Think global, act local: one global plan, with local adjustments. Think global, act global: everything is standardized.

The three options lead straight to the question of his next printed sheet: how far should a firm standardize?

Where you plan, and where you adjust

"Think" is about the plan. "Act" is about the execution in each market.

OptionWhoWhat it means
Think local, act localA domestic companyIt stays home.
Think global, act localA global strategy with local execution"You go global and you act local": one global plan, local adjustments.
Think global, act globalA fully standardized company"Everything is globalized": a standardized business strategy, marketing strategy, generic strategy and competitive strategy.
Think global, act local

A global brand that makes only minor alterations, such as writing 7UP in Arabic script.

Standardized means the same everywhere. So the third option is one product and one way of doing business for the whole world.

How far should a firm go toward the third option? That is the subject of the sheet he handed out in the same lecture, "The Myth of Globalization", in the last part of this lecture.

The three options

  1. Think local, act local: a domestic company.
  2. Think global, act local: global, with minor alterations (the brand name in Arabic script).
  3. Think global, act global: a fully standardized strategy. "Everything is globalized."

Name the three think and act options.

Think local, act local (domestic); think global, act local; think global, act global (fully standardized).

Which option is it? (Think, then act.)

  • A domestic company that stays home
  • 7UP written in Arabic script
  • One standardized strategy for the whole world
  • One global plan, local adjustments
  • "Everything is globalized"

In "think global, act global", what is standardized?

  1. Only the product
  2. Only the advertising
  3. The business, marketing, generic and competitive strategies
  4. Nothing: each country gets its own strategy

"Everything is globalized ... You develop a standardized business strategy ... standardized marketing strategy ... standardized generic strategy ... standardized competitive strategy."

Which of the three options describes a company that is not international at all?

Think local, act local: the domestic company. It stays home.

His words
"Any company has three options ... To think local and act local ... domestic company ... To think global and act local ... To think global and act global ... Everything is globalized ... You develop a standardized business strategy ... standardized marketing strategy ... standardized generic strategy ... standardized competitive strategy."
A modern example of "think global, act local"

"Think global, act local" is the usual description of McDonald's: one global brand and system, with local menu items. In India it sells no beef. The textbook (2014) describes the mutton "Maharaja Mac"; today the menu there is mainly chicken and vegetarian.

In 1983 a Harvard professor, Theodore Levitt, made a bold claim: technology is pushing the world toward one market, so the winners will sell the same standardized product everywhere at a low price.

Four years later Susan Douglas and Yoram Wind answered him in an article called "The Myth of Globalization". This is the printed sheet Prof. Abu Qahf handed out. Its message: think globally, yes, but standardizing everything is "naive and oversimplistic". Standardization is one option on a scale, not the only road.

A claim, and a reply in five steps

To standardize means to do the same thing everywhere: the same product, sold the same way, in every country.

Levitt's claim (1983). Technology "drives the world toward a single converging commonality". Global firms will win through "enormous economies of scale" and lower world prices. Economies of scale means that each unit gets cheaper when you make more of the same product.

The reply of Douglas and Wind (1987). A global view is right. But one standard product for the whole world is only one of the options. Their article goes through five steps:

Two poles since the 1960s

Since the 1960s, international strategy has swung between two poles:

Standardize

One strategy worldwide. It gains synergies from operating in many countries, and it was seen as the multinational's key advantage.

Adapt

Change the strategy to fit each country's special conditions. It is needed to succeed locally.

Synergies are the extra gain when parts work together (1 + 1 = 3). For example, one good idea used in ten countries.

A middle way: pattern standardization. One global theme or positioning, executed locally. Positioning is the place a product takes in the customer's mind.

The critics of Levitt said standardization fits some products better than others (industrial goods, luxury items), and some markets better than others (the Triad: the three rich blocs of the USA, Europe and Japan).

Who said what

Levitt (1983): technology drives the world toward one market; sell the same standardized product everywhere, at a low price, with enormous economies of scale.

Douglas and Wind (1987), "The Myth of Globalization": standardizing everything is "naive and oversimplistic". Standardization is one option on a scale.

The old debate

Standardize (one strategy worldwide, synergies) or adapt (to each country's conditions). In the middle: pattern standardization, one global theme executed locally.

The five steps of the article

  1. The old debate.
  2. Three assumptions and their pitfalls.
  3. Requisite conditions.
  4. Constraints: external (4), internal (2).
  5. The framework: a continuum and a checklist.

What did Levitt claim in 1983, and what did Douglas and Wind answer in 1987?

Levitt: technology drives the world toward one market, so winners sell the same standardized product everywhere at a low price, through enormous economies of scale. Douglas and Wind: think globally, but standardizing everything is "naive and oversimplistic"; standardization is one option on a scale.

Which pole of the old debate does each line belong to?

  • One strategy worldwide
  • Fit each country's special conditions
  • Gains synergies from operating in many countries
  • Needed to succeed locally
  • Levitt's "enormous economies of scale"

What is pattern standardization?

The middle way: one global theme or positioning, executed locally.

What is the Triad?

  1. The three assumptions of standardization
  2. The three rich blocs: the USA, Europe and Japan
  3. Levitt, Douglas and Wind
  4. Product, price and promotion

The three rich blocs. Critics of Levitt said standardization fits these markets, and products such as industrial goods and luxury items, better than others.

What are synergies?

The extra gain when parts work together (1 + 1 = 3), for example one good idea used in ten countries.

Who named the two forces (the authors the article cites)

Fayerweather (1969). Unification (the internal pressure to integrate) against fragmentation (country differences, and relations with the host society).

Doz (1980). The economic imperative (rationalize across borders to survive) against the political imperative ("national responsiveness" to host governments). A third option: administrative coordination, deciding each case on its own merits.

Porter (1980, 1985). Forces for global competition (scale economies, learning, lower transport costs, global segments) against barriers (government rules, tariffs, local preference, transport costs, different demand) that call for "protected niche" strategies.

The case for global products and brands rests on three key assumptions. Prof. Abu Qahf dictated them in class, and one of his exams asked for exactly these three.

People's needs are becoming the same everywhere. People will give up their preferences for a lower price at high quality. And supplying the whole world brings big economies of scale.

Same needs, price beats preference, scale savings

An assumption is something taken as true without proof. Levitt's philosophy of global standardization stands on three:

  1. Customer needs and interests are becoming increasingly homogeneous worldwide.
  2. People around the world are willing to sacrifice preferences in product features, functions, design and the like for lower prices at high quality.
  3. Substantial economies of scale in production and marketing can be achieved through supplying global markets.

Three words. Homogeneous means alike. To sacrifice preferences means to give up what you would have liked (a feature, a design). Economies of scale means each unit costs less when you make more.

To remember it

S-P-S: Same needs, Price beats preference, Scale savings.

Explain it simply

Levitt's dream: everyone wants the same thing, everyone will take a cheaper standard version, and making one version for the world is much cheaper.

The three assumptions of global standardization

  1. Customer needs and interests are becoming increasingly homogeneous worldwide.
  2. People around the world are willing to sacrifice preferences in product features, functions, design and the like for lower prices at high quality.
  3. Substantial economies of scale in production and marketing can be achieved through supplying global markets.

List the three assumptions of the global standardization philosophy.

(1) Customer needs and interests are becoming increasingly homogeneous worldwide. (2) People will sacrifice preferences in features, functions and design for lower prices at high quality. (3) Substantial economies of scale in production and marketing from supplying global markets.

In the second assumption, what are people willing to sacrifice, and for what?

  1. Quality, for a lower price
  2. Preferences in features, functions and design, for lower prices at high quality
  3. A low price, for more features
  4. Local brands, for global brands

They give up preferences (features, functions, design), not quality. The price is lower and the quality stays high.

What does S-P-S stand for?

Same needs, Price beats preference, Scale savings: the three assumptions.

Whose philosophy rests on these three assumptions?

  1. Douglas and Wind's
  2. Levitt's
  3. Porter's
  4. Prof. Abu Qahf's own

Levitt's (1983). Douglas and Wind list the three assumptions in order to knock each one down.

His words in class
"The developing global standardization philosophy is actually built upon or based upon three major assumptions. The first assumption is this: customers' needs worldwide is becoming increasingly homogeneous. The second assumption is people are actually willing to sacrifice preference, function, design for lower prices. The third assumption is there is a substantial economies of scale will be enjoyed."
"For lower prices", or "for lower prices at high quality"?

In class he said only "for lower prices". The printed sheet says "lower prices at high quality", and a classmate's summary of the sheet keeps those words. Write the sheet's full wording.

Douglas and Wind, the authors of the printed sheet Prof. Abu Qahf handed out, knock down each of the three assumptions.

People are not becoming the same: diversity is even growing inside countries. People pay for quality and features, and a "cheap" position is easy to attack. And modern factories make small runs efficiently, while in many industries production is only a small part of the cost.

Needs are becoming the same? Little evidence

Global segments exist, but they are small and upscale. A segment is a group of customers with the same needs. The worldwide ones buy Rolex, Omega, Dior, YSL. Apart from a few products like Classic Coke and McDonald's, that is all.

Many firms sell local products.

  • Nestlé's Findus sells fish fingers in the UK and coq au vin in France.
  • Coca-Cola in Japan sells Georgia, a canned coffee.

Diversity is growing inside countries. The American VALS study found 9 value segments inside the USA alone. VALS is a survey that groups people by their Values And LifeStyles.

So people are not becoming alike, even inside one country.

Price does not beat everything, and scale is not everything

Assumption 2: price beats preferences

  1. No evidence that price-sensitive buyers are increasing. Interest in features, quality and service is growing. PIMS, a large database of business results, shows that quality drives success.
  2. A low-price position is vulnerable: to new technology, to cheaper rivals, to subsidies. And price buyers are not loyal.
  3. One standardized low price ends up overpriced in some countries and underpriced in others.

Assumption 3: big economies of scale

  1. Flexible factory automation makes small runs efficient. You no longer need one giant run of one product.
  2. Production is often a small part of total cost (cosmetics, detergents, drugs, banks). Distribution and brand management matter more (P&G, Avon).
  3. The idea is product-driven: it forgets the rest of the marketing mix, which is price, promotion and distribution.
Explain it simply

Douglas and Wind reply to Levitt: people are not becoming the same; people pay for quality and features, and a "cheap" positioning is easy to attack; modern factories can make many versions cheaply, and in many industries the real money is spent on distribution and marketing, not in the factory.

One pitfall for each assumption (at least)

  1. Same needs: little evidence. Global segments are small and upscale; firms sell local products (Findus, Georgia coffee); diversity is growing inside countries (VALS: 9 segments).
  2. Price beats preference: buyers value quality (PIMS); a low-price position is vulnerable and price buyers are not loyal; one price is too high in some countries and too low in others.
  3. Scale savings: flexible automation makes small runs efficient; production is often a small part of total cost; the idea forgets the rest of the marketing mix.

Give one pitfall for each assumption.

(1) Diversity is growing within countries (VALS: 9 segments). (2) Low-price positioning is vulnerable and price buyers are not loyal. (3) Flexible automation removes the need for one standard product; production is often a small share of cost.

Which assumption does each pitfall attack?

  • Nestlé's Findus sells fish fingers in the UK and coq au vin in France
  • Price buyers are not loyal
  • Flexible factory automation makes small runs efficient
  • The VALS study found 9 value segments in the USA
  • PIMS: quality drives success
  • Production is a small part of total cost in cosmetics and banks
  • One price is overpriced in some countries, underpriced in others

What do Douglas and Wind say about global segments?

  1. They do not exist
  2. They exist, but are small and upscale (Rolex, Omega, Dior)
  3. They cover most products
  4. They exist only in Japan

They exist but are small and upscale, apart from a few like Classic Coke and McDonald's.

What are VALS and PIMS, and which assumption does each one weaken?

VALS is a survey that groups people by values and lifestyles; it found 9 segments in the USA, which weakens "needs are becoming the same". PIMS is a large database of business results; it shows quality drives success, which weakens "price beats preference".

Standardization is a "winning" strategy only under certain conditions. The printed sheet Prof. Abu Qahf handed out gives three requisite conditions, which simply means the conditions that must exist.

There must be a global market segment. There must be synergies to gain from standardizing. And there must be an international communication and distribution infrastructure to reach the whole world. One of his exams asked for exactly these.

What "global standardization" asks for

"Global standardization" means selling the same product, in the same way, in every country: one design, one brand, one advert. It is cheaper than making a different version for each country. But it only pays off when three things are true.

1. The existence of a global market segment. A market segment is a group of customers with the same needs. A global segment is such a group spread over many countries. Examples: rich people who want the same luxury watch in Dubai, Paris and Cairo; people who travel a lot and want the same hotel everywhere; big companies that want the same supplier in every country they work in. The group must be big enough, loyal enough and reachable at a profit.

2. Potential synergies from standardization. Synergy means the whole is worth more than the parts (1 + 1 = 3). A good idea found in one country can be reused in the others: American washing-powder makers took a formula made for Europe's hard water back to America, and the Marlboro cowboy advert works in many countries. The company also learns from many markets at once, and one team of experts (on currencies, or on the risks of each country) can serve them all.

The roads to reach the whole world

3. The availability of an international communication and distribution infrastructure. Infrastructure means the basic services that everything else runs on.

You need worldwide "roads" for selling: advertising agencies that work in many countries (the sheet names Saatchi and Saatchi, and McCann Erickson), banks, market-research firms, shipping companies and freight forwarders, containers, satellites. In 1987, when the article was written, also telex and fax.

Without them you cannot advertise and deliver the same way everywhere.

To remember it

S-S-I: a Segment to sell to, Synergies to gain, Infrastructure to deliver.

In one line

One product for the whole world works only if the same kind of buyers exist across countries, sharing brings real gains, and the means to reach them all are there.

The three requisite conditions for global standardization

  1. The existence of a global market segment (big enough, loyal enough, reachable).
  2. Potential synergies from standardization (transfer of good ideas, experience, expertise).
  3. The availability of an international communication and distribution infrastructure.

His class version, to add in one line

In class: the core product must be capable of being globalized. (The full class version is under "More".)

List the three requisite conditions for global standardization.

A global market segment exists; synergies from standardization; an international communication and distribution infrastructure.

Which of these is a global market segment?

  1. All the people of one country
  2. International travellers who want the same hotel everywhere
  3. The employees of a multinational
  4. The customers of one corner shop

A global segment is a group of customers with the same needs, spread over many countries: luxury buyers, international travellers, multinational companies that want the same supplier everywhere.

A global segment is not enough by existing. Which three things must be true of it?

It must be big enough, loyal enough and reachable, so that serving it is profitable.

Which condition does each example belong to?

  • A hard-water washing formula from Europe reused in America
  • Advertising agencies that work in many countries
  • Buyers of the same luxury watch in Dubai, Paris and Cairo
  • Containers, satellites, shipping companies
  • The Marlboro cowboy advert works in many countries
  • Companies that want the same supplier in every country

What did he give in class as the three requisite conditions, and what should you write in the exam?

In class: the product must be standardized; the marketing program must be standardized; the company must have a global brand. In the exam write the printed sheet's three (segment, synergies, infrastructure), and add one line: "in class: the core product must be globalizable".
