What to write. Write the sheet's three conditions. This is the content of his printed sheet, and both the classmate's notes (which he says he reviewed against the recording) and another classmate's summary of the article give the same three. The recording may have garbled this part, or he may really have said it; that is not confirmed. You may add one line: "in class: the core product must be globalizable".

His words in the recording:

"However, there are requisite conditions. The requisite conditions for global standardization. The first condition is this: the product must be standardized. The second condition is the marketing program must be standardized. The third condition is the company must have a global brand."

Even when a company wants to sell the same product the same way everywhere, some things stop it. A constraint is something that limits what you can do.

The printed sheet Prof. Abu Qahf handed out lists four external constraints, which come from the countries and markets, and two internal ones, which come from the company itself.

Four external constraints

  1. Governmental and trade restrictions. Taxes on imported goods (tariffs), limits on how much you may bring in (quotas), rules that part of the product must be made in the country (local content), and rules on what products and adverts may say.
  2. Differences in the marketing infrastructure. The media and the shops differ. In some countries there were no TV adverts, or few people had a TV, or many could not read. In many countries people shop in small corner shops بقالة, not supermarkets, and the post or the roads are poor. So one campaign and one sales method cannot work everywhere.
  3. Interdependencies with resource markets. What materials and workers cost, and what is available, differs. Where wood is scarce, packaging is made from jute or sugar cane. Where workers are cheap, salespeople visiting shops can be cheaper than TV adverts. So the design, the packaging and the selling change.
  4. The nature of the competitive structure. If cheap local rivals exist, you may need a simpler, cheaper version of your product. "The existence of global competition does not necessarily imply a need for global standardization."
To remember it

External G-I-R-C: Government, Infrastructure, Resources, Competition.

Two internal constraints

  1. Existing international operations. What the company already has abroad: joint ventures, licences, exclusive distributors, and local brands it bought. They cannot be dropped overnight. Ironically, the longer and wider a firm's international history, the less standardization suits it.
  2. Local management motivation and attitudes. If head office imposes one plan on everyone, local managers answer "it won't work here, things are different". And it conflicts with local autonomy, the freedom that exists to make them work hard for their market.
To remember it

Internal O-M: Operations already in place, Managers' attitudes.

In one line

Laws, shops, media, materials and competitors differ from country to country, and the company's own partners and managers resist. So "one way everywhere" almost always has to bend.

External constraints (4)

  1. Governmental and trade restrictions.
  2. Differences in the marketing infrastructure.
  3. Interdependencies with resource markets.
  4. The nature of the competitive structure.

Internal constraints (2)

  1. Existing international operations.
  2. Local management motivation and attitudes.

His class version, in two lines

Internal: operational constraints from the firm itself, and lack of enthusiasm among local management.

External: government-imposed trade restrictions, and poor infrastructure or workers in the host country.

Name the four external and the two internal constraints.

External: government and trade restrictions; marketing infrastructure; resource markets; competitive structure. Internal: existing international operations; local management motivation and attitudes.

External or internal constraint?

  • Tariffs, quotas and local-content rules
  • Local managers say "it won't work here, things are different"
  • People shop in small corner shops, not supermarkets
  • An exclusive distributor already under contract
  • Cheap local rivals
  • Wood is scarce, so packaging is made from jute
  • A local brand the company bought years ago

What does the sheet say about a firm with a long and wide international history?

  1. Standardization suits it best
  2. Ironically, standardization suits it less
  3. It has no constraints
  4. It must sell its local brands

The longer and wider its history abroad, the more partners, licences, distributors and local brands it already has, and these cannot be changed quickly.

Does global competition mean a company must standardize?

No. "The existence of global competition does not necessarily imply a need for global standardization." Low-cost local rivals may call for stripped-down models or lower prices.

Give his short class version of the constraints.

Internal: operational constraints from the firm itself; lack of enthusiasm among local management. External: government-imposed trade restrictions; poor infrastructure or workers in the host country.

The sheet's examples for the four external constraints

Governmental and trade restrictions. Tariffs, quotas, local-content rules (a set share of the product must be made locally), product and advertising regulation (Japanese trade-body standards; strict advertising rules in Germany and Switzerland), cartels (European steel, Swiss chocolate), and grey markets. A cartel is a group of companies that agree prices among themselves. A grey market is the firm's own goods, bought cheaply in one country and resold by unofficial sellers in another, below its price: Wilkinson razor blades were undercut this way in India.

Differences in the marketing infrastructure. At the time of the article (1987): no TV adverts in Scandinavia, few TVs in Nigeria or Indonesia, and illiteracy limits print. Mom-and-Pop shops, not supermarkets: over 75% of retail sales went through small shops even in Japan, Italy and Spain. Poor mail (Brazil, Italy), poor roads.

Interdependencies with resource markets. The cost and availability of materials and labour change the design and the packaging: jute or sugar cane in place of wood fibre; plastic against paper in Europe; cheap labour favours personal selling over mass media.

The nature of the competitive structure. Low-cost local rivals call for stripped-down models or lower prices.

The sheet's examples for the two internal constraints

Existing international operations. Joint ventures, licences, exclusive distributors and acquired local brands (P&G owns the British brand Domestos) cannot be changed quickly.

Local management motivation and attitudes. A strategy "imposed" by headquarters meets "it won't work here, things are different", and conflicts with local autonomy, which exists to encourage local entrepreneurship.

No. A global perspective means planning for markets worldwide, not country by country. It does not mean global products and brands everywhere.

The options form a continuum ("continuum means scale", Prof. Abu Qahf said) from pure standardization to pure differentiation. Most real choices fall in the hybrid middle. In class he drew it as three options: standardization, a cluster of countries, differentiation.

A scale with two ends and a wide middle

Differentiation is the opposite of standardization: each country gets its own product and its own marketing. Hybrid means mixed.

The first chart of the printed sheet shows the scale. Each row is one element of the marketing mix. A company can place each element at a different point:

  • Pure standardization: every element is the same worldwide. A global strategy.
  • Pure differentiation: every element is adapted for each country.
  • A mixed (hybrid) strategy: some elements standardized, some adapted, some shared by a cluster of countries.

The class version: three options

In class he turned the scale into three options. A cluster is a group of similar countries treated as one.

Option I: standardization (global strategy)

Product: same. Price: same. Packaging: same. Advertising: one strategy worldwide.

Option II: a cluster of countries (hybrid)

Product: same within the cluster. Price: different. Packaging: same. Advertising: one strategy for each cluster.

Option III: differentiation (multidomestic)

Product: different. Price: different. Packaging: different. Advertising: different for each country.

Multidomestic means the company treats each country as a separate home market.

The continuum

"Continuum means scale": from pure standardization to pure differentiation, with most options in the hybrid middle. A global perspective means planning for markets worldwide, not global products everywhere.

His three options

  1. Standardization (global strategy): the same product, price, packaging, and one advertising strategy worldwide.
  2. Cluster of countries (hybrid): the same product within the cluster, different prices, the same packaging, one advertising strategy per cluster.
  3. Differentiation (multidomestic): everything adapted for each country.

What are the three positions on the continuum?

Pure standardization, mixed (hybrid), pure differentiation.

Which of his three options is it?

  • One advertising strategy worldwide
  • The same product within a group of countries, at different prices
  • Multidomestic
  • A different product and a different advert for each country
  • One advertising strategy per cluster
  • The same price everywhere

What does a "global perspective" mean in the printed sheet?

  1. Selling global products and brands everywhere
  2. Planning for markets worldwide, not country by country
  3. Adapting everything to each country
  4. Entering every country at once

Planning for markets worldwide. It does not mean global products and brands everywhere.

What did he say "continuum" means, and where do most options fall on it?

"Continuum means scale." Most options fall in the hybrid middle, between pure standardization and pure differentiation.

Most companies are hybrids. They standardize some things and adapt others: by element of the marketing mix, by region, or by customer segment.

The printed sheet Prof. Abu Qahf handed out ends with two tools. A chart that decides element by element whether to be global. And a checklist of four questions: a global segment? synergies? no external constraints? no internal constraints? Only four times "yes" means: consider global.

Ways to be in the middle

  • Standardize some mix elements, adapt others. Apple sold the same product line worldwide, but with different positioning, promotion and distribution in each country.
  • By region or cluster of countries. Ford built separate models for Europe (Fiesta, Granada, Taurus).
  • By customer segment. Revlon's Charlie line for working women worldwide; Almay for sensitive skin.
  • Combinations. Pampers: the same product, regional promotion. Kellogg's Corn Flakes: standard themes in Latin America and the Far East, country-specific ones in Europe. Virginia Slims: "You've Come a Long Way Baby" became "Oh, So Slim and Sexy" in Japan.
  • Plus unique local lines. White tooth powder for India (P&G, Colgate); bar soaps for developing countries.

The marketing mix is the set of things a company decides about a product: the product itself, its price, its promotion and its distribution.

Decide element by element, then ask four questions

The second chart of the sheet takes the elements one by one. For each, the company decides: global, or non-global?

And its last table is a checklist of four questions:

  1. Is there a global market segment for your product?
  2. Are there synergies associated with a global strategy?
  3. Are there no external constraints or government regulations?
  4. Are there no internal constraints?

One "no" means standardization is not appropriate. Yes to all four: consider global.

The conclusion of the article. Success comes from carefully analysing the forces toward globalization, the obstacles, and the company's own strengths and weaknesses, and then choosing where its differential advantage lies.

Hybrid strategies

  1. Standardize some mix elements, adapt others (Apple).
  2. By region or cluster (Ford in Europe).
  3. By customer segment (Revlon's Charlie).
  4. Combinations (Pampers, Kellogg's, Virginia Slims), plus unique local lines.

The checklist of four questions

  1. A global market segment?
  2. Synergies?
  3. No external constraints?
  4. No internal constraints?

Yes to all four: consider global. Any no: standardization is not appropriate.

What are the four checklist questions at the end of the sheet?

Global segment? Synergies? No external constraints? No internal constraints? Yes to all four: consider global.

Give one example of a hybrid strategy.

Apple: the same product, local promotion and distribution. Or Ford's separate models for Europe, Revlon's Charlie line, Pampers with regional promotion.

A company answers yes to three of the four checklist questions and no to "are there no internal constraints?". What does the sheet say?

  1. Go global: three out of four is enough
  2. Standardization is not appropriate
  3. Leave the foreign markets
  4. Standardize the product only

Only "yes" to all four means "consider global". Any "no" means standardization is not appropriate.

Ford built separate models for Europe. Which kind of hybrid is this?

  1. Standardizing some mix elements
  2. Standardizing by region or cluster of countries
  3. Standardizing by customer segment
  4. Pure differentiation

By region or cluster of countries: separate models (Fiesta, Granada, Taurus) for Europe as one group.

Which elements does the second chart decide one by one?

Positioning, product, brand name, packaging, pricing, advertising and P.R., customer and trade promotion, distribution. Each is decided as global or non-global.

Optional. Open what you want.

A modern example of a hybrid

Netflix runs one global platform and brand, but buys and produces local shows and dubs them for each country. That is a standardized product system with differentiated content and promotion: a hybrid on the first chart.

To standardize means to do the same thing in every country: the same product, the same price policy, the same advertising, the same way of distributing.

Prof. Abu Qahf says a global firm is required to standardize all its procedures. But six factors decide how far it can go: the type of product, how similar the markets are, the media, government restrictions, infrastructure services, and the political relationship between the countries.

The list is not closed. He said these six come "in addition to many other" factors.

Standardize everything, as far as the factors allow

A global firm is required to standardize all its procedures, like the marketing mix, among other things. He set the two sides against each other: a standardized or an unstandardized plan, product, distribution, policy.

Marketing mix

Here it means "product, price, promotion, distribution".

Other functions can be standardized too, such as human resources management and public relations.

But some factors govern the degree of standardization of the marketing program. To govern here means to decide how far the firm can go. The next two steps give his six.

The product, the markets, the media

1. Type of product. Can it be standardized or not? Look at the core, the first of the three levels of a product (core, formal, augmented). If the core can be standardized, "go global. If it is not, stop. You are required to produce product for each country." He kept saying "convenience product" here. The next lesson explains it.

2. Degree of heterogeneity or homogeneity of markets. Heterogeneous markets are different from each other. In them it is impossible to standardize. Homogeneous markets are similar. In them you can. His example of a homogeneous market: the Arab world.

3. Media characteristics. Marketing needs media. Does television cover the whole country, in one language?

  • If television cannot cover the whole country or region, you deal with each country.
  • With several languages, television in one language is not enough. You need versions: one in Arabic, one in the regional language, a third in French.
  • Culture can stop it too. Culture means "local habits, domestic habits, domestic customs, the norms".
His example

A Thai advert for a motor car cannot be shown in Egypt. It is "out of our ethics", "completely against our religion". So a new advert is made for the Arab culture.

The government, the infrastructure, the neighbours

4. Government restrictions. The government may step into business "in order to protect its national companies":

  • a price ceiling: a highest price the company is allowed to charge;
  • a production quota: a limit on how much the company may produce. A quota stops mass production, and so it stops the economies of scale of a standard product;
  • restrictions on imports and exports.

Economies of scale means the cost of each unit falls when you produce very large quantities.

5. Availability of marketing infrastructure services. Communication and transport, highways, telecom, television and radio, newspapers with wide coverage, advertising agencies. If they are not available, the company either does not invest, or establishes its own, which means "a lot of money ... which the company cannot afford".

6. Type of political relationship between the countries of a region. "Is it hostile or friendly?" Using Egypt as a production base to serve its neighbours with the same product and the same marketing mix depends on Egypt's relations with them.

The six factors that govern the degree of standardization

  1. Type of product (can the core be standardized?).
  2. Heterogeneity or homogeneity of markets (the Arab world is homogeneous).
  3. Media characteristics (coverage, language, culture: the Thai car advert).
  4. Government restrictions (price ceiling, quota, limits on imports and exports).
  5. Availability of infrastructure services.
  6. Type of political relationship (hostile or friendly).

The list is not closed: "in addition to many other" factors.

To remember it

P-M-M-G-I-P: "Please Make More Global Investment Plans". Product, Markets, Media, Government, Infrastructure, Political relationship.

Give the six factors that govern the degree of standardization of the marketing program.

Type of product; heterogeneity or homogeneity of markets; media characteristics; government restrictions; infrastructure services; type of political relationship.

Does each situation help the firm to standardize, or block it?

  • The core of the product can be the same everywhere
  • The markets are heterogeneous
  • The markets are homogeneous
  • The government sets a production quota
  • The country speaks several languages
  • Television covers the whole region in one language
  • Hostile relations between the countries of the region

A Thai advert for a motor car cannot be shown in Egypt, so a new advert is made for the Arab culture. Which factor is this?

  1. Type of product
  2. Media characteristics
  3. Government restrictions
  4. Type of political relationship

Media characteristics. Culture is part of this factor, together with coverage and language. The advert is "out of our ethics".

Why does a production quota work against a standardized product?

A quota limits how much the company may produce. That stops mass production, and so it stops the economies of scale that a standard product is meant to give.

What can a company do when the marketing infrastructure services are not available?

Either it does not invest, or it establishes its own services, which means "a lot of money ... which the company cannot afford".

How his six relate to the constraints on his printed sheet

His printed sheet "The Myth of Globalization" lists external constraints on standardization. Three of his six are those constraints in other words:

  • government restrictions = the sheet's government and trade restrictions;
  • media, and infrastructure services = the sheet's differences in the marketing infrastructure.

New in his list: type of product, homogeneity of markets, political relationship.

If the question is "the factors that govern the degree of standardization", write his six.

When Prof. Abu Qahf explained the first factor, the type of product, he kept saying "convenience product". It is a cheap, everyday product that people buy often, quickly and with little thought: a soft drink, bread, soap.

Such products are often easy to standardize. But he warned against making it a rule: "Somebody may argue that all convenient products can be standardized. I would say no."

Easy to buy, and no loyalty at all

Convenience product

"Goods and services that is easy to buy, without actually walking around or spending time or spending more money ... There is no loyalty at all. If you are asking for a bottle of Pepsi ... there is a Coca-Cola. Take a Coca-Cola."

In plain words: a cheap, everyday product that people buy often, quickly and with little thought, from the nearest shop. Soft drinks, bread, soap, toothpaste, razor blades. People do not compare brands for long.

That is why his favourite examples of global products are convenience products: Coca-Cola, Pepsi, pens, razor blades. The need, and the way the product is bought, are the same almost everywhere. So they are often easy to standardize.

"I would say no"

"Somebody may argue that all convenient products can be standardized. I would say no."

Many convenience products cannot be standardized. And some need minor alterations that do not touch the core, as McDonald's and Cadbury did in Egypt.

Do not mix them up

A car or a house is the opposite of a convenience product. Buyers compare, ask and negotiate. That is his story of buying a Pepsi and buying a Kia.

Convenience product

Goods and services that are easy to buy, without walking around, spending time or spending more money. "There is no loyalty at all."

Examples: Coca-Cola, Pepsi, pens, razor blades, bread, soap, toothpaste.

His warning

Not all convenience products can be standardized. Some need minor alterations that do not touch the core (McDonald's and Cadbury in Egypt).

What is a convenience product, in his words?

Goods and services that are easy to buy, without walking around, spending time or spending more money. "There is no loyalty at all": if there is no Pepsi, you take a Coca-Cola.

"All convenience products can be standardized." What does he say?

  1. Yes, always
  2. "I would say no"
  3. Yes, if the price is low
  4. Only in homogeneous markets

No. Many cannot, and some need minor alterations that do not touch the core, as McDonald's and Cadbury did in Egypt.

Is it a convenience product?

  • A bottle of Pepsi
  • A Kia car
  • Razor blades
  • A house
  • Toothpaste
  • Bread

Why are convenience products often easy to standardize?

The need, and the way the product is bought, are the same almost everywhere.

Where the term comes from

In marketing textbooks the convenience product is one of the four classes of consumer products: convenience, shopping, specialty and unsought. A car or a house is a shopping or a specialty product.

Prof. Abu Qahf opened the fifth lecture with three short ethics scenarios from a printed sheet. The class worked in groups. Each group read one scenario, one member presented the group's answer, and then he gave his own view.

This lesson is the first scenario: a bribe at a port. His answer is three words: "Bribe is bribe." Refuse, advise the captain, and tell your boss officially.

The "tip" at the port

It is your first day as distribution manager in a foreign port. A ship's captain makes you an offer: skip the official shipping fee of 1,000 dollars, and split the money with you.

The question: do you take half and keep quiet, refuse, or report him?

What the class said

  1. Take the 500 dollars and keep quiet. Some might, "because my salary is lower than anybody can accept".
  2. Refuse, and report to your boss.
  3. A student's idea: if it is the captain's first visit to this port, refuse, warn him, and do not report.

Several groups chose the third option.

"Bribe is bribe"

He did not accept the soft option. His answer has three parts, all at the same time:

  1. Refuse.
  2. Advise the captain.
  3. Tell your boss officially, so the ship owner learns what his captain does. A spoken report is enough. No written report is needed.

Why report? To protect the whole economy and the ship owner, and to give the seaport an ethical image.

Why not forgive him quietly? It is a weak answer. He may try it again, here or in another port, and word of mouth spreads.

"Bribe is bribe ... Such type of events must be actually dealt quite hardly ... tell your boss as well at the same time ... Just to protect the whole economy in the future, to protect the ship owner in the future, and also to establish an ethical image about this seaport."

His answer to the bribe

"Bribe is bribe."

  1. Refuse.
  2. Advise the captain.
  3. Tell your boss officially. A spoken report is enough.

Why

To protect the whole economy and the ship owner, and to give the seaport an ethical image. Forgiving quietly is weak: he may try again, and word of mouth spreads.

The captain offers to split the fee. What was his answer, and why?

"Bribe is bribe": refuse, advise the captain, and tell your boss officially (a spoken report is enough), to protect the economy and the ship owner and give the port an ethical image.

Several groups said: if it is the captain's first visit, refuse, warn him, and do not report. What did he think of that?

  1. It is the best answer
  2. It is a weak answer: he may try again, here or in another port
  3. It is right only if the amount is small
  4. He gave no opinion

Weak. The captain may try it again, here or in another port, and word of mouth spreads. So you tell your boss officially as well.

Does the report to your boss have to be written?

No. A spoken report is enough. What matters is that it is official, so the ship owner learns what his captain does.

How did the class work on the three scenarios?

In groups. Each group read one scenario, one member presented the group's answer, and then he gave his own view.

The printed sheet with the three scenarios

The second scenario is a Japanese textile plant in a developing country, where workers complain of abuse. Prof. Abu Qahf said the problem is clear. What he wants in the answer is the how: "Easy to answer what, and easy to answer why, but it is not easy to answer how."

The scenario is also the classic charge against multinationals: an exploitative relationship with the developing host country.

The Japanese textile plant

You are the president of a Japanese textile maker. It moved production to a developing country to save labour costs.

  • Workers complain of verbal and physical abuse, and of poor safety.
  • The plant managers deny it.
  • A local labour group says workers were threatened with jail and harm.

The questions: do you improve conditions or shut the plant? How does it affect your relations with officials, and your future there?

What the class said

One group: send an independent audit team, protect the workers, suspend the accused supervisor, reject the shutdown and upgrade safety, agree an ethical standard with the local government, protect the brand.

Another student: collect information first.

He wants the "how"

He said the complaint is clear "even without collecting information". There are three problems:

  1. Low pay: no fair compensation.
  2. A supervisor who "dehumanizes" people.
  3. Unhealthy working conditions.
"Easy to answer in few words ... but this is not what is required ... Easy to answer what, and easy to answer why, but it is not easy to answer how ... How is very important."

So the answer must say how:

  • Retrain the supervisor, or replace him, even for a while.
  • Improve lighting, noise, safety and the sanitary system.
  • Build a fair salary system and an incentive system.
  • Develop industrial relations (the relations between the company and its workers).
  • Tell workers, supervisors and stakeholders that there is a mutual interest, not an exploitative relationship.

The classic charge against multinationals

This scenario is the classic charge against multinationals: an exploitative relationship with the developing host country. Bad conditions, low pay, abuse. It belongs to the advantages and disadvantages of foreign direct investment, which he discussed later in the course.

He was careful about the other side. Going abroad for cheap labour and profit is a legitimate goal, "the main driving force". And the host country gains jobs and gets its needs met.

But:

"Never ever assume that any foreign investor, or even national investor, is going to behave as an ideal citizen."

The three problems

Low pay; a supervisor who "dehumanizes" people; unhealthy working conditions.

The how

  1. Retrain or replace the supervisor.
  2. Improve lighting, noise, safety and sanitation.
  3. A fair salary system and an incentive system.
  4. Better industrial relations.
  5. The message of mutual interest, not exploitation.

His two sentences

"Easy to answer what, and easy to answer why, but it is not easy to answer how."

"Never ever assume that any foreign investor, or even national investor, is going to behave as an ideal citizen."

In the textile plant scenario, what did he say the answer must show?

The how, not only the what: retrain or replace the supervisor; improve lighting, noise, safety and sanitation; a fair salary and incentive system; better industrial relations; and the message of mutual interest, not exploitation.

Which three problems did he see in the complaint, "even without collecting information"?

Low pay (no fair compensation); a supervisor who "dehumanizes" people; unhealthy working conditions.

Is going abroad for cheap labour and profit wrong in itself, according to him?

  1. Yes, it is always exploitation
  2. No, it is a legitimate goal, "the main driving force"; but do not expect an "ideal citizen"
  3. Only if the host country is rich
  4. He did not say

It is a legitimate goal, and the host gains jobs and gets its needs met. But no investor, foreign or national, should be expected to behave as an ideal citizen.

What is "the classic charge against multinationals" that this scenario shows?

An exploitative relationship with the developing host country: bad conditions, low pay, abuse.

Links to the rest of the course

These links are not his words. They are connections worth noticing.

  • Justice in the working climate ("no justice, no satisfaction; no satisfaction, no productivity") and creative human resources management, two pillars of the World Class Organization, are this scenario's answer.
  • The Nike case, asked in a past exam, shows what sweatshops cost a brand.

The third scenario puts you in the chair of a newly elected president who wants to open the country to trade. Prof. Abu Qahf's answer: "pave the way" before the decision is issued, and step back if the public still refuses.

For a foreign investor this is "golden information": a government that cannot convince its own people is a reason not to enter the country.

The new president

You are the newly elected president of a developing country that used to avoid imports. You want to open trade.

The questions: how do you convince the public? And do you go ahead if they resist?

What the class said

  • Show the benefits and the lower prices of imports.
  • Involve community influencers.
  • One student suggested heavier taxes on local goods. He rejected it: "this is benefiting the foreign markets".

"Pave the way"

Before the decree is issued (a decree is an official order of the president), others explain and sell the idea:

  • academics and universities;
  • conferences and public debates;
  • journalists;
  • public opinion leaders and non-profit associations.

If the public still refuses, step back. You keep your dignity and your integrity.

If they accept, go ahead, and they will be grateful.

"Think big ... act as a president." He compared it with President Sadat's opening of the Egyptian economy.

"Golden information for any foreign investor"

Why does a company care about this? Because it tells the investor how safe the country is.

  • A government that cannot convince its people is ineffective, and is threatened by social turmoil. That is a reason not to enter.
  • Strong public acceptance of the leadership encourages foreign firms to come.

This is political risk again.

"If the government is not quite able to govern the country, and to get the public convinced with its policies ... this is actually represent a threat for any company to decide to enter this country as an investor, and vice versa."

How to answer such questions

He complained that the answers read like a school reading exercise, copying lines from the text. His word was "Think": a master's answer should differ from an undergraduate's.

His answer

  1. "Pave the way" before the decree: academics, conferences and debates, journalists, opinion leaders, non-profit associations.
  2. If the public refuses, step back: you keep your dignity and integrity.
  3. If they accept, go ahead.

The lesson for an investor

Whether a government can convince its people is "golden information". If it cannot, it is ineffective and risks social turmoil: a reason not to enter.

How to answer

"Think." Do not copy lines from the text. A master's answer should differ from an undergraduate's.

Why does a foreign investor care whether a president can convince the public?

It is "golden information": a government that cannot convince its people is ineffective and risks social turmoil, a reason not to enter.

Who "paves the way" before the decree is issued?

Academics and universities, conferences and public debates, journalists, public opinion leaders and non-profit associations. They explain and sell the idea.

The way has been paved, and the public still refuses. What should the president do?

  1. Issue the decree anyway
  2. Put heavier taxes on local goods
  3. Step back, and keep his dignity and integrity
  4. Resign

Step back. He rejected heavier taxes on local goods, because that benefits the foreign markets.

What was his complaint about the way students answered the scenarios?

The answers read like a school reading exercise, copying lines from the text. "Think": a master's answer should differ from an undergraduate's.

Prof. Abu Qahf went back to the management team of a global firm. It still pursues its three objectives, but it is made of four kinds of manager: the business manager, the country manager, the functional manager and the corporate manager.

This is the answer of the best-known paper on the question: "there is no such thing as a universal global manager". The job is too big for one person.

"There is no such thing as a universal global manager"

The management team of a global firm still pursues the three objectives he gave at the start of the course ("we took them before"): search the world for opportunities, keep a presence in the key markets, and look for similarities among countries.

But who is "the global manager"? The best-known paper on the question is by Christopher Bartlett, of Harvard, and Sumantra Ghoshal: "What Is a Global Manager?", Harvard Business Review, 1992.

Its answer: "there is no such thing as a universal global manager". The job is too big for one person. So the firm needs four kinds of manager, and each kind has three jobs.

Four managers, three jobs each

1. The business manager: strategist, architect, coordinator. He looks at the whole world and builds one shared strategy, so the firm makes and sells the same way wherever it can.

2. The country manager: sensor, builder, contributor. He knows one country well. He senses what local customers and governments want, and adapts the firm's work to fit.

3. The functional manager: scanner, cross-pollinator, champion. He is an expert in one area (finance, people, information). He finds a good idea in one country and spreads it to the others. Examples: the global marketing, production and operations, human resources and finance managers.

4. The corporate (top) manager: leader, talent scout, developer. He leads the other three, settles their disagreements, and finds and grows the managers of the future.

Cross-pollinator

Someone who carries a good idea from one place to another, as a bee carries pollen between flowers. His own explanation: "leading by edge ... by advantage".

To remember it

B-C-F-C. The Business manager pulls toward "the same everywhere". The Country manager pulls toward "change it for my market". The Functional manager carries ideas between them. The Corporate manager decides where the line falls. It is the "standardize or adapt" choice, given to people.

The four roles (Bartlett and Ghoshal, 1992)

  1. Business manager: strategist, architect, coordinator.
  2. Country manager: sensor, builder, contributor.
  3. Functional manager: scanner, cross-pollinator, champion.
  4. Corporate manager: leader, talent scout, developer.

The sentence

"There is no such thing as a universal global manager."

Give the four roles of the global manager, and who wrote them.

Business, country, functional and corporate manager. Bartlett and Ghoshal, "What Is a Global Manager?", 1992.

"Sensor, builder, contributor" are the three jobs of:

  1. The business manager
  2. The country manager
  3. The functional manager
  4. The corporate manager

The country manager. He senses what local customers and governments want, and adapts the firm's work to fit.

Which manager is the "cross-pollinator", and what does it mean?

  1. The corporate manager: he hires talent
  2. The country manager: he knows local customers
  3. The functional manager: he spreads a good idea from one country to the others
  4. The business manager: he builds the strategy

The functional manager. He finds a good idea in one country and spreads it to the others. His explanation: "leading by edge ... by advantage".

What are the three jobs of the business manager, and what does he stand for?

Strategist, architect, coordinator. He looks at the whole world and builds one shared strategy, so the firm makes and sells the same way wherever it can.

Why four managers and not one?

"There is no such thing as a universal global manager." The job is too big for one person.

Another version you may meet: one person with seven qualities

The revision material passed on from earlier classes describes "the successful global manager" as one person with 7 qualities: a global mindset, long-term vision, negotiation skills, understanding each culture, emotional intelligence, motivating others, and accepting foreign assignments.

The paper looks from the opposite angle: no single person has it all, so build a team.

After the four roles, Prof. Abu Qahf gave his own conclusion: the global manager is the corporate manager. He is a leader, a talent scout and a developer, and those three jobs include the characteristics of the other three managers.

He also said why there is no single ideal global manager, and what was wrong with most of the reports the class wrote on this question.

The global manager is the corporate manager

"The global manager is actually representing the corporate manager. He's a leader, he's a talent scout, and he's a developer."

Those three jobs include the characteristics of the other three managers.

A talent scout is someone who looks for gifted people.

Why there is no single ideal global manager

  • Nobody can guarantee that one manager will do all of it without weaknesses.
  • An unhealthy working climate stops anyone from doing it.

And all four roles deal with people.

What was wrong with the reports

The class had written an assignment on the question "who is the global manager?". His feedback:

  • Most reports did not answer the question clearly.
  • One listed responsibilities that "any manager" has: strategic planning, team management, decision making, performance evaluation, risk management.
  • Choose the right sources: references and periodicals. Not everything on the internet is right.
  • Do not let artificial intelligence do the thinking: "keep yourself the brain".

He covered the paper up to the end of the table of the four roles. The later views on the global manager, from 2003 onward, were not taught.

His conclusion

The global manager is the corporate manager: leader, talent scout, developer. These three jobs include the characteristics of the other three managers.

Why no single ideal global manager

Nobody does all of it without weaknesses, and an unhealthy working climate stops anyone from doing it.

In his view, which of the four roles is "the global manager"? Give its three jobs.

The corporate manager: leader, talent scout, developer. Those three jobs include the characteristics of the other three managers.

Why is there no single ideal global manager?

Nobody can guarantee that one manager will do all of it without weaknesses, and an unhealthy working climate stops anyone from doing it.

One report answered "who is the global manager?" with: strategic planning, team management, decision making, performance evaluation, risk management. What was his criticism?

  1. The list was too short
  2. These are responsibilities that "any manager" has
  3. The list was copied from the textbook
  4. It had no examples

They describe any manager, so they do not answer who the global manager is.

What two pieces of advice did he give about writing reports?

Choose the right sources (references and periodicals), because not everything on the internet is right. And do not let artificial intelligence do the thinking: "keep yourself the brain".

Learn, Evaluate (be aware), Able to decide, Develop, Encourage, Remunerate, Sustain, Hear, Invest in people, Punish when required.

Which of the three jobs does each letter belong to?

  • Learn
  • Evaluate

Some handwritten notes of the class have "Educate" for the first E, "Aware" for A and "Health" for H. The recording makes the letters clearer: "educate" belongs to L, A is "able to decide", and H is "hear". Write the version of this lesson.

How it fits his other lists

It is not in the revision material. It fits his earlier lists: "creative human resources management" and "justice in the working climate" in the World Class Organization, and the corporate manager's jobs of talent scout and developer.

A company that wants to do business in another country has to choose a form to go in. It can simply sell there. It can sign a contract with a local company. Or it can own a business there.

Prof. Abdel Salam Abu Qahf, who teaches this course, puts every possible form on one drawing of his own: 17 ways, called modes of entry, in 3 groups, called options.

This lesson gives you the whole map. The next lessons walk through it piece by piece.

Three options: sell, sign, or own

A mode of entry طريقة الدخول للأسواق الأجنبية is the form a company uses to get into a foreign market. Any company is free to choose among three big options.

Option I: Commercial

Also called trading. His printed sheet says "Export".

You only sell to that country. Somebody else, or the internet, carries your product to the customer.

1 Trading houses2 Agent3 Distributor4 International exhibition5 E-commerce16 Marketing branch17 Assembly plant

Option II: Contracting

His printed sheet says "No ownership".

You sign a contract with a company there. It does the work. You own nothing, or only a share.

6 Licensing7 Franchising8 Management and manufacturing contracts9 Turnkey project10 International subcontracting11 Strategic alliance12 Joint venture

Option III: Equity

His printed sheet says "Ownership". Equity means an ownership share.

You own the business in that country.

13 Wholly owned subsidiary14 Merger15 Acquisition

That makes 17 modes. The numbers are his: he wrote them on the board, and you will see in lesson 3 why they run in this order.

The colours stay the same in all 11 lessons: green for selling, purple for contracts, red for owning. A mode with a ring around it is one where the company puts its own money into the country. Lesson 3 explains that too.

To count them

5 ways to sell (1 to 5), then 6 contracts (6 to 11), then 6 ways to put your own money in (12 to 17). 5 + 6 + 6 = 17.

The same thing, the way he draws it

This is his model. You only need to recognise it now. The next step builds it one stroke at a time, which is how you will learn to draw it.

Three things to notice:

  • Owning is drawn in the middle, between selling on the left and contracts on the right. The middle is where the money, the risk and the profit are highest.
  • Each side box has a dashed line. Under it sit the modes that go deeper than the rest of their box: the marketing branch and the assembly plant on the left, the joint venture on the right.
  • There is one extra shape, the free-zone project. He leaves it out of the course, so it has no number.

The three names of this topic

He uses three names for the same thing: modes of entry, strategies of entry, and degrees of international commitment (he also says involvement, or engagement).

Commitment means how much of its money and people the company ties to that market: very little if it only ships goods there, a lot if it owns a factory there.

The three options

  1. Option I: Commercial (trading, export). The company only sells.
  2. Option II: Contracting (no ownership). The company signs a contract.
  3. Option III: Equity (ownership). The company owns.

The 17 modes, in his order

1 Trading houses. 2 Agent. 3 Distributor. 4 International exhibition. 5 E-commerce.

6 Licensing. 7 Franchising. 8 Management and manufacturing contracts. 9 Turnkey investment project. 10 International subcontracting. 11 Strategic alliance.

12 Joint venture. 13 Wholly owned subsidiary. 14 Merger. 15 Acquisition. 16 Marketing branch. 17 Assembly plant.

Draw it stroke by stroke

His past exams ask for this drawing "by drawing only". Tap through the eight strokes, then try it on paper.

Give the three names he uses for this topic.

Modes of entry into foreign markets. Strategies of entry. Degrees of international commitment (or involvement, or engagement).

Name the three options, and say in one word what the company does in each.

Option I, commercial (trading, export): it sells. Option II, contracting (no ownership): it signs a contract. Option III, equity (ownership): it owns.

In which box of his drawing does each mode sit?

  • Trading houses
  • Agent
  • Distributor

  • E-commerce
  • Marketing branch
  • Assembly plant

  • Management and manufacturing contracts

How many modes are in his model?

  1. 7, like most textbooks
  2. 15, because the marketing branch and the assembly plant are not counted
  3. 17, not counting the free-zone project
  4. 18, with the free-zone project

17. The free-zone project is on the drawing but he leaves it out of the course. Most textbooks list only five to seven modes.

What does "commitment" mean in "degrees of international commitment"?

How much of its money and people the company ties to the foreign market. Shipping goods there is a low commitment. Owning a factory there is a high one.

Optional. Open what you want.

Why he is proud of this drawing

He developed it himself, so it is an Egyptian model, and it has been taught in universities abroad. Most textbooks list only five to seven modes. His has 17, and it ties them to information, control, money, risk, profit and government incentives, all in one picture.

Why the free-zone project has no number

A free zone is an area inside a country with its own special rules. He calls it "a state within a state". The course deals only with investment inside the country itself, which he calls "inland", so he leaves the free-zone project out.

If a question still asks about it: older revision material for this course counts a company that produces and sells inside a free zone as direct investment.

His printed sheet and the whiteboard

Prof. Abu Qahf's drawing of the 17 modes is more than a list. Its arrows carry one message: the deeper a company goes into a foreign market, the more it learns, the more it controls, the more money it needs, the more it risks, and the more it can earn.

Two more arrows, on top, say that governments push companies with incentives. He calls them "pressures", which is the word to watch.

Think of a shop in a city you do not know

You can send your goods to a trader there. It is cheap and safe, but you learn nothing about the customers and you cannot set the price.

Or you can rent and run your own shop there. It is costly and risky, but you meet every customer, you decide everything, and all the profit is yours.

The drawing says the same about countries. Each arrow is one part of that trade-off.

1. The two arrows on top: government "pressures"

The host country is the country the company enters. The home country, also called the parent country, is the country the company comes from.

"Pressures" here does not mean political pressure. It means the incentives and privileges that governments offer. Every host government offers incentives to attract foreign investors. Home governments encourage their own companies to invest abroad.

2. The arrow on the left: market information

The deeper the company goes in, the more information it collects, in amount and in kind. A trading house tells you very little. An agent tells you about the market, the competitors and the prices.

3. The arrow on the right: control of the market

The deeper the company goes in, the more freedom it has to decide how many units to produce, how many to sell, and at what price.

4. The double arrow underneath: investment, risk and profit

All three rise together as the company moves toward the middle of the drawing, where owning sits. He calls the middle the "hot area".

ModeWhat the company pays
Trading houseNothing.
AgentA little: training the agent (even abroad), decorating the showroom, a promotion plan.
ExhibitionOnly the fees.
E-commerceOnly the internet fees.
Direct entryThe money needed jumps, and so do the profit and the risk.

5. The small arrows from one mode to the next

On his printed sheet, small arrows link each mode to the next one. They show a company moving on to the next step when everything stays stable. Lesson 4 comes back to this.

One sentence

The higher the commitment, the more information, the more control, the more money needed, the more risk, and the more profit.

The arrows

  1. On top, two arrows: host government pressures and home (parent) government pressures. Pressures = incentives and privileges, not political pressure.
  2. On the left: market information. It grows as the company goes deeper.
  3. On the right: control of the market. It grows as the company goes deeper.
  4. Underneath, a double arrow: investment requirements, risk and profit. None or little at the two ends, high in the middle (the "hot area").
  5. Between the modes: small arrows, the move to the next step when things stay stable.

Host and home

Host country: the country the company enters. Home (parent) country: the country it comes from.

On the drawing, "host government pressures" means:

  1. Political pressure on the foreign company
  2. The incentives and privileges the host offers to attract foreign investors
  3. The taxes the host collects from foreign companies
  4. The limits the host puts on foreign ownership

Pressures are incentives. The host offers them to attract investors, and the home government offers them to push its own companies abroad.

What rises as a company moves toward the middle of the drawing?

Investment requirements, risk and profit (the double arrow underneath). With deeper commitment, market information and control of the market rise too (the side arrows).

Toshiba of Japan sells in Egypt. Which is the host country and which is the home country?

Egypt is the host: the country the company enters. Japan is the home, or parent, country: where the company comes from.

A company reaches a foreign market only through a trading house. What does it invest, and what does it learn about that market?

  1. It invests a lot and learns a lot
  2. It invests a lot and learns very little
  3. It invests nothing and learns a lot
  4. It invests nothing and learns very little

This is the lightest end of the drawing: no investment, almost no risk, but also almost no information and no control.

A company uses an agent. What does it pay for?

A little: training the agent (even abroad), decorating the showroom, and a promotion plan.

How this becomes a paragraph in an exam answer

When a question says "discuss the modes of entry", close the answer with what the model shows:

"The deeper the commitment, the more market information the company collects, the more control it has over the market, and the higher the investment requirements, the risk and the profit. Host and home governments push with incentives."

The same four arrows as a list of factors

The arrows can also be written as the four things that affect a company's decision to enter and its choice of a mode:

  1. How important control over the market is to management.
  2. The pressures of the host and the parent governments.
  3. The information available about the market.
  4. The investment requirements, profit and risk.

Lesson 6 gives the longer lists of factors.

Prof. Abu Qahf numbered the 17 modes on the board so that he could split them in two ways.

By ownership: modes 1 to 11 are indirect investment, where the company earns from the foreign market without owning a business inside it. Modes 12 to 17 are direct investment, where it owns one, fully or partly.

By how a direct investment starts: greenfield means building something new. Brownfield means joining or buying a company that already exists.

First split: does the company own something there?

Indirect: modes 1 to 11

Also called indirect modes, or indirect strategies, of entry

The company earns from the foreign market without owning a business inside it. All the ways to sell (1 to 5) and all the contracts up to the strategic alliance (6 to 11).

Direct: modes 12 to 17

Foreign direct investment, FDI الاستثمار الأجنبي المباشر

The company owns, fully or partly, a business inside the country.

12 Joint venture 13 Wholly owned subsidiary 14 Merger 15 Acquisition 16 Marketing branch 17 Assembly plant

Three modes look out of place

The joint venture (12) is drawn in the contracts box. The marketing branch (16) and the assembly plant (17) are drawn in the selling box. All three are still direct, because in each of them the company puts its own money into something it owns, or co-owns, inside the country.

So follow the numbers, not the boxes. That is what his numbers are for: 1 to 11 are the indirect modes, 12 to 17 the direct ones.

Second split: how does a direct investment start?

Greenfield

"Start from scratch"

You set up something new.

12 Joint venture 13 Wholly owned subsidiary 16 Marketing branch 17 Assembly plant

Brownfield

He says "brown investment"

You come in by joining or buying a company that already exists.

14 Merger 15 Acquisition

To remember it

A green field is empty land: you build on it. A brown field already has a building on it: you take it over.

Indirect and direct

1 to 11 = indirect foreign investment. The company does not own a business in the country.

12 to 17 = direct foreign investment (FDI). The company owns one, fully or partly: joint venture, wholly owned subsidiary, merger, acquisition, marketing branch, assembly plant.

Greenfield and brownfield

Greenfield (start from scratch): 12 joint venture, 13 wholly owned subsidiary, 16 marketing branch, 17 assembly plant.

Brownfield (take over what exists): 14 merger, 15 acquisition.

The rule

Follow the numbers, not the boxes. Putting your own money into something you own or co-own inside the country makes the mode direct.

Indirect or direct?

  • Agent
  • Licensing
  • Franchising
  • Turnkey project
  • Strategic alliance
  • International subcontracting
  • Joint venture
  • Wholly owned subsidiary
  • Merger
  • Acquisition
  • Marketing branch
  • Assembly plant

Greenfield or brownfield?

  • Joint venture
  • Wholly owned subsidiary
  • Marketing branch
  • Assembly plant
  • Merger
  • Acquisition

The joint venture is drawn in the contracts box. Why is it direct investment?

Because the company puts its own money into a project it co-owns inside the country. Ownership, full or partial, is what makes a mode direct. Follow the numbers (12 to 17), not the boxes.

The McDonald's, Pizza Hut and Starbucks shops in Egypt are:

  1. Licensing contracts, and direct investment
  2. Franchise contracts, and indirect investment
  3. Both of these

They are franchise contracts (mode 7). The foreign company owns nothing in Egypt, so it is indirect investment.

Setting up lines to assemble cars inside a host country is:

  1. Indirect entry
  2. Direct entry, like merger, acquisition and full ownership

An assembly plant is mode 17: direct. Do not mix it up with a manufacturing contract, where a local factory produces on the company's behalf. That one is a contract, so it is not direct entry.

Optional. Open what you want.

What about a project inside a free zone?

He left free zones out of the course. But a multiple-choice question from older revision material asks it, and there the answer is that a company producing and marketing inside a free zone counts as direct investment inside the country.

The textbook's words for the same choice

The textbook calls it "purchase or build". Purchase: buy an existing business, which comes with a plant, people and a reputation. Build: set up a new one from the ground up, a greenfield investment. It is the same brownfield or greenfield choice.

No. The 17 modes are not a ladder. A company may enter a foreign market "anytime, using any mode of entry": by owning on day one, through a licence, or through an agent.

But companies that avoid risk prefer to go in gradually. They start light, learn the market, and only then go deeper.

Free to start anywhere, wise to start light

The small arrows on Prof. Abu Qahf's drawing do not force anyone to climb step by step. A rich, experienced company can buy a local firm on its first day in the country.

His example of the careful way is some Japanese companies. They start with an agent, a distributor or a licence, to collect information and get familiar with the market. Only then do they move to a deeper mode.

His second printed sheet shows this gradual path as one rising line over time:

As the company moves up the line, everything on the upright axis rises with it: investment, risk, profit, information and control. These are the same arrows as in lesson 2, now placed on a timeline.

His real example: Toshiba in Egypt

The late Hajj Mahmoud El-Araby began as the agent of Toshiba in Egypt. He sold so well that the Toshiba name became known in Egypt, Sudan and Libya.

Toshiba saw a promising market and moved up to a joint venture with him: an assembly plant in Egypt for televisions, refrigerators and whatever else can be assembled.

The rule

A company can enter "anytime, using any mode of entry". It need not climb step by step.

The gradual path

Risk avoiders, such as some Japanese companies, enter gradually:

  1. Export or licensing (an agent, a distributor, a licence): no ownership.
  2. Joint venture or assembly plant: shared ownership.
  3. Wholly owned subsidiary: full ownership.

Along the path, investment, risk, profit, information and control all rise.

The example to quote

Toshiba in Egypt: first an agent (El-Araby), then a joint venture with him, an assembly plant.

Must a company climb the modes one by one? Who chooses to?

No. It may enter anytime, using any mode. Companies that avoid risk choose to go gradually. His example: some Japanese companies, which start with an agent, a distributor or a licence.

Tell the Toshiba story in two steps.

Step one: Hajj Mahmoud El-Araby was Toshiba's agent in Egypt, and made the name known in Egypt, Sudan and Libya. Step two: Toshiba moved up to a joint venture with him, an assembly plant in Egypt.

A company has no international experience, and its management always avoids risk. How should it enter a new market?

  1. Buy a local company, because it is the fastest way in
  2. Build a wholly owned subsidiary, to keep full control
  3. Gradually: an indirect mode first, a deeper mode once it knows the market
  4. It should not enter at all

No experience and risk avoidance both point to the gradual path: an agent, a distributor or a licence first. These need little money, carry little risk, and bring information about the market.

On his second sheet, what is on the two axes of the rising line?

Across: time. Upward: investment, risk, profit, information and control. The line rises from export or licensing, to a joint venture or assembly plant, to a wholly owned subsidiary.

The link with the Uppsala idea

The gradual path is the same idea as the Uppsala model, one of the theories that explain why and how companies go abroad. It says a company goes deeper into a market as its experience of that market and its information about it grow. Those are its two success factors: prior experience, and enough information and knowledge.

His second printed sheet

Before a company chooses a mode of entry, it has to choose where to go and what to sell there. Prof. Abu Qahf says it must "look at the world and search for opportunities everywhere".

He gives three phases, in this order: screen the markets and sites, decide between standardization and differentiation, then pick one of five product planning options.

Phase 1: screen the markets and the sites

Screening means examining every possible country and removing the weak ones. A market is a place to sell in. A site is a place to produce in. There are four steps.

Step 1. Identify the basic appeal

Why this country and not that one? What attracts the company there?

Step 2. Assess the national business environment

Three sides:

  • Cultural. Is the culture friendly or hostile to foreigners? Countries that were once occupied often feel that "foreign investment means foreign occupation".
  • Economic. Market size, monetary policies, taxation policies, natural resources and raw materials.
  • Political. How stable is the country?

Step 3. Measure the market size and the site potential

His example is a canned food company looking at Egypt. It must know how much the industry sells now, how many companies are in it, how they compete, who would work for it, and where the raw materials come from. It must also check whether the country can carry its marketing: distribution, transport, storage, advertising, media.

Step 4. Select the market or the site

If steps 1 to 3 come out positive, somebody senior (the chief executive, or the manager in charge) makes a field trip to the country, at least to study the competition on the ground.

Phase 2: the same everywhere, or different in each market?

Standardization means selling the same product in the same way everywhere. Differentiation means a different product, or different marketing, for each market. To decide, the company asks five questions:

  1. The type of product. Can my product be standardized at all?
  2. How similar are the markets? If the countries are alike (homogeneous), standardize. If they are very different (heterogeneous), there is no standardization: a product for each market.
  3. The media through which the product will be promoted.
  4. Government restrictions on pricing, on production, on imports and exports, and on employing foreigners.
  5. The services available: banking, insurance, storage, transport.

Phase 3: the five product planning options

Two things can change: the product and the promotion message. That gives five options.

OptionThe productThe message
1SameSame
2SameRedesigned
3Adapted (redesigned, or a minor alteration)Same
4, "dual adaptation"AdaptedAdapted
5A completely redesigned or brand new product
To remember it

Change nothing. Change the message. Change the product. Change both. Or start again with a new product.

The three phases of analysing an international opportunity

  1. Screening markets and sites.
  2. Standardization or differentiation.
  3. The product planning options.

Phase 1: the four steps of screening

  1. Identify the basic appeal.
  2. Assess the national business environment: cultural, economic, political.
  3. Measure the market size and the site potential.
  4. Select the market or the site, with a field trip.

Phase 2: the five questions

  1. The type of product.
  2. How similar the markets are.
  3. The media.
  4. Government restrictions.
  5. The services available.

Phase 3: the five options

  1. Same product, same message.
  2. Same product, redesigned message.
  3. Adapted product, same message.
  4. Adapted product, adapted message (dual adaptation).
  5. A completely redesigned or brand new product.

Name the three phases of analysing an international opportunity.

(1) Screening markets and sites. (2) Standardization or differentiation. (3) The product planning options.

Give the four steps of screening, in order.

(1) Identify the basic appeal. (2) Assess the national business environment: cultural, economic, political. (3) Measure the market size and the site potential. (4) Select the market or the site, with a field trip by somebody senior.

In "screening markets and sites", a site is:

  1. A place to sell in
  2. A place to produce in
  3. The company's website
  4. A free zone

A market is a place to sell in. A site is a place to produce in.

"Dual adaptation" means:

  1. The same product with a redesigned message
  2. An adapted product with the same message
  3. An adapted product with an adapted message
  4. A brand new product

Dual means two: both the product and the promotion message are adapted. It is option 4 of the five.

The countries a company wants to enter are very different from each other (heterogeneous). It should:

  1. Standardize: one product for all of them
  2. Differentiate: a product for each market
  3. Stay at home

Alike markets (homogeneous): standardize. Very different markets (heterogeneous): no standardization, a product for each market.

Optional. Open what you want.

Culture has two sides

When the company assesses the cultural environment, culture has a material side and a non-material side.

  • Material: the infrastructure. Electricity, drainage, transport, media, roads, distribution channels.
  • Non-material: habits, customs, attitudes, language, religion.
The full list for step 3 (the canned food company in Egypt)

To measure the market size and the site potential, the company must know:

  • The current sales of the industry.
  • How many companies are in it.
  • The market model: competition, monopoly, or oligopoly, which means a few big sellers.
  • Whether demand is elastic (buyers react strongly to a price change) or inelastic.
  • The workforce.
  • The raw materials.

It must also check the marketing infrastructure: the distribution channels, the quality of transport and storage, the advertising and promotion agencies, and how far the broadcast media reach.

Two examples of government restrictions

A company that wants to use a country as a base for exporting must first ask whether exports of its product are restricted there.

Some governments protect their young local industries, called infant industries, by giving every foreign firm a quota: for example, no more than 1,000 units a day.

The textbook says the same four steps

The textbook chapter on analysing international opportunities gives the same four screening steps: (1) identify basic appeal, (2) assess the national business environment, (3) measure market or site potential, (4) select the market or site. For step 4 it adds a visit to each remaining location, an analysis of the competitors and a financial evaluation.

The choice of a mode of entry "is dependent upon a wide variety of factors". Prof. Abu Qahf sorts them into three groups: factors that come from the company itself, from the host country, and from the parent (home) country.

His exam cases describe a company and ask for the suitable mode. The clues in the case are these factors. Learn to read them and the answer follows.

Three groups, each pushing the choice

1. Firm-specific factors: the company itself

  1. Its financial resources.
  2. Its previous experience and information.
  3. The attitude of its top management.
  4. The aptitude of its top management.
  5. Skilled people who can be sent abroad.

How they push. A company short of money cannot enter directly: only the indirect modes are open to it. A company with no experience picks a lighter mode. If top management has a negative attitude toward going abroad, it prefers indirect modes: "you can make licensing, you can use an agent".

Attitude and aptitude, in his words

Attitude is how you feel about something. Aptitude الاستعداد is your readiness to actually do it.

"I want to drink tea, and I like tea, so my attitude toward tea is positive. But I am too lazy to make it: I have no aptitude."

2. Host-country factors

  1. How healthy the business environment is: political, economic, social.
  2. Restrictions on foreign ownership.
  3. A hostile culture or attitude toward foreigners.
  4. Government restrictions on business, pricing and production.
  5. Political stability, and relations with neighbouring countries.
  6. Market size.
  7. Everything that makes a location attractive (the location theory).

How they push. Most companies want to control and manage their own project. But where foreign ownership is strictly prohibited, the company cannot enter directly. Where the market is small, the company uses an agent, a distributor or a licence, because it will not invest a lot of money for a small profit.

3. Parent-country factors

The relationship between the home country and the host country. A hostile relationship can stop companies from entering.

His example

When Ronald Reagan was president of the USA, he asked American companies not to invest in the Soviet Union, so that it would not get the new technology. The companies obeyed.

Read the clues, pick the mode

Four small cases. Each one has appeared in his past exams or in the revision material for them. Find the clue, then name the mode.

Case 1

An Egyptian food company wants to enter Jordan. Which mode?

No mode can be proposed until four things are known: the company's financial capabilities, its human capabilities, its competitive advantages, and its experience in that market. If it has huge financial capabilities, it enters by direct investment. If not, by exporting and agents.

Case 2

A company has no international experience, and its management always avoids risk.

Both clues point to going in gradually: start with an indirect mode (an agent, a distributor or a licence), learn the market, then go deeper.

Case 3

A company has 200 registered patents, little money and few employees. The countries it wants to enter do not restrict foreigners.

It has something valuable to offer (the patents) but no money and no people to produce abroad. So it lets others produce for a fee: licensing. More exactly, licensing by choice, because the reasons come from the company, not from the country. Lesson 8 explains the two types.

Case 4

A company with no plan and no experience at all.

The mode that can make it international without any plan is the trading house. Lesson 7 shows how.

The three groups

Firm-specific: financial resources; previous experience and information; attitude of top management; aptitude of top management; skilled people who can be sent abroad.

Host-country specific: health of the business environment; restrictions on foreign ownership; hostile culture toward foreigners; government restrictions on business, pricing, production; political stability and relations with neighbours; market size; the location factors.

Parent-country specific: the relationship between the home country and the host country (Reagan and the Soviet Union).

The clues and where they point

  • Little money: indirect modes only.
  • No experience, or a management that avoids risk: a lighter mode first, then deeper.
  • Foreign ownership prohibited: no direct entry.
  • Small market: an agent, a distributor or a licence.
  • No plan and no experience at all: trading houses.
  • Many patents, little money, few people, no restrictions: licensing by choice.

Name the three groups of factors that decide the mode, with one example each.

Firm-specific: a shortage of money leaves only the indirect modes. Host-country: where foreign ownership is prohibited there is no direct entry, and a small market calls for an agent or a licence. Parent-country: hostile relations between home and host, as when Reagan asked American companies not to invest in the Soviet Union.

Which mode can make a company international although it has no previous experience and no plan?

  1. Licensing
  2. Management and manufacturing contracts
  3. Merger
  4. Acquisition
  5. Trading houses

Trading houses. A local trader exports the product, and the producer becomes international without ever planning to.

A home-appliance company has 200 patented products, little money and few staff. The markets it wants place no limits on foreign ownership. Which mode suits it?

  1. A wholly owned subsidiary
  2. Licensing by necessity
  3. Licensing by choice
  4. An acquisition

Licensing by choice. The reasons are the company's own: no money for direct investment, not enough people, and a very high ability to innovate. The host countries place no restrictions, so it is not licensing by necessity.

A host country strictly prohibits foreign ownership. A foreign company that wants this market:

  1. Must build a wholly owned subsidiary
  2. Should acquire a local firm
  3. Cannot enter directly, so it uses an indirect mode
  4. Should open a marketing branch

Direct entry means owning, and owning is prohibited. Only the indirect modes are left: an agent, a distributor, a licence, another contract.

What is the difference between attitude and aptitude? Give his example.

Attitude is how you feel about something. Aptitude is your readiness to actually do it. "I like tea, so my attitude toward tea is positive. But I am too lazy to make it: I have no aptitude."
