I tried it. Open the model answer

"Determinants of foreign investment" means what makes a country attractive to foreign investors. Write the three lists.

Host-country factors (14). The main ones: restrictions on full or shared foreign ownership; restrictions on exporting, importing and imported raw materials; the degree of state intervention; political stability; customs tariffs and exemptions; investment incentives, climate and laws; distribution channels; marketing infrastructure; political relations with neighbours; culture and the public's attitude to foreign products; the name and reputation of the country.

Home-country factors (3). The home government's support and incentives for its companies; how far the state pays for the first studies; pressures, positive or negative.

Foreign-company factors (4). Financial, technical and human resources; previous experience; competitive advantages; the ability to invest directly and indirectly.

The full numbered lists are in lesson 6, under "More".

Discuss

"Discuss" wants a short essay with a clear skeleton: an opening definition, the parts in order, his example for each part, and a closing line. Build the skeleton first, then fill it.

Worked for youAsked in two past exams

"Any company thinking of invading the international markets faces several alternative options. What are they, what are the strategies of entry, and what are their most important advantages and disadvantages?"

Another past exam asked the same thing in fewer words: "Discuss: entry models, strategies of invading international markets."

See how the answer is built

The skeleton: introduction, Option I, Option II, Option III, what the model shows, advantages and disadvantages.

Introduction. Modes of entry, also called strategies of entry or degrees of international commitment, are the forms a company can use to enter a foreign market. Any company is free to choose among three options that contain 17 modes.

Option I, commercial (export). The company only sells. Trading houses (a local trader exports the product, and the producer becomes international without any plan); agents (work for a commission and do not own the product); distributors (buy the product and resell it for their own account); international exhibitions; e-commerce. Deeper: a marketing branch, an assembly plant.

Option II, contracting (no ownership). Licensing (permission to produce and market a product for a royalty); franchising (the use of a trademark, as in McDonald's); management contracts (running someone else's project for fees) and manufacturing contracts (a local factory produces on the company's behalf); turnkey projects (build the plant and hand it over when it starts producing); international subcontracting (part of an order is produced by another party to the same specification); strategic alliances (each party uses the other's strength); joint ventures (a project owned together with a local investor).

Option III, equity (ownership). A wholly owned subsidiary; merger; acquisition, friendly (by negotiation) or hostile (through the stock market).

What the model shows. The deeper the commitment, the more market information the company collects, the more control it has over the market, and the higher the investment requirements, the risk and the profit. Host and home governments push with incentives. Modes 1 to 11 are indirect investment and 12 to 17 are direct investment. Direct investment is greenfield (from scratch) or brownfield (merger, acquisition). A company need not climb step by step, but risk avoiders enter gradually (Toshiba in Egypt: an agent first, then a joint assembly plant).

Advantages and disadvantages. The light modes need little money and carry little risk, but give little control and a lower return, and may create a future competitor. Ownership gives full control and all the profit, at high cost and high risk (nationalization, confiscation). Then give two or three points for each main mode, from lesson 11.

With gapsAsked in two past exams

"Discuss in detail the situational factors or conditions that determine the choice of an entry strategy or model."

Open the answer and fill the gaps

Say each hidden word, then tap it to check.

The choice depends on three groups of factors.

Firm-specific factors: its financial, technical and human resources; its previous experience and information; the attitude and the aptitude of its top management toward going abroad; its competitive advantages. A firm short of money or experience can use only the indirect modes.

Host-country factors: restrictions on foreign ownership, full or partial; restrictions on exporting, importing and imported materials; the degree of state intervention; political stability; tariffs, exemptions and investment incentives; distribution channels and marketing infrastructure; relations with neighbours; culture and the public's attitude to foreign products; market size. Where foreign ownership is prohibited, direct entry is impossible. Where the market is small, an agent, a distributor or a licence is enough.

Parent-country factors: the support and incentives the home government gives its companies, and its relations with the host country (Reagan stopped American companies from investing in the Soviet Union).

From the model itself: the importance of control to management, the pressures (incentives) of the two governments, the information available about the market, and the investment requirements, profit and risk.

YoursAsked in one past exam

"What are the types of licensing contracts, and when is each type used?"

I tried it. Open the model answer

Definition. A licensing contract is a permission from one company (the licensor) to another (the licensee) to produce and market a certain product in a certain market, in return for a fee (royalty). It is an indirect mode of entry, common in industrial projects.

Licensing by necessity (forced). Used when the reasons come from the host country: (1) a small market, not profitable in the long run; (2) political and economic instability; (3) foreigners are not allowed into strategic industries; (4) restrictions on foreign ownership, full or partial; (5) restrictions on exporting and importing.

Licensing by choice. Used when the reasons come from the company: (1) no money for direct investment; (2) weak marketing ability and experience in that market; (3) high ability in research and innovation; (4) not enough people to work abroad; (5) no wish or ability to exploit the market itself; (6) selling licences instead of exporting; (7) testing the market before direct investment; (8) entering with no investment cost and the least risk.

A third case: mixing licences with industrial assembly operations.

Case

A case describes a company and asks what it should do. Answer in three moves: restate the clues in one line, name the choice, then give the reasons, each one tied to a clue.

Worked for youAsked in one past exam

"An Egyptian company wants to internationalize for the first time. It found four markets: A, B, C and D. It has no experience, and its management always avoids risk. Explain the suitable strategies to enter the market it will choose."

See how the answer is built

Move 1: the clues. First time abroad. Four candidate markets. No experience. Management avoids risk.

Move 2: the choice. First choose the market by screening the four: basic appeal, national business environment, market size and site potential, then a field trip. Then enter gradually, through indirect modes: exporting through trading houses, then an agent or a distributor, international exhibitions, e-commerce, or a licence.

Move 3: the reasons, each tied to a clue.

  • No experience: the company lacks experience and information, which are needed before a deep commitment (the Uppsala idea).
  • Avoids risk: indirect modes need little investment and carry little risk.
  • First time: indirect modes bring market information for the next step.

Closing line. When the market proves promising, the company can move to a joint venture or an assembly plant, and later to a wholly owned subsidiary.

YoursAsked in one past exam

"A canned food company will enter an Asian market by licensing in 2027. Discuss the situational factors that determine licensing, by its types."

I tried it. Open the model answer

State the type first. If the Asian country restricts foreign ownership or is unstable, it is licensing by necessity. If the company itself lacks money or people, it is licensing by choice. The case does not say, so give both.

Licensing by necessity, when the reasons come from the host country: a small market; political and economic instability; strategic industries closed to foreigners; restrictions on foreign ownership; restrictions on exporting and importing.

Licensing by choice, when the reasons come from the company: no money for direct investment; weak marketing ability and experience there; high ability in research and innovation; not enough people; no wish or ability to exploit the market itself; licences instead of exporting; testing the market; no investment cost and the least risk.

"An Egyptian food company wants to enter the Jordanian market. Which mode do you propose?"

I tried it. Open the model answer

No mode can be proposed until four things are known: the company's financial capabilities, its human capabilities, its competitive advantages, and its experience in that market.

If it has huge financial capabilities, it enters by direct investment. If not, by exporting and agents.

Multiple choice

The tricky ones. His options often end with "a or b" and "none", so read every option before you choose. The other tricky questions on this topic sit inside the lessons and come back in Review.

Which kind of agent sells from a catalogue and keeps no stock?

  1. The commission agent
  2. The commission agent who guarantees payment
  3. The spare parts and services agency
  4. The commission agent who holds stock

The plain commission agent: a catalogue, no stock, a commission. The four kinds are in lesson 7, under "More".

A company producing and marketing in a free zone is:

  1. Direct investment inside the country
  2. Indirect investment
  3. Fast direct invasion
  4. None of these

Direct investment, in the revision material for his exams. In class he left free zones out of the course.

Strategic alliances with suppliers or customers are:

  1. A way of entering international markets
  2. A tool for keeping competitive advantage
  3. Either of the two above
  4. None of these

Both. An alliance is mode 11 of entry, and partnering with suppliers and customers is also one of the ways a company keeps its competitive advantage.

International subcontracting is:

  1. Direct entry
  2. A kind of acquisition
  3. A kind of merger
  4. None of these

None. It is an indirect mode of its own, mode 10: another party produces part of the order to the same specification.

Discuss

"Discuss" wants a short essay with a clear skeleton: an opening definition, the parts in order, his example for each part, and a closing line. Build the skeleton first, then fill it.

Worked for youAsked in four past exams

"Opinions have differed on the feasibility of foreign investments and the role of multinational companies in development in developing countries. Discuss in detail."

The three other exams asked it this way: "The traditional viewpoint on the feasibility of foreign investments" (20 marks). "Discuss briefly, with examples, the feasibility of foreign investments for developing host countries." "Discuss in detail the feasibility of foreign investments through multinational companies, especially for the Third World, and how this feasibility can be measured."

See how the answer is built

The skeleton: introduction, the traditional view, the modern view, the benefits, examples, how feasibility is measured, conclusion.

Introduction. "Feasibility" asks whether foreign investment is worth it for the host country. All countries, developed and developing, compete to attract it, yet 80% goes to North America, the European Union and Japan, 16% to China, and only 4% to all the other countries. Two views explain the relationship between multinational companies and developing host countries.

1. The traditional (classical, radical) view. The relationship is a zero-sum game played from one side: the multinational wins and the host country loses; the companies take more than they give.

  • Hood and Young: the relationship is exploitative, a form of imperialism: the companies use local resources at the host's expense, create technological dependency, and bring consumption patterns (fast food, snacks) that raise consumption, cut savings and so starve national projects of finance.
  • Leontiades: do not expect multinationals to behave like an "ideal citizen". Their exemptions from taxes and customs duties take away the money that would finance national development, and they may bribe officials.
  • Baliga: a colonial point of view: the host is a source of cheap raw materials and cheap labour; national workers get the routine jobs; the investment is kept small.
  • Frank: exploitation; investment concentrated in extractive industries, with no links to the rest of the economy, so dependency grows.
  • Biersteker: little capital comes in and much is transferred out; research stays at headquarters; high salaries create social class division and pull skilled workers from national firms.

2. The modern view. The relationship is one of mutual interest ("win to win"): the company seeks profit, expansion and lower risk, the host seeks development, and each gains according to the policies of the other. Mikesell, Vernon and Wells: foreign investment plays a vital role in development if the country directs it well (foreign currency, a new class of businessmen, modern technology, export markets). Stopford: it raises capital formation. Hood and Young add that even if some exploitation exists, there is no one-sided game.

3. The benefits. Five benefits solve five problems: hard currency (the shortage of foreign currency); new jobs (unemployment); technology transfer (the technology gap between North and South); a better balance of payments (its chronic deficit); managerial development (bad management). Derivative benefits: a higher standard of living, less crime and corruption, no "social fury".

4. Examples (for the exam that asks "with examples"). The host decides how much it gains by differentiating its incentives: the same tax exemption for an iron and steel project and for a snack factory pushes investors to the snacks; the same incentives in Cairo and in Marsa Matrouh push them to Cairo; a firm creating 1,000 jobs should get more than a firm creating 5. Evidence from the Harrison reading: in Mexico and Venezuela multinationals paid up to 30% more than local firms and helped local firms to export, but their technology did not spread to local competitors by itself.

5. How feasibility can be measured (for the exam that asks how). By comparing benefits with costs on each effect: the balance of payments (capital and export earnings coming in, against profits and foreign salaries transferred out and borrowing from national banks); the jobs created; the technology and skills transferred; the growth of national product and tax revenue; the links built with local sectors. Look at the first effects and the later effects. Some benefits are hard to measure in numbers, but they must not be overlooked. And study where foreign investment actually flows, and how much.

Conclusion. Both views hold some truth. Foreign investment helps development provided the right investment climate and policies exist. "The ball is in your field, not in the field of the multinational corporation": the result depends on how the host manages foreign investment.

Part 5 is put together from the four-benefit version and the comments on the two views (lessons 2 to 4, under "More"). The revision material has no separate section on measurement.

With gapsAsked in one past exam, for 20 marks

"The traditional viewpoint on the feasibility of foreign investments."

Open the answer and fill the gaps

Say each hidden word, then tap it to check.

The assumption. The traditional view is also called the classical or the radical view. It sees the relationship between multinationals and developing host countries as a zero-sum game played from one side, "just like gambling". The winner is the multinational companies, and "they take more than they give".

Hood and Young. The relationship is exploitative, a form of imperialism. Multinationals export capital because profits at home are falling, search for new profitable markets, create technological dependency, and bring a consumption pattern that does not fit national development: people consume more and save less, so the banks have less to lend (Pizza Hut, KFC, McDonald's, Chipsy).

Leontiades. Do not expect them to behave like an "ideal citizen". Their exemptions from income tax and customs duties, and infrastructure services bought at cost, take away the money of the national development programmes. And they may bribe national officials.

Baliga. A colonial point of view: the host is a source of cheap raw materials and a profitable market; the foreign share must be the larger one and keep management and control; they choose countries with cheap labour, give national workers only the routine jobs, and keep the investment small to avoid risk.

Frank. Exploitation in every part of the relationship. Investment is concentrated in the extractive industries (oil, mining), builds no strong links with the rest of the economy, and so the host's dependence on the advanced countries grows.

Biersteker. Little capital comes in and a lot is transferred home; research and development stays at headquarters; higher salaries create social class division and pull trained workers away from national companies.

Freeman, Persen and Livingstone. Unethical practices: bribery, gifts, commissions, even trying to overthrow the regime. And they obstruct economic planning by obtaining customs and tax exemptions.

Comments on this view. (1) It is wrong to expect multinationals to be ideal in their behaviour. (2) Their concentration in extractive industries feeds the feeling of exploitation. (3) They want to dominate, so they prefer direct investment. (4) Their fear of nationalization and confiscation makes them prefer joint investment. (5) They do not care about the host's economic and social development. (6) They often create a market monopoly. (7) How sincere they are can be judged by studying where foreign investment flows and how much: 80% to the three globalization centres, 16% to China, 4% to all the others.

Closing line. The modern view answers that the relationship is a mutual interest, and that what the host gains depends on how it manages foreign investment.

YoursAsked in three past exams

"Can international companies be held accountable for social responsibility?"

It came as the last part of longer questions about globalization. It was not taught in class.

I tried it. Open the model answer

Assuming globalization is accepted in thought and practice, holding international companies accountable needs three things.

1. A global tax system that collects from the industrial countries and the host countries and spends the proceeds on the pollution and poverty these firms cause.

2. Accountability for environmental performance: measure environmental contributions (pollution and waste control); give each area its assets and liabilities; publish reports and disclose to society; adjust the statement of financial position for environmental and social contribution.

3. Accountability for the "pollution of minds" is "a kind of the impossible", because globalization's mechanisms produce rebellion, escape and alienation.

Short answers

He often writes "the answer must not exceed two words", or "mention without explanation". Give the term or the list and stop.

The classical view and the modern view of foreign investment: two words each.

Zero-sum game. Mutual interest.

Name the five benefits of foreign direct investment.

Hard currency, new jobs, technology transfer, a better balance of payments, managerial development.

How should a host country use its incentives?

Differentiate them by sector, by region and by the number of jobs created. "The ball is in your field."

Multiple choice

The tricky ones. His options often end with "a or b" and "none", so read every option before you choose. The other questions on this topic sit inside the lessons and come back in Review.

A foreign company borrows from foreign banks, not from local ones. This hurts:

  1. The balance of trade
  2. The balance of payments
  3. Both
  4. None of these

None. What hurts the host's balance of payments is borrowing from its national banks, and transferring profits and foreign employees' salaries abroad.

"The traditional theory assumes foreign investment is a zero-sum game whose winner is the host countries." This statement is:

  1. Correct
  2. Wrong

Wrong. It is a zero-sum game from one side, and the winner is the multinational companies.

Foreign companies pay salaries far above those of national companies. According to the traditional view this leads to:

  1. Social class division
  2. The flight of trained labour from the national companies
  3. Both
  4. None of these

Both: social class division, and trained workers leaving the national companies.

How can the sincerity of multinationals' intentions toward developing countries be judged?

By analysing the direction and the size of foreign investment flows among the countries of the world.

Textbook exercises

He asked the class to read chapter 7 of the textbook, "Foreign Direct Investment", and to solve the exercises at its end "for yourselves". He will not collect them, but the class expects exam questions from them.

Below are model answers to all of them: the 15 Quick Study questions inside the chapter, Talk It Over 1 to 3, Teaming Up 1 and 2, Take It to the Web, Ethical Challenges 1 to 3, and the case "Driving the Green Car Market in Australia".

They are written the way he asks: define first in the book's words, obey the command word, a fact sheet for the case, and "how" for the ethics questions. The opinion answers are examples, written in the first person. Write your own position in your own words.

Where a point ends with "My judgment", it is reasoning written for this answer, not something taken from the book or from the class.

Part A. Quick Study questions (inside the chapter)

Quick Study 1

1. What is the difference between foreign direct investment and portfolio investment?

  • FDI is "the purchase of physical assets or a significant amount of the ownership (stock) of a company in another country in order to gain a measure of management control".
  • Portfolio investment is "an investment that does not involve obtaining a degree of control in a company".
  • The difference is control. Countries draw the line at different shares: the U.S. Commerce Department counts 10 percent of the stock as FDI; most other governments use 10 to 25 percent.
  • In the professor's model, FDI is modes 12 to 17 (joint venture, wholly owned subsidiary, merger, acquisition, marketing branch, assembly plant); modes 1 to 11 are indirect investment.

2. What factors influence global flows of FDI?

  • Globalization. When trade barriers rose, firms invested inside markets to get around them; when the Uruguay Round of GATT lowered barriers, firms moved production to the most efficient, low-cost locations and exported from there. Globalization also pushes firms from emerging markets to invest abroad (Acer of Taiwan had 10 subsidiaries 20 years after it started).
  • Mergers and acquisitions. Cross-border M&As are "the main vehicle through which companies undertake FDI"; their value peaked at about $1.2 trillion in 2000.
  • The business cycle. Financial crises and slow growth cut FDI (2008, 2009); strong profits lift it.
  • Entrepreneurs and small businesses also invest abroad (the "Cowboy of Manchuria" candy factory in China).
  • From class: host and home government "pressures", which the professor defined as incentives, not political pressure.

3. Identify the main destinations of FDI. Is the pattern shifting?

  • Book (2011 data): developed countries received 49 percent ($748 billion of more than $1.5 trillion); developing countries 45 percent ($684 billion); transition economies of Southeast Europe about 6 percent. The EU is the largest recipient ($421 billion, nearly 28 percent). Developing Asia got $423 billion (China more than $124 billion, India nearly $31 billion); Latin America 14.2 percent; all of Africa 2.8 percent.
  • His class version: 80 percent goes to the three "globalization centers" (North America, the EU, Japan), 16 percent to China, 4 percent to all other countries, and Egypt gets a fraction of that 4 percent. The book's numbers are newer and show a bigger developing-country share; write the book's figures and add his three-centers point in one line.
  • Yes, it is shifting: toward developing and emerging markets (low-cost production, big new consumer markets), and emerging-market firms are now investors too.

Quick Study 2

1. Explain the international product life cycle theory of FDI. A company begins by exporting its product and later undertakes FDI as the product moves through its life cycle:

  • New product stage: made at home, because demand is uncertain and production should stay close to the research department.
  • Maturing product stage: the firm builds plants in countries where demand is big enough.
  • Standardized product stage: competition forces costs down, so the firm produces in low-cost developing countries and serves the world from there.
  • Weakness: it does not explain why a firm chooses FDI rather than licensing (a local firm could pay for the right to make the product) or exporting more from the home plant. From class: it does not apply to unique goods (Rolls-Royce, French perfume); VW Beetle production moving to Brazil is the class example.

2. How does the theory of market imperfections (internalization) explain FDI?

  • A market imperfection is anything that stops a market from working at peak efficiency. When an imperfection makes a transaction less efficient, the firm undertakes FDI to internalize the transaction and remove the imperfection.
  • Trade barriers: NAFTA required enough local content to avoid tariffs, so Korean manufacturers built plants in Tijuana, Mexico.
  • Specialized knowledge: when the know-how is in the firm's people, FDI may be the only way to use it abroad; and selling the knowledge for a fee can create a future competitor (Japanese firms paid Western firms for technology after the Second World War and became leaders in electronics and cars).
  • From class: this is the internalization idea he taught with the theories (protection theory, the Xerox lesson: do not license your patent).

3. Explain the eclectic theory, and identify the three advantages necessary for FDI to occur. Firms undertake FDI when the features of a location combine with ownership and internalization advantages. All three must be present:

  • Location advantage: natural (oil in the Middle East, timber in Canada, copper in Chile) or acquired (a productive workforce).
  • Ownership advantage: a special asset: brand recognition, technical knowledge, management ability.
  • Internalization advantage: doing the activity inside the firm instead of leaving it to an inefficient market.
  • From class: John Dunning's O-L-I (a past exam asked for the common factor with protection theory: "internalization advantage").

4. How does the theory of market power explain the occurrence of FDI?

  • A firm undertakes FDI to establish a dominant market presence in its industry; the benefit is higher profit, because it can dictate the cost of its inputs and/or the price of its output.
  • The usual route is vertical integration: backward (into the stages that supply its inputs) or forward (into the stages that absorb its output, for example its own distribution).
  • From class: this is the professor's "controlling the market" arrow (deciding units produced, units marketed, price).

Quick Study 3

1. Why is control important to companies considering the FDI decision?

  • Firms want the product marketed the same way and sold at the same price as at home; many believe more ownership (up to 100 percent) gives more control.
  • But ownership does not guarantee control: the host may force the hiring of local managers or require all output to be exported.
  • Partnership requirements: IBM once insisted on 100 percent ownership; it got 100 percent in Guadalajara, Mexico, only after many concessions.
  • Benefits of cooperation: Interbrew (Belgium) bought Hungary's Borsodi brewery on the condition that local management stayed in charge, then trained them.
  • From class: control rises with the degree of commitment; contracting modes give little control, equity modes the most.

2. What is the role of production costs in the FDI decision? Define rationalized production.

  • Costs differ by country: labour rules, benefit packages beyond wages, training time; cheap land and low taxes cannot be assumed to last (rising wages in China pushed some firms to Vietnam).
  • Rationalized production: "a system of production in which each of a product's components is produced where the cost of producing that component is lowest", then assembled in one place (a Chinese-assembled stuffed toy: eyes from Japan, outfit from France, stuffing from Germany or the U.S., fur from Korea).
  • Its risk: a stoppage in one country stops everything (the UAW strike at GM's brake-pad plant threatened assembly plants across North America).
  • Related: Mexico's maquiladora border region, and R&D costs (SmithKline Beecham paid about $68 million for access to Cadus's gene research).
  • From class: this is "globalization of supply" (subcontracting, component specialization), and the professor's international subcontracting example (Honda makes 600 cars and asks another plant to make the other 400 to the same specification).

3. Explain the need for customer knowledge, following clients, and following rivals in the FDI decision.

  • Customer knowledge: a local presence teaches you what home cannot (tastes that differ by country). Country image also matters: German automotive engineering, Italian shoes, French perfume, Swiss watches; a perfume maker may bottle in France for the image.
  • Following clients: suppliers invest where their customers have invested (German parts makers followed Mercedes to Tuscaloosa, Alabama).
  • Following rivals: in industries with few large firms, staying out when the first mover enters may shut you out (firms returned to South Africa after apartheid; Pepsi went back in 1994 and left in 1997, beaten by Coke).
  • From class: market information grows with commitment; an agent tells you much more than a trading house.

Quick Study 4

1. What is a country's balance of payments? Briefly explain its usefulness.

  • "A national accounting system that records all receipts coming into the nation and all payments to entities in other countries". Inflows add to it; outflows reduce it.
  • Usefulness (my wording, from the book's argument): it shows whether a country earns more from abroad than it pays abroad, and it is the main reason governments intervene in FDI (to protect foreign-exchange reserves).

2. Explain the difference between the current account and the capital account.

  • Current account: exports and imports of goods and services, income received on assets abroad, and income paid on foreign assets inside the country (a foreign subsidiary sending profits home is a negative entry). Surplus = you export and earn more than you import and pay; deficit = the opposite.
  • Capital account: purchases and sales of assets (a citizen buying foreign shares is a capital outflow; a foreigner buying local real estate is a capital inflow).
  • The two balances should be equal.

3. For what reasons do host countries intervene in FDI?

  • To control the balance of payments: the first inflow is a boost; local content rules cut imports; exports from the new plant help; but profits sent home drain reserves, so hosts may restrict profit removal or encourage reinvestment.
  • To obtain resources and benefits: technology (Siemens' design center and Texas Instruments' semiconductor plant in Singapore), management skills and employment; critics add that FDI can also destroy jobs when weaker local firms close.
  • From class: the professor's five benefits of FDI (hard currency, new jobs, technology transfer, a better balance of payments, managerial development), which solve five problems (currency shortage, unemployment, the North-South technology gap, the chronic balance-of-payments deficit, bad management).

4. For what reasons do home countries intervene in FDI?

  • To discourage outward FDI: resources leave the country; the foreign plant may replace exports (a VW plant in the U.S. replaces German-made cars, though repatriated profits later help); jobs may move abroad, the most sensitive point, although the effect is usually regional and may be offset by parts exports (Hyundai's plant in Brazil).
  • To promote outward FDI: long-term competitiveness (Japanese firms treat every venture as a learning opportunity); moving out "sunset" industries (old technology, low-skill jobs) to upgrade toward "sunrise" industries.
  • From class: Reagan told American firms not to invest in the Soviet Union so it could not get new technology (a parent-country factor).

Quick Study 5

1. Identify the main methods host countries use to promote and restrict FDI.

  • Promote: financial incentives (tax incentives such as lower rates or tax holidays of five years or more; low-interest loans) and infrastructure improvements (ports, roads, telecoms; Malaysia's Multimedia Super Corridor). Downside of incentives: bidding wars between locations; the cost to taxpayers can be several times what the jobs pay.
  • Restrict: ownership restrictions (bans in cultural and defence industries; foreign stake below 50 percent) and performance demands (local content, a share of output exported, technology transfer to local firms). Ownership rules are being dropped because investors can go elsewhere (Indonesia scrapped one for GM because China and Vietnam were also courting GM).
  • From class: offer incentives selectively: the same tax holiday for iron and steel and for a Chipsy-type snack factory pushes investors to the quick-payback snack; the same incentives in Cairo and Marsa Matrouh push everyone to Cairo. Differentiate by sector, region and number of jobs. "The ball is in your field, not in the field of the multinational".

2. What methods do home countries use to promote and restrict FDI?

  • Promote: insurance (expropriation, war, kidnapping, terrorism); loans and loan guarantees; tax breaks on foreign profits and treaties against double taxation; political pressure on other countries to open up (the U.S. pressing Japan).
  • Restrict: differential tax rates (foreign earnings taxed higher) and sanctions banning investment in certain countries.
Part B. Talk It Over

Talk It Over 1. "Fed up with companies sending jobs abroad... no national pride?" vs "every company's duty is maximum profit". Do you agree with either? Where do you stand?

In plain words: one manager says moving factories and services to cheap countries is unpatriotic; the other says a company's only duty is profit. Take a side and defend it.

My position: I agree with neither as stated. Both describe the relationship as a zero-sum game, where one side's gain is the other's loss. The professor taught that this is the old "radical" or "classical" view; the modern view is that the firm and the countries involved have a mutual interest, and how much each gains depends on how skilfully each side manages the deal.

Why the first manager is wrong:

  • The book shows outward FDI does not only destroy jobs at home. The effect is "rarely national", it can be offset by parts exports to the new plant (Hyundai's Brazil plant can add jobs in Korea that supply it with parts), and repatriated profits later improve the home balance of payments.
  • Moving "sunset" industries abroad and retraining workers lets the home economy move up to "sunrise" industries.
  • Firms that refuse to go where costs are lowest lose to rivals who do (rationalized production, following rivals).

Why the second manager is also wrong:

  • "Never ever assume that any foreign investor, or even national investor, is going to behave as an ideal citizen". A firm that chases cost alone runs into the problems of the ethics cases: abuse of workers, damaged brand, lost licence to operate.
  • Profit is legitimate, "the main driving force", but long-term profit needs the host's acceptance: fair wages, safe work, justice ("no justice, no satisfaction; no satisfaction, no productivity").
  • The evidence in our handout supports responsible FDI, not exploitation: in Mexico and Venezuela multinationals paid as much as 30 percent more than domestic firms, and average wages rose with foreign investment.

Where I stand: going abroad is a normal business decision and can be good for both countries, if it is managed: keep high-value work at home, retrain displaced workers, behave in the host country as a partner, not an exploiter. For governments, the professor's point applies to the home country too: the ball is in its field (training, incentives for sunrise industries), not in the hands of the firm.

Talk It Over 2. Your automaker invests in an assembly plant in Costa Rica with a local partner. Reasons? How much control, and in which areas would you keep or cede control?

In plain words: your car company builds an assembly plant in Costa Rica together with a Costa Rican partner. Why do it, and what should you keep in your own hands?

Where it sits in the professor's model: a joint venture investment project (mode 12) running an assembly plant (mode 17): direct investment, higher investment, risk and profit than exporting, more market information and more control. It is the Toshiba path: El-Araby was first Toshiba's exclusive agent, and when the market proved promising Toshiba set up a joint-venture assembly plant in Egypt.

Potential reasons for the investment (book Chapter 7 issues; the Costa Rica details are assumptions to check, as he wants in a case):

  1. Production costs: lower labour and land costs; assembly is labour-intensive (rationalized production: parts come in, cars are assembled locally).
  2. Market imperfections / trade barriers: if finished cars face tariffs but kits do not, or if a regional trade agreement rewards local content, local assembly avoids them (the Tijuana logic). Assumption: check Costa Rica's tariff and trade-agreement rules.
  3. Host incentives: tax holidays, low-interest loans, infrastructure, free-zone status.
  4. Customer knowledge and market access: a base to learn and serve Central American buyers.
  5. Why a partner: the host may demand shared ownership; the partner brings local knowledge, government contacts, suppliers and dealers, and shares the investment and risk; a risk-averse firm enters gradually (the Japanese way).
  6. Following rivals if competitors are already there.

Control: yes, a great deal, but selectively. Full control is neither possible (a partner and a host government) nor necessary.

  • Keep control of: product design and technology (internalization: do not let the partner become a future competitor); quality standards and the brand; supply of the key parts; financial reporting and profit repatriation terms.
  • Cede to the partner: human resources and labour relations under local law and custom (the Manager's Briefcase "surprises": mandated benefits, unions, dismissal rules); relations with government and permits; local suppliers of simple parts; local marketing and dealers. Interbrew's success in Hungary came from leaving local management in charge and training them.
  • Lesson: control what creates your competitive advantage; share what the partner knows better.

Talk It Over 3. Which FDI theory is most appealing to you? Why? Which companies fit it? What faults do the other theories have?

My choice: the eclectic theory (John Dunning's O-L-I). It is the most complete: it asks three questions at once (what do we own that others lack, why this location, and why do it ourselves instead of licensing) and says FDI happens only when all three are answered. It also combines the other theories: internalization is the market-imperfections idea, and location is the location theory.

Companies that fit:

  • Volkswagen in China (chapter opening): ownership advantage = strong brands and a modular production system; location = the biggest car market and low costs; internalization = it builds its own plants (four new assembly plants) instead of licensing its designs.
  • Toyota in Australia (the chapter case): engine technology (ownership), a government fund and an existing plant (location), production kept inside Toyota (internalization).

Faults of the alternatives:

  • International product life cycle: explains why some firms follow their product abroad, but not why they choose FDI over licensing or more exports; it does not apply to unique goods.
  • Market imperfections: explains why the firm keeps the activity inside, but not where it invests (it is silent on location). My judgment.
  • Market power: fits industries with a few large firms and vertical integration; it says little about small firms and entrepreneurs, who also invest abroad. My judgment.
Part C. Teaming Up

These are group research projects (a 2 to 3 page report; a simulation report). They are not exam questions as written, but the content behind them is. Below: how to answer, with book or sourced facts.

Teaming Up 1. Research a cross-border merger or acquisition from the past year: reasons, equals or not, post-deal issues, performance.

Method (his fact-sheet approach): pick one deal from the business press; build a table with the factors: buyer and target (country, size), price, type (merger or acquisition; friendly or hostile), each side's stated reasons, the integration problems, results since.

Frame for the reasons (the book's four M&A motives): a foothold in a new geographic market; greater global competitiveness; filling gaps in the product line; lower R&D, production and distribution costs.

Frame for the classification (class): merger and acquisition are brownfield ("brown") investment, buying something that exists, as opposed to greenfield, "start from scratch"; acquisitions are hostile (buying shares on the stock market, no negotiation) or friendly (negotiated). Merger is chosen for speed of entry.

Frame for post-deal issues (book): obsolete equipment, poor relations with workers, an unsuitable location reduce the appeal of buying; goodwill, brand and existing staff increase it; the Manager's Briefcase surprises (HR policies, mandated benefits, unions, unreliable data, political contacts).

Book examples if no current deal is at hand: Cemex (Mexico) buying Spain's two largest cement companies, Valenciana and Sanson, for $1.8 billion, "buy big globally, or be bought" (a larger firm absorbing smaller ones); Interbrew buying Hungary's state-owned Borsodi brewery and keeping local management (a friendly deal managed with respect for national pride). A real deal "from the past year" was not researched here; that part needs a current news search if you ever do it as a report.

Teaming Up 2. Market Entry Strategy Project: for your country, FDI attraction, FDI source, balance of payments, current and capital account, causes, effects, trade policy.

Example country: Egypt, with the latest published figures.

  • Does it attract large amounts of FDI? Yes, for Africa. UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2026 puts Egypt's FDI inflows at $46.578 billion in 2024 (revised) and $15.453 billion in 2025, a fall of 66.8 percent, because the 2024 figure was inflated by the $35 billion Ras El-Hekma deal with the UAE; Egypt was Africa's largest FDI recipient for the fourth year in a row but dropped out of the world's top 20 in 2025. In 2024 it ranked ninth in the world.
  • Is it a major source of FDI? Not established here (Unknown); not a major outward investor in the sources read.
  • Balance of payments / current account: fiscal year 2024/25 (July to June) current account deficit $15.4 billion, down 25.9 percent from $20.8 billion; overall balance of payments a $2.1 billion deficit after a $9.7 billion surplus the year before, which the Central Bank linked to the one-off inflows of the previous year.
  • Possible causes of the deficit (from the same reports): a large trade deficit; pressure on Suez Canal receipts; remittances from Egyptians abroad were a major support. Capital account balance: Unknown (not in the sources read).
  • Effects (book logic): a chronic current-account deficit drains foreign-exchange reserves, which is why hosts court FDI and may restrict profit repatriation; the professor's first FDI benefit, hard currency, answers exactly this problem.
  • How the government encourages or restricts: incentives such as tax holidays and customs exemptions ("all countries compete with incentives") and the free zones, which the professor excluded from the course as "a state within a state".
Part D. Take It to the Web

Take It to the Web 1. Watch a Chapter 7 video on the book's YouTube channel and write a half-page report.

Not done here (it depends on a video). How to write it: one line on what the video shows; then map it to the chapter's headings: which FDI pattern (destination), which theory (IPLC, imperfections, eclectic, market power), which management issue (control, purchase-or-build, costs, customers, clients, rivals), which government action (promotion or restriction); end with what a company should do with that information.

Take It to the Web 2. The Philippines and its neighbours: strong sectors, complement or compete, management issues for an investor; what Southeast Asian governments can do against China; an article on a company relocating.

No country data was fetched for this (the CIA World Factbook, which the book suggests, announced in February 2026 that it had been discontinued). So this answer gives the method and the book-based parts only.

  • Strengths and complement vs compete: build a table: country, main sectors, wage level, workforce skills, market size. Countries with similar sectors and wage levels compete for the same investors; countries at different stages complement each other (rationalized production can place different components in different countries).
  • Management issues (book Chapter 7 checklist): control and partnership rules; purchase or build; production costs (wages, mandated benefits, unions); reliability of data in developing countries; personal and political contacts and the ethical dilemmas they bring.
  • What governments can do to compete with China: infrastructure rather than bidding wars of tax breaks (Malaysia's Multimedia Super Corridor); stable rules and pro-growth policy, bilateral investment treaties; and the professor's advice: target incentives to your objectives (regions, sectors, jobs created) instead of giving everyone the same. China's own advantage in the book is a low-wage workforce and a huge domestic market.
  • Relocation article: state the reasons given (costs, markets, incentives) and whether the company planned for the workers left behind (retraining, the "sunset industry" argument).
Part E. Ethical Challenges

Ethical Challenge 1. A Dubai textile firm may buy a struggling Pakistani factory that dumps waste into a river. Buy and replace all staff, buy and retrain the staff, or walk away?

In plain words: you can buy a polluting factory cheaply. Do you buy it and fire everyone, buy it and train the same people to work cleanly, or not buy it at all?

Brief. This is a purchase-or-build decision (an acquisition, brownfield) with an environmental and a human problem attached.

Fact sheet

FactorFacts in the caseWhat it means
The assetStruggling factory on a major riverCheap entry, existing plant and people
EnvironmentRecently found dumping waste into the riverLegal, reputational and moral liability; must be fixed whatever we choose
PeopleCurrent managers and workersKnow the plant and the local market; the polluting decisions came from management, not from every worker
Firing everyone"Replace the management and hire all new employees"Mandated benefits and generous dismissal rules can make this expensive and are "typically not negotiable"; destroys local goodwill
Our strengthsMajor textile manufacturerWe can bring cleaner technology and management systems (multinationals tend to use cleaner energy and are more energy efficient)

Options compared (weighted table; weights and scores are my judgment, as in his Gdansk method)

Factor (weight)A: buy, replace all staffB: buy, keep staff, retrain, replace only those responsibleC: walk away
Fix the river (25)20220 (nothing gets fixed)
Cost and speed (20)81520
Local acceptance and reputation (20)51710
Productivity potential (20)15140
Fairness to workers (15)2137
Total (100)508137

Answer: buy the factory, keep the workers, and retrain them; replace the managers who ordered or allowed the dumping. The how, which he says matters most:

  1. Before signing: an environmental audit and a price that reflects the clean-up cost.
  2. Day one: stop the dumping; install waste treatment; agree a clean-up plan with the local authority and publish it.
  3. Management: bring in an environmental and operations manager from Dubai; retrain or replace the managers responsible; keep the local managers who were not.
  4. Workers: training in clean processes; fair pay and incentives; tell them the plant's future depends on it being clean ("no justice, no satisfaction; no satisfaction, no productivity").
  5. Stakeholders: show the town and the government that this is a mutual-interest relationship, not exploitation.

Why not A: it treats the workers as the cause of a management failure, it is costly under local labour rules, and it confirms the radical charge that multinationals exploit host countries. Why not C: nothing improves for the river or the people, and we lose a cheap entry. Lesson: an acquisition buys the plant's problems along with its assets; price them in and fix them openly.

Ethical Challenge 2. Your boss orders you to sell a large rice shipment to Japan fast, below market price; you overhear that it may be contaminated (the firm has had E. coli problems before). What do you do, and whom do you contact?

In plain words: you may be about to sell possibly poisoned rice abroad. Do you obey?

Answer: no shipment until the rice is tested and cleared. As the professor said of the port bribe, "bribe is bribe": some things are not negotiable, and the answer is to act openly and at once, not quietly.

How:

  1. Ask the quality assurance manager directly for the test results on that shipment; do not act on a rumour.
  2. Tell your boss, in writing, that you will not sell it until it is cleared, and why. The low price and the hurry are themselves warning signs.
  3. If the boss insists, go above him: senior management, the head of quality, the company's compliance or legal function. In the bribe case the professor's rule was to tell your boss officially at the same time, to protect "the whole economy", the owner and the port's ethical image.
  4. If the company still ships, report to the food-safety authority. Your duty to the people who will eat the rice comes before your duty to obey.

Why (the business side): one food-poisoning case in Japan could close that market to the firm and damage the image of Thai rice in general; country reputation is an asset that sells products. It also exposes the firm to the legal action and loss of trust that cost far more than one shipment. Lesson: a sales target never justifies a safety risk; the cheapest moment to stop a bad shipment is before it leaves.

Ethical Challenge 3. You are the French ambassador to Malaysia. Malaysia offered tax breaks and a "union-free" workforce to attract semiconductor firms; union leaders at Harris Electronics were fired; Thomson closed a unionized plant and moved to Vietnam. Discuss the governments' problem and advise.

The problem. A newly industrialized country needs FDI for jobs, technology, hard currency and skills (the professor's five benefits), but investors are mobile: if one country raises labour standards, the firm moves to a cheaper one (Thomson to Vietnam). So governments compete by lowering standards, which is the "race" the radical school warns about: the multinational wins and the host's citizens lose. Leontiades: "don't expect these companies to behave like an ideal citizen".

My advice as ambassador (modern view: mutual interest, and the host decides the terms, "the ball is in your field"):

  1. Compete on what lasts, not on weak workers: infrastructure and skills. Malaysia's own Multimedia Super Corridor is the right kind of incentive; skilled, productive workers are an acquired location advantage.
  2. Make incentives conditional and selective: give the deepest tax breaks to firms that bring technology and training and create many jobs, not to those that only want cheap, silent labour.
  3. Allow real worker representation: protect in-house unions by law (no dismissal of elected leaders); start with company-level dialogue if national unions are too much for now.
  4. Use the evidence: in our handout, foreign firms in developing countries paid up to 30 percent more than domestic firms and raised average wages. Good investors do not need a union-free guarantee.
  5. Avoid the bidding war: escalating concessions can cost taxpayers more than the jobs pay.

Another nation that supports the case for unions: Germany. It keeps a large car industry (Volkswagen, the book's opening case) while workers sit on company boards by law: elected works councils in firms with at least five employees, half of the supervisory board seats for employees in large firms (the 1976 Codetermination Act) and one third in mid-sized firms. The book's own opening case shows Volkswagen thriving with close ties between government, management and labour.

Part F. Case: "Driving the Green Car Market in Australia"

Brief

High fuel costs and climate concerns shifted demand to smaller, fuel-efficient cars, and trade protection that had sheltered Australian car making since 1985 was being cut. Mitsubishi closed its last plant in 2008, leaving only Ford, Toyota and GM; Ford announced 450 job cuts and sales fell 11 percent. The government created a $3.4 billion fund (2011 to 2020) to turn the industry toward "green" cars. Toyota, aiming at 1 million hybrid sales a year, had been weighing importing engines from its Kamigo plant in Japan (helped by the strong Australian dollar). In September 2010 it announced a $300 million upgrade of its Altona plant in Melbourne, partly funded by $63 million from the Green Car Innovation Fund and cash from the Victorian government, to make 100,000 hybrid and new four-cylinder engines a year from 2012 for export to countries that build the Camry. Toyota said the fund was the main factor; the government said 3,300 jobs would be secured.

Fact sheet

FactorFacts in the caseWhat it means
Market trendDemand moving to small, fuel-efficient cars, at home and abroadHybrid engines are the growth product
Toyota's goal1 million hybrid sales; must more than double productionNeeds capacity fast
Existing baseAltona plant in Melbourne; Camry hybrid already made in Japan, Kentucky and a China joint ventureUpgrade is faster than greenfield
Host incentives$63 million from the federal fund + Victorian state cashFinancial incentive lowers the investment
Host objectiveSave jobs (3,300) and keep a car industry after protection is cutMutual interest: jobs for Australia, subsidized capacity for Toyota
CostsStrong Australian dollar made importing from Japan attractiveCurrency risk for exporting from Australia
Industry healthMitsubishi gone, Ford cutting jobs, sales down 11%Weak local market; the plant must export to survive
Output useEngines exported to Camry plants in other countriesRationalized production
AlternativesImport engines from Japan; move production homeThe fund tipped the decision

Thinking Globally 1. What were the chief factors in Toyota's decision to undertake FDI in Australia rather than build its hybrids in Japan?

  1. Government incentives: the $63 million grant and Victorian support, which Toyota itself called "the major factor". Host promotion through financial incentives.
  2. An existing plant and workforce (location advantage, acquired) and Toyota's engine technology (ownership advantage), kept inside the firm (internalization): the eclectic theory.
  3. Capacity need and speed: Toyota had to more than double hybrid output; another plant adds capacity without overloading Japan.
  4. Rationalized production: Altona engines feed Camry plants elsewhere, so each component is made where it fits best.
  5. Market presence and relations: staying as one of only three local producers keeps Toyota close to Australian customers and government (customer knowledge, cooperation with the host).

Against it: the strong Australian dollar, which made imports from Japan look cheaper.

Thinking Globally 2. Why upgrade the existing Melbourne plant rather than build one from the ground up elsewhere in Australia?

This is the book's purchase-or-build choice, here "upgrade or build":

  1. Existing plant, equipment, trained personnel and supplier links: no need to hire and train a new workforce.
  2. Speed: production from the second half of 2012.
  3. Lower investment and risk: $300 million upgrade, part paid by taxpayers, versus a full greenfield plant.
  4. No new permits, land or financing problems, which the book lists as greenfield "headaches".
  5. The grant and state support were tied to this plant and to protecting existing jobs (Melbourne, Victoria).
  6. Goodwill: keeps relations with workers, the community and the Victorian government.
  7. Location already suits exports (an established industrial city). My judgment.

A greenfield plant makes sense only when adequate facilities do not exist (GM in Poland); here they did.

Thinking Globally 3. What will manufacturing in Australia rather than Japan do to Toyota's reputation at home? Do international customers care where cars are assembled?

  • At home: some Japanese may see it as exporting jobs, the home country's most sensitive issue. But the effect is limited: it is an addition of capacity, not a closure in Japan; key parts and technology still come from Japan (which supports Japanese jobs, like Hyundai's Brazil example); and Japanese firms are known for treating ventures abroad as learning opportunities that build long-term competitiveness. My judgment: little damage.
  • International customers: country of origin matters for image ("German automotive engineering"), but for a global brand most buyers judge the brand and its quality system, not the assembly site. Toyota's risk is low as long as Altona engines meet Toyota's standards. My judgment.

Thinking Globally 4. What are the pros and cons of Toyota's approach to managing FDI?

Pros

  • Shares cost and risk with governments (grant + state cash).
  • Fast, cheaper capacity through an existing plant.
  • Rationalized production: one plant supplies engines to Camry plants in several countries.
  • Strong relations with the host government; a "mutual interest" deal.
  • Fits its green, fuel-efficient strategy and Australia's new demand.

Cons

  • Dependence on subsidies: a decision driven by incentives lasts only as long as the incentives; the book warns that low costs and tax terms "cannot be assumed" to stay.
  • Currency risk: the strong Australian dollar raises the cost of exports from Australia.
  • A shrinking local industry: fewer local carmakers means a thinner supplier base and a small home market.
  • Rationalized-production risk: a stoppage at Altona would hit every plant that depends on its engines (the GM brake-pad strike).
  • Exit cost: if the subsidies end, leaving means job losses and reputation damage.

What happened afterwards (real world): in February 2014 Toyota announced it would stop making vehicles and engines in Australia by the end of 2017, and the Altona plant closed on 3 October 2017, the end of Toyota manufacturing in Australia after 54 years; the site became a training and product development centre.

Suggestions and lessons

  1. For hosts: incentives buy time, not loyalty. Tie them to lasting advantages (skills, suppliers, infrastructure) and differentiate them by objective, as the professor taught ("the ball is in your field").
  2. For firms: count the subsidy as temporary; test the plant's economics without it, including the exchange rate.
  3. Before accepting a host's money, agree what happens if the market or the policy changes (exit terms, retraining).
  4. Rationalized production needs a back-up source for critical components.
How these may come up in his exam
  • Definitions and lists, in the book's words: FDI against portfolio investment; rationalized production; the balance of payments, with the current account against the capital account; the four FDI theories; the ways host and home countries promote and restrict FDI.
  • Essay links he taught: the five benefits of FDI and the five problems they solve; the radical view (zero-sum: Hood and Young, Leontiades) against the modern view (mutual interest); selective incentives (Chipsy against iron and steel, Cairo against Marsa Matrouh). These match the book's "reasons for intervention" and "policy instruments" sections, so one answer can combine both.
  • Purchase or build is his brownfield against greenfield.
  • A case (he said a case is possible): use the fact sheet, then answer, then lessons, as in the Australia case above.
  • Past exams already asked about the value of FDI for developing host countries (four times) and the determinants of FDI (once). Quick Study 4 and 5, with his benefits and the two views, are the material for those.
