Behind the lessons

How this course works, the whole course as one short story, the glossary, and where every part comes from.

How this course works

  • Lecture by lecture. The course follows the six lectures, each split into its parts in the order Prof. Abu Qahf taught them. Inside a part the lessons are short and build on each other.
  • Every lesson has the same parts: in one minute, the idea, what to keep, check yourself. The extras sit at the end of the lesson, under "More", and are optional.
  • Nothing was cut. Everything the first study page had is here. What does not fit the main text is under "More" in its lesson.
  • Review brings questions back on the right day, so you do not have to plan what to revise.
  • To read a lesson as one page, or to print it, open the lesson and tap "One page" at the top.
  • Your progress is saved in this browser, on this device only. A second device starts empty.

The course as one story

The whole course told as one short story about Karim, who wants to sell his father's juice outside Egypt. He meets each idea of the six lectures in turn. Good for a first read, and for a last one.

Read the story (about 12 minutes)

Karim had just finished his EMBA when his father, who owned a small juice company in Alexandria called Nile Juice, asked him whether they should start selling outside Egypt. Karim realized he was being asked to enter international business, and he wanted to understand what that really meant.

He found that it was nothing new. The merchants of Quraysh travelled to Syria in summer and to Yemen in winter, buying in one land and selling in another, and the Phoenicians and Greeks had traded abroad long before them. Only the name was new. He learned that international business is the application of all managerial functions, theories and principles in different environments: a manager abroad plans, organizes, motivates and decides exactly as at home, and only the environment around him changes. In practice, any organization doing business in one or more foreign countries, directly or indirectly, is an international business. He also came across an old definition by a scholar named Vernon, by which a firm is international only if it works in six or more countries with sales of 100 million dollars a year, and he saw why it was wrong: the line was drawn at a random place, and one foreign country is enough.

His father asked why, if the job is the same, so many companies fail abroad. Karim told him about an HR manager at MIDOR whose money-based bonus plan worked well in Egypt but failed when she copied it in the UAE, where people already earn more and a little extra money does not move them. He told him how Gaddafi forced 7-Up, Mirinda and Coca-Cola to take Arabic names in Libya, how Pepsi painted its cans blue for the Philippines, how McDonald's dropped beef in India, and how Cadbury replaced pig fat with vegetable oil in Egypt. He explained that Western and Egyptian companies give each worker one boss, while Japanese companies decide nothing until everyone agrees, and that this consensus style, invented in America, succeeded only in Japan, because Japanese culture puts the group first while American and Arab cultures put the individual first. The principles of management are the same everywhere, but culture, economy, politics and society change how they work.

So Karim learned not to trust only the facts in front of him. Like the puzzle of joining nine dots with three lines, the answer often lies outside the picture you are given. He remembered a case from his EMBA about an American company choosing between Jane and Bill to run marketing for its Saudi subsidiary. The answer depended on questions the case did not answer: cosmetics would favour Jane and steel or cars would favour Bill, and conservative Riyadh would favour Bill while Jeddah would favour Jane. A good manager asks, assumes and imagines scenarios, and does not judge people by stereotypes.

Before going anywhere, Karim had to ask whether the core of his product could travel. A product is anything, tangible or intangible, that satisfies a human need, and it has three layers: the core benefit people buy it for, the formal features such as size and colour, and the augmented services such as a guarantee. The core must stay the same abroad, while the features and services can adapt. He also learned that a market is not a place but a group of people with a need, a desire to buy and the money to pay. People in Sudan and Saudi Arabia wanted a cheap, tasty, healthy drink and could pay for it, so the core of his juice could travel.

There were two ways to go. He could go indirectly, by exporting juice made in Alexandria, or directly, by building his own plant abroad, either fully owned or as a joint venture with a local partner, who could even pay for the plant while Nile Juice brought its know-how. Karim started by exporting to Sudan.

Years later Nile Juice had companies in several countries, and people started calling it a multinational, which means a cluster of companies in different countries controlled by one headquarters. Karim learned the difference between a multidomestic company, where each country unit runs its own way, and a global company, which makes its products and policies the same worldwide, like Coca-Cola and McDonald's. The United Nations prefers the word transnational, because in poor countries that were once colonies the word foreign sounds like colonization. A global company looks for similarities between countries, such as one Arabic advert for all Arab countries, because making one product for many markets lowers the cost of each unit. Companies also differ in who decides: in an ethnocentric company headquarters decides everything, in a polycentric one each country decides for itself, in a regiocentric one each region decides, and a geocentric company is a large company integrated vertically, owning more steps of its chain from farm to shop, or horizontally, repeating the same operation in many places.

A consultant told Karim to make everything the same everywhere, because the world had become a small village. Karim checked. Globalization means the free movement of everything between countries without any restriction, yet people still need visas, products must meet the standards of each bloc, like the CE mark in Europe, and conflicts between countries are everywhere. Faster flights and cheap calls had brought the death of distance, not globalization. Trade agreements like GATT and GATS push toward it, and burgers and jeans everywhere only look like it. Agreements between rich and poor countries give equal opportunities but never equal results, as Egyptian exporters learned when their potatoes were rejected by European standards, or when a shipment of fine Egyptian cotton undershirts was refused in England because the pins rusted at sea. Globalization, Karim concluded, is a myth.

That did not mean a different juice for every country. A global product can be sold worldwide with small local touches, and a company can think global and act local. Karim read an old debate on this. In 1983 Theodore Levitt claimed that needs were becoming the same everywhere, that people would accept a standard product for a lower price, and that one product for the world would bring huge savings. In 1987 Douglas and Wind replied in "The Myth of Globalization" that people are not becoming the same, that cheap prices are easy to attack, and that modern factories can make many versions cheaply. Standardizing works only when there is a group of similar buyers across countries, real gains from sharing, and worldwide channels to reach them, and it is blocked by government rules, different shops and media, different materials and competitors, existing partners and resisting local managers. The choice is a scale, not yes or no, and most companies sit in the middle. Karim kept one juice and one brand but adapted bottle sizes, prices and adverts.

He then mapped what surrounds his company. Every organization lives inside its own internal environment, a task environment of its customers, suppliers, competitors and government agencies, and a general environment of economy, politics, culture, society and technology. He saw politics at work in Egypt between 2011 and 2013, when instability drove foreign firms out and kept new ones away. He also remembered buying a can of Pepsi without a question and then questioning a Kia salesman about everything: the same man was two different customers, because one purchase was emotional and the other rational. When he studied a rival in Saudi Arabia, he did not just summarize it; he built a fact sheet comparing both companies on their origin, business, customers, diversification, entry methods, strengths and weaknesses, the way Illy and Starbucks can be compared, and only then drew his conclusions.

When Nile Juice built a plant abroad, the government soon capped its prices and limited the profits it could send home. Karim was facing political risk, the likelihood that the host country's political decisions or events will hurt a foreign firm's investment, operations or profit transfers. Unlike uncertainty, a risk can be predicted and calculated, which is why insurers cover risks. It can hit every firm in the country, through violence, corruption or constant political change, or target only certain firms, through a special tax or the seizure of a plant. Governments can block imports, fix prices, impose quotas, block profits and salaries, expropriate a company with compensation, or confiscate and nationalize it without compensation. Karim learned to watch for warning signs: unemployment and inflation, frequent changes of government, deep cultural divisions, and hostility between his home country and the host. To protect himself he could integrate into the country, with local partners, suppliers, workers and research, or defend himself by keeping a small footprint, borrowing from local banks and spreading production across countries. He chose a mix, and he learned that keeping something the host cannot do without, such as technology, keeps the government's hands off. When the terms had to be agreed, he negotiated patiently, knowing that culture shapes every step of a deal.

Competition was the other danger. Companies like Coca-Cola have lived for more than a century because they can compete any time, anywhere, any way and against anybody, built on total quality management, continuous learning and world-class standards. Quality needs a vision shared by every worker, a variety of products, empowered employees and constant comparison with the best, and money spent on quality saves more than it costs, as Xerox learned when Japanese copiers forced it to improve. Karim also read Richard Watson's forecast that by 2027 only 25 of 500 large American companies and 24 of 100 British ones would survive. The dying ones show clear signs: skilled people leaving, cuts in marketing, no new customers for six months, poor service, no new products for a year, rejected ideas, piling stock, an aging board, dependence on one supplier, flattery instead of truth, weak information and fighting owners. When Karim found that 94 percent of his bottles came from a single supplier, he found a second one the same week.

Surviving was only the start. The companies that last adapt all the time, and they learn by improving in small steps rather than waiting for one big leap. That needs people who are free to create and who believe they can make a difference, and an open eye on everything that goes in and comes out: if the results are poor, change the inputs or the process. A company with quality and learning joins the club of the world's best, which puts the customer first, manages its people creatively, uses modern technology, treats its suppliers as partners and keeps justice at work. Justice at work mattered more than equal treatment, because without justice nobody is satisfied and nobody produces. Getting in is easy and staying is hard, so Karim kept up his research, made his production leaner, built good information, sold covers and cups beside the juice, stayed close to his customers because none of them is loyal and a new one costs twice an old one, moved fast, kept things simple, made one promise and kept it, kept his offices clean and tidy, and smiled. When he planned a factory abroad he knew that every country competes for investors with tax holidays and cheaper services, yet most investment still flows to the rich nations; he scored each candidate country out of 100, weighting the economy above politics, and chose the highest. For each new market he also asked how much of his marketing could stay the same: it depended on the product, how alike the buyers were, which media reached them and in what language, the government's rules, the roads and services, and the relations between the two countries.

Karim also stopped believing in the perfect global manager. No one person could know every market, so he built a team: a business manager who kept one strategy for the whole world, country managers who knew what each market and government wanted, functional experts who carried good ideas from one country to the next, and himself at the top, balancing them, finding talent and growing it. The one who led them all was the real global manager: a leader, a talent scout and a developer. A leader, he told them, learns so that he can teach, stays aware, decides, develops, encourages, rewards, keeps his people, listens, invests in people and, when he must, punishes. When a manager abroad was offered a bribe, he told him to refuse it and report it, because a bribe is a bribe. When workers in a partner's plant complained of low pay and an abusive supervisor, he did not stop at saying what was wrong: he worked out how to fix it, retraining or replacing the supervisor, improving the light, noise, safety and pay, and showing everyone that the firm and the country shared one interest. And before entering a country he watched whether its government could win its own people over, because a government that cannot is a risk. Then he asked himself why Nile Juice should go abroad at all. Old answers spoke of countries: nations once hoarded gold, and each country gains by selling what it makes cheaply, as Egypt does with potatoes, or what nobody else has, like the pyramids. Better answers spoke of markets: go where a need has no product, where demand beats supply, or where the existing products are poor or overpriced, because profit lives where competition is weak. Keep your recipe at home and license it to no one, or a local partner will copy it. Look at what each country offers, its market, costs, tariffs, attitude to foreigners and incentives, and sort those factors into what the product and country allow, what drives your firm, and what governments permit. Products also travel through a life. When sales at home decline, a firm can stop, improve the product, or cut its price and promote it; when none of that works, it takes the product abroad: invented and exported from one country, copied by another, finally made cheaply in a third that sells them back, as Volkswagen did with the Beetle in Brazil, though a Rolls-Royce never leaves Britain. Before entering, gain experience and information. And to invest at all, own something special, find the right place for it, and keep it inside the company. Only then would Karim choose how to enter.

Choosing how to enter was not one decision but a menu of seventeen, and Karim sorted them into three groups. He could simply sell: through a trading house that buys his juice in Egypt and ships it abroad on its own, through an agent who finds customers for a commission but never owns the juice, through a distributor who buys it and resells it, at an international fair, or over the internet. He could sign a contract: license his recipe to a local bottler for a royalty, franchise his brand, send his managers to run someone else's plant, have a local factory make his juice, build a complete plant for a client and hand over the key, pass part of a large order to another producer, ally with a company that had what he lacked, or share a new company with a local partner. Or he could own: open his own marketing branch or assembly plant, build a wholly owned subsidiary from scratch, or get in fast by merging with a local firm or buying one, in a friendly deal or through the stock market. The first eleven left him owning nothing abroad, and the last six were direct investment. The deeper he went, the more he learned about the market and the more he controlled it, but the more money he needed and the more he risked for a higher profit. Nothing forced him to climb step by step, yet careful companies do, as Toshiba did in Egypt when it began with an agent and ended with a shared assembly plant. Before choosing, he studied each candidate country: what attracted him to it, its culture, economy and politics, the size of its market, and then he flew there to see the competition himself. He decided how much of his juice and his advertising could stay the same. Then three things settled the choice: his own money, experience, people and willingness; the host country's rules, stability and market size; and the relations between Egypt and that country. Where he was short of money he licensed, and where the market was large and open he built.

The countries, he noticed, wanted him as much as he wanted them. Every country competes for foreign investment, because it brings hard currency, jobs, technology, a healthier balance of payments and better management, which answer the five problems of a poor country: no foreign currency, unemployment, old technology, a constant deficit and bad management. Some people called this a game in which the foreign company wins and the country loses: it uses up local resources, teaches people to spend instead of save, takes tax exemptions that could have paid for development, and sometimes bribes officials. Others saw two partners who both gain. Karim understood that both could be true. A country that hands the same gifts to every investor gets snack factories in its capital, while a country that keeps its best incentives for heavy industry, remote regions and projects with many jobs gets what it needs. The ball is in the host's field, and the answer, as always, is good management.

Nile Juice now sells in four countries, and before every decision Karim still asks himself what he does not know yet.

Glossary, A to Z

Every key term of the course in one place, 128 of them, for a last look before the exam. The wording is his where he gave one.

Open the glossary

Absolute advantage المزايا المطلقة

A country has something no other country has, like the Giza pyramids. (Textbooks use the term differently.)

Acquisition الاستحواذ

Buying an existing company. Hostile: through the stock market, with no negotiation. Friendly: negotiated between seller and buyer. Brownfield.

Adaptive vs generative organization

Adaptive reacts to required changes but fails to anticipate them; generative (learning) anticipates change and has learned how to learn.

Agent الوكيل

The link between the producer and the final customer in a foreign market. Works for a commission and does not own the product. Inclusive (works with all companies in the field) or exclusive (one company only).

Aptitude الاستعداد

Readiness to actually do something. Attitude is how you feel about it. "I like tea (attitude) but I am too lazy to make it (no aptitude)."

Augmented product المنتج المدعم

The extra services around a product: guarantee, instalments, free cover.

Balance of payments ميزان المدفوعات

The national record of all the money entering a country and all the money leaving it. FDI improves it and solves its chronic deficit.

Benchmarking البنشماركية / الأطر المرجعية

Continually measuring internal processes and products against industry leaders; "the standard or reference point against which things can be compared".

Brownfield investment

He says "brown investment": entering by merger or acquisition, taking over a company that already exists.

Case fact sheet

His comparison table of factors (origin, business, diversification, customers, commitment, entry modes, competitors, SWOT, potential), built before answering a case.

Classical (radical) view of FDI وجهة النظر التقليدية

The relationship between multinationals and developing host countries is a zero-sum game: the company wins, the country loses (Hood and Young; Leontiades).

Conditional, driving and governing factors (modified location) العوامل الشرطية / الدافعة / الحاكمة

Conditional: product, host features, international relations. Driving: the firm's strengths and competitive position. Governing (he also says "controlling"): host and home countries' investment features.

Confiscation مصادرة

Taking a foreign investment project with no compensation (his class definition). Careful: the Arabic revision material uses the word مصادرة for taking with meagre compensation; answer in English.

Continuous improvement vs development التحسين المستمر

Improvement = small changes made all the time; development = huge changes. A learning organization = adaptation + continuous improvement.

Continuum (standardization-differentiation)

"Continuum means scale": from pure standardization to pure differentiation, with hybrid strategies in between.

Convenience product سلع ميسرة

His definition: goods bought easily, "without actually walking around or spending time", with no brand loyalty ("no Pepsi, take a Coca-Cola"). Often easy to standardize, but not always: "I would say no" (McDonald's and Cadbury changed small things in Egypt). One of the four classes: convenience, shopping, specialty, unsought.

Core product المنتج الجوهري

The product "why": its function, the benefit the buyer enjoys.

Creativity vs innovation الإبداع والابتكار

Creativity = something new with no previous example, the ideation component of innovation; innovation = the application of creativity, "not canned ideas" (Giza pyramid: new, no precedent, passes the time test).

Cross-pollinator

One of the functional manager's three jobs (Bartlett and Ghoshal): carries a good idea from one country to the others.

Customer intimacy

The fourth way to sustain world class: manage the customer's expectations, let him participate, put yourself in his shoes, respond to his needs.

Customer retention الاحتفاظ بالعملاء

Keeping existing customers through continuous added value; "customer loyalty is an old school term": "the customer is actually loyal to his or her self-interest". Keeping a customer costs about half of attracting a new one.

Death of distance موت المسافات

Transport and communication make distance feel smaller; geographic and cultural distance remain. What we live in, "rather than globalization".

Degree of international commitment

How much of its money and people a company ties to a foreign market. Another name for the mode of entry.

Direct and indirect foreign investment الاستثمار الأجنبي المباشر وغير المباشر

In his model, modes 1 to 11 are indirect (the company owns nothing inside the country) and modes 12 to 17 are direct (it owns or co-owns a business there).

Direct international business الأعمال الدولية المباشرة

Own plant, subsidiary or branch abroad, wholly owned or a joint venture.

Direct vs indirect competition

Direct = companies in the same industry; indirect = all companies, regardless of nationality, size, ownership or industry.

Distributor الموزع

A link between producer and customer who buys the product and resells it for his own account, so he owns the product.

Driving forces of globalization القوى الدافعة للعولمة

What pushes toward globalization (GATT, GATS, transport and communication technology); not globalization itself.

Eclectic (OLI) theory نظرية الانتقاء

John Dunning: to go abroad a firm needs three advantages: a unique asset (Ownership), a distinctive Location, Internalization (use it yourself, no licence).

Economies of scale وفورات الحجم

Lower unit cost from larger volume; global firms reach it by exploiting similarities among countries.

Empowerment التمكين

Delegating authority, no micromanagement, accountability based on results.

Empowerment التمكين

The process of giving employees the resources, information, and authority needed to carry out their jobs effectively.

Ethnocentric المركزي وحيد الجنسية

Centralized: all decisions and strategies made at headquarters. Weakness: cannot adapt to the host.

Expropriation نزع الملكية

His class definition: taking a foreign project with compensation. The reading's definition: seizure "with little, if any, compensation".

External flexibility ratio نسبة المرونة الخارجية

(Single supplier / total suppliers) x 100; a higher ratio means less flexibility.

Factors governing the degree of standardization

Type of product; heterogeneity or homogeneity of markets; media characteristics; government restrictions; infrastructure services; type of political relationship.

Foreign direct investment (FDI) الاستثمار الأجنبي المباشر

A lasting interest (10% or more ownership) in an enterprise in another economy; long-term, with the right to manage.

Formal product المنتج الشكلي

The features: size, colour, weight, design.

Franchising الامتياز التجاري

The franchiser supplies the franchisee with intangible property (mainly the brand) and other assistance over an extended period. More control than licensing, mostly in services.

GATT / GATS

General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (goods) / General Agreement on Trade in Services: driving forces of globalization.

Geocentric الجغرافي / العالمي التوجه

Large, integrated (vertically and/or horizontally). Weakness: imposes home-country culture.

Global company الشركة العالمية

A very large company that standardizes and integrates its operations, products, marketing and HR policies worldwide.

Global manager (4 roles)

Bartlett and Ghoshal (1992): no universal global manager; a team of business, country, functional and corporate managers.

Global market segment شريحة سوقية عالمية

A group of buyers with similar needs in many countries; the first requisite condition for standardization.

Global product

A product that can be marketed worldwide, satisfying customer needs on a worldwide basis.

Global sourcing التوريد العالمي

The use of worldwide suppliers, regardless of where they are located, who are best able to provide the needed output.

Globalization العولمة

The free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions; or the tendency toward integrating the world.

Glocalization العومحلية

Giving things a local character within globalization.

Greenfield investment

Starting from scratch: a wholly owned subsidiary, a marketing branch, an assembly plant or a joint venture.

Hard currency العملة الصعبة

Strong foreign money such as the dollar. Bringing it in is the first benefit of FDI.

Horizontal integration التكامل الأفقي

The same operation spread to different places.

Host country and home (parent) country الدولة المضيفة والدولة الأم

The host country is the one the company enters. The home or parent country is the one it comes from.

Indigenization laws

Laws requiring nationals to hold a majority interest in the operation.

Indirect international business الأعمال الدولية غير المباشرة

Selling abroad without one's own operation there, e.g. exporting.

Integrative techniques الأساليب التكاملية

Making the operation part of the host's infrastructure, "less foreign": local relations, suppliers, JVs, local R&D.

Internalization المورد الذاتي

Dunning's I: keep the unique asset inside the company: no licence to others (Xerox), R&D at home. The same idea as protection theory.

International business الأعمال الدولية

(1) The application of all managerial functions, theories and principles in different environments. (2) Any organization doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly.

International product life cycle دورة حياة المنتج الدولي

The life cycle of one good in three countries: invented and exported at home, copied by another advanced country, then made by developing countries that export it even to the inventor (VW Beetle in Brazil). Not for unique goods (Rolls-Royce).

International subcontracting التعاقد من الباطن

A company that cannot fill a whole order has part of it made by its own branch in another country or by another company, to the same specification (Honda: 600 cars itself, 400 by others). Only the first of its four forms is required.

Internationalization التدويل

A company moving its marketing or production activities outside its home country. The theories explain why and where.

Joint venture (JV) المشروع المشترك

An investment project owned together by a foreign company and a local investor (a new, separate company). Mode 12; direct and greenfield. Example: the Toshiba and El-Araby assembly plant.

Latent customer

A potential customer. "In this moment, he or she is your customer. Before, is not, is a latent customer."

LEADERSHIP (acrostic)

Learn, evaluate (be aware), able to decide, develop, encourage, remunerate, sustain, hear, invest in people, punish when required.

Learning organization منظمة التعلم

An organization able to adapt and improve continuously; needs creativity, openness, learning and self-confidence. His class version: adaptation + continuous improvement; creativity, openness, self-efficacy. The reading's definition: "able to transform itself by anticipating change and discovering new ways of creating products and services; it has learned how to learn"; openness, creativity, personal efficacy.

Licensing التراخيص

The licensor gives the licensee permission to produce and market its product in a given market for a fee (royalty). The textbook's definition: the right to use intangible property for a specified period.

Location theory نظرية الموقع

The FDI decision depends on the host's location factors: market, cost, protection measures, investment climate, incentives, others.

Macro political risk الخطر السياسي الكلي

Risk that affects all foreign and national firms across the economy.

Management by consensus الإدارة بالإجماع

No decision without 100% yes from everyone; success and failure are everyone's responsibility.

Management contract عقد الإدارة

One company supplies another with managerial expertise for a specific period, for a lump sum or a fee based on sales.

Market السوق

A group of people with needs to satisfy, desire to buy and purchasing power. "Not a place."

Market fundamentalism أصولية السوق

The belief that the market and profit should rule everything. It is where utilitarianism leads globalization.

Market imperfection عدم كمال السوق

"Having no or less competition". Firms invest where a need has no product, demand exceeds supply, or the supply is poor.

Marketing ecology

The whole environment around a product in a market (culture, income, use, competition, infrastructure).

Marketing myopia

Short-sightedness: looking at your own product instead of at what customers want (red flag 7 of company death).

Mass customization

Tailor-making a standard product to each customer's expectations (Dell) so it is not seen as a generic offering.

Mercantilists التجاريين

The oldest trade view: a country's wealth is its gold stock, so it should export to gain gold.

Merger الاندماج

Joining with a company that already operates in the country: the fast way in. Brownfield.

Micro political risk الخطر السياسي الجزئي

Risk targeted at particular foreign firms or industries.

Mode of entry طريقة الدخول للأسواق الأجنبية

The form a company uses to get into a foreign market. Also called a strategy of entry or a degree of international commitment. His model has 17, in 3 options: commercial, contracting, equity.

Modern view of FDI وجهة النظر الحديثة

Multinational and host country have a mutual interest; how much the host gains depends on its skill. It should differentiate incentives by sector, region and jobs.

Monopolistic characteristics الخصائص الاحتكارية

The technological, financing, organizational-managerial and integrative strengths that let multinationals win in developing markets.

Multidomestic company الشركة متعددة المحلية

Affiliates in many countries, each with its own strategies, based on perceived differences between countries.

Multinational corporation الشركة متعددة الجنسيات

A cluster of companies spread in different countries and held by the headquarters.

Nationalization التأميم

Turning private (foreign) ownership into state ownership; no compensation.

Negotiation التفاوض

Bargaining with one or more parties to arrive at a solution acceptable to all.

Niche النيش (ركن سوقي متخصص)

A distinct, special corner of a market. (Niche marketing = تسويق النيشات.)

Objective vs target

Objective = long-term result (business continuity); target / aim / goal = short-term result (immediate profit).

Pattern standardization التوحيد النمطي

One global theme or positioning, executed locally.

Personal efficacy

The belief that one both can and should learn to influence significantly the world in which one lives; built by self-awareness and proactive problem-solving.

Political risk الخطر السياسي

The likelihood that host-country political decisions or events will negatively affect a foreign firm's investment, disrupt its operations, or block its profit transfers.

Political system النظام السياسي

The structure, processes and activities by which the nation governs itself.

Polycentric اللامركزي

Decentralized: each subsidiary sets its own policies and strategies. Weakness: hard to control.

Portfolio investment

Buying shares only to earn from them, with no control over management. The opposite of FDI.

Product المنتج

Anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need.

Product proliferation

Creating a wide array of product versions that competitors cannot copy quickly enough (Canon); one of three approaches to innovation.

Protection theory نظرية الحماية

Multinationals keep their innovations from leaking: R&D at headquarters and no licences to other firms (Xerox).

Protective and defensive techniques الأساليب الدفاعية والوقائية

Discouraging host interference by staying non-integrated: small local plant, R&D outside, local borrowing, spread production.

Push vs pull (retail)

Push: manufacturers push goods onto stores and customers. Pull: the retailer identifies needs and customers pull goods from the store (Wal-Mart).

Regiocentric

Organized and decided by region.

Relative advantage المزايا النسبية

A country specializes in and exports what it makes at a lower cost than others (Egypt exports potatoes).

Relative bargaining power قوة المركز التفاوضي

Keeping the firm's bargaining power above the host's, e.g. through proprietary technology.

Risk الخطر

An event that can be predicted and whose occurrence can be calculated.

Royalty إتاوة

The fee a licensee pays the licensor, usually a percentage of the sales made with the licensed property.

Screening markets and sites

Examining every possible country and removing the weak ones, in 4 steps: basic appeal; national business environment; market size and site potential; select with a field trip.

Self-efficacy الكفاءة الذاتية

His class name for the third requirement of the learning organization, tied to empowerment. The same thing as "personal efficacy" in the reading and "self-confidence" in the revision material.

Self-reference criterion

Judging a foreign market through your own culture's eyes.

Selling appeal

A promise to the buyer (a price discount, free delivery, a three-year guarantee). One promise kept beats six made.

Six sigma

Motorola's quality target: under 3.4 defects per million parts (3 sigma = 66,810; higher sigma, fewer defects).

Strategic alliance التحالف الاستراتيجي

Two companies cooperate so that each uses the other's competitive advantage, without creating a new company (EgyptAir and Thai Airways in the Star Alliance).

Target costing (Japan)

Planned selling price minus desired profit = target cost; every component is costed with designers, engineers and suppliers, then cost is cut continuously.

Task environment بيئة المهام

The external competitive or specific environment: customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies.

Tax holiday إعفاء ضريبي مؤقت

A period in which a foreign investor pays no tax on the income it earns; one of the incentives every country offers to attract FDI.

Technology paradox

High-tech MNCs can thrive while their prices fall fastest: cut prices, win share, profit from the follow-on market.

Total business environment بيئة الأعمال الكلية

Internal environment plus external (public / general and task / specific) environment.

Total Quality Management (TQM) إدارة الجودة الشاملة

Pillar 1 of the new model firm; requires quality vision, diversification, empowerment, benchmarking.

Trading house

A commercial company that buys and sells inside its own country and may export what it buys, making the producer international "without any previous plan".

Transnational corporation الشركة عابرة القوميات / عبر الوطنية

His class meaning: the UN's term for an international firm, chosen to avoid the colonial image of "multinational" or "foreign". Another meaning you may meet: a firm combining global integration with local responsiveness.

Turnkey project مشروع تسليم المفتاح

A foreign company builds a complete plant "from A to Z" and hands it over to the local owner when it produces the first unit.

Uncertainty عدم التأكد

An event that cannot be predicted, so its occurrence cannot be calculated.

Unity of command وحدة الأمر

Each subordinate takes orders from one manager only, to avoid contradictory orders.

Uppsala model نموذج جامعة ابسالا

Swedish model: going abroad needs prior experience of the market and enough information about it; firms enter similar markets first, step by step.

Utilitarianism النفعية

Judging every action only by the benefit it brings ("the greatest good for the greatest number": Bentham and Mill). It is the governing principle of globalization, so there is no theory of it.

Vertical integration التكامل الرأسي

Upward toward the market, downward toward raw materials.

Virtual organization المنظمة الافتراضية

Does business as if it were a very large enterprise while it is much smaller: core competencies kept, the rest outsourced.

Weighted fact sheet (country scoring)

For the Gdansk case: factors weighted out of 100 (political stability 20, economic environment 60, ...), each country scored, highest total chosen.

Wholly owned subsidiary

An investment project completely owned by the foreign investor. Highest investment, risk and profit. Greenfield.

World Class Organization (WCO) طبقة الصفوة من الشركات

The elite of world companies, able to compete anywhere, any time, any way, against anybody. The reading's definition: "enterprises that are able to compete with anybody, anywhere, anytime, anyway", with 6 pillars. In class he gave 5 pillars, ending with justice, "not equality".

Zero-sum game

"Just like gambling": one party wins and the other loses. The assumption of the classical view of FDI.

Lecture 5, part 1: Three ethics scenarios

Lecture 6, part 2: Foreign direct investment

The 8 lessons are the second topic of lecture 6, the last lecture, given on Wednesday 11 November 2026: foreign direct investment, and the two views on whether it is worth it for the host country.

  • The lecture itself (lessons 1 to 4): the written-out recording of lecture 6. The "80, 16, 4" figures and the list of incentives were first given in lecture 4 (28 October 2026).
  • The textbook (lessons 5 and 6, and the textbook exercises in the Exam tab): Wild and Wild, International Business: The Challenges of Globalization, 7th edition (Pearson, 2014), chapter 7, "Foreign Direct Investment", pages 200 to 221. He told the class to read it and to solve its exercises.
  • The second reading (lesson 7): Ann Harrison, "The Role of Multinationals in Economic Development: The Benefits of Foreign Direct Investment", Columbia Journal of World Business, Winter 1994, handed out in class.
  • The revision booklet: a 45-page Arabic booklet passed on from earlier batches of this course. Its chapter 7 (pages 40 to 43) covers the feasibility of foreign investment: from it come the four-benefit version (lesson 2), and the extra names and comments on the two views (lessons 3 and 4). Lesson 8, global social responsibility, comes from its page 8 and from a model-answer page among the past exam papers.

Where the lecture and the booklet or the textbook differ (for example the "80, 16, 4" figures), the lesson gives the lecture's version, and the other version is under "More".
